הדבר אשר, הוא האיש וכדומה: ויאמר אלהם יוסף הוּא אשר דברתי אלכם לאמר מרגלים אתם בראש' מב יד. ויאמר משה אל אהרן הוּא אשר דבר יי' לאמר בקרבי אקדש ויקר' י ג. וכי תאמר אלי אל יי' אלהינו בטחנו הלוא הוּא אשר הסיר חזקיהו את במתיו ואת מזבחתיו ישע' לו ז. — *וקצת במשמ' ולכן: ומה אם יעקב אבינו שהבטיחו הקב"ה ואמר לו הנה אנכי עמך ושמרתיך בכל אשר תלך נתיירא אנו עאכ"ו הוא שהנביא מקנטרן ואומר להם ותשכח ה' עושיך פסיק' דר"כ, אנכי אנכי. והוא שדוד אמר כי אבי ואמי עזבוני מד"ר ויקר' יד. — *ובכלל במקום דבר זה: שתגלחת הנגע דוחה תגלחת הנזיר בזמן שהוא ודאי אבל בזמן שהוא ספק אינו דוחה נזיר ח ב. עמד רבי יהושע על רגליו ואמר לא בושה וכלימה הוא לנו שנגזור טומאה על עיר אבותינו זבח' קיג.. שכשם שהוא רחמן על האדם כך מרחם על הבהמה תדע לך שהוא כן שבשעה שבקש הקב"ה לאבד עולמו וכו' תנחומא נח ח. — ובמשמ' אותו הדבר הנזכר: אימתי (משחק בקוביה ומלוה ברבית פסול להעיד) בזמן שאין להם אומנות אלא הוא אבל יש להן אומנות שלא הוא כשרין סנה' ג ג. — ובמשמ' דבר זה אינו אלא בתנאי זה: ג' שנים שאמרו (בחזקה) הוא שאכלן רצופות ב"ב כט.. — והוּא שֶׁ, במשמ' מה שאמור למעלה אינו אלא בתנאי: בריכה שנוטפת מים משדה בית השלחין זו מותר להשקות ממנה שדה בית השלחין אחרת וכו' אמר אביי והוא שלא פסק מעיין ראשון מו"ק ד.. פול המצרי שהביא שליש לפני ר"ה אם זרעו לזרע מתעשר לשעבר וכו' והוא שליקט ממנו לפני ראש השנה רמב"ם מע"ש ונט"ר א י. ישראל שהיה לו קרקע בסוריא והוריד לה אריס ושלח לו האריס פירות הרי אלו פטורים שאני אומר מן השוק לקחם והוא שיהיה אותו המין מצוי בשוק הוא, תרומ' א יט. נשתברו שש (צלעות) מיכן ושש מכאן או אחת עשרה מכאן ואחת עשרה מכאן טרפה והוא שנשברו מחציין של מול השדרה הוא, שחיט' י א. — ב) כנוי לאלהים: אני אני הוּאאעפ"י שאפשר לפרש מלת הוא שבכל המשלים הבאים גם פשוט במשמ' מלת הקשור, מכל מקום נראה שהיה צרוף זה גם כנוי להאלהות, ולכן אולי הרכבת השמות עם הוא בסוף: אביהוא, אליהוא ועוד. ואין אלהים עמדי דבר' לב לט. אני הוא יי' הוּא שמי וכבודי לאחר לא אתן ישע' מב ח. שמע אלי יעקב וישראל מקראי אני הוּא אני ראשון אף אני אחרון שם מח יב.
en: Whereas in the first two persons, the speaker and the one addressed [printed in the source as "סנכח"], all the Semitic languages agree and use the same two words with only slight changes, in the third person, of the absent masculine and absent feminine, the sister languages divided into three groups: that of שׁ (שׂ), that of ה, and that of both together, both ש and ה. In Akkadian (Assyrian) שׁ (and in Minaean שׂ) serves to mark the third person for masculine and feminine; in Arabic, Aramaic, Hebrew etc. ה for masculine and feminine; and in Mehri for masculine and feminine שׂ. And some of the moderns, Jensen, Brockelmann, Ungnad (Jensen, Brokelman, Ungand), hold that in the ancient common Semitic language the use of the person sign for the third person masculine and feminine was as it is in Mehri, that is, ה for the masculine and ש for the feminine; and besides this there was a further difference in the vowel sound, the masculine using shuruk and the feminine hiriq. And afterwards, when the sister languages separated and each began to go its own particular way, only Mehri preserved the custom of the ancient mother language of marking the masculine third person with a letter of its own and the feminine third person with a letter of its own; most of the sister languages abandoned the doubled sign of the third person in the letter itself, and some of them (Akkadian and Minaean) kept the letter ש for masculine and feminine, and some (Arabic, Aramaic, Hebrew and others) the letter ה for masculine and feminine, and were content to distinguish between masculine and feminine by the vowel alone, shuruk for the masculine and hiriq for the feminine. And it is natural that the sign of the masculine third person in the ancient language, the letter ה, tipped the scale against the sign of the feminine, the letter ש, and in most of the Semitic languages only the letter ה is used, and only in a few languages, Akkadian and Minaean, did the use of the letter ש for both genders remain, and only in one of them did the old usage of the ancient Semitic language remain, with both letters together, one for the masculine and one for the feminine. And from the spelling of this pronoun in Hebrew with א at the end after the ו — and there is no doubt that it was pronounced at first and only afterwards weakened and became quiescent (some scholars hold that this א is the protective א, alif al-wiqaya in Arabic, but this is not clear) — one may learn that the ancient form of the pronoun for the third person masculine and feminine was hu-a, shi-a (a being the demonstrative particle), and from this הוּא, היא in Hebrew (C Brock. Gruudr. § 104). And the scholars have already discussed the nature of the third-person feminine pronoun in the Torah, which is also written everywhere like the spelling of the masculine pronoun, only the vocalization distinguishing between them, the feminine word being vocalized with hiriq thus: הִוא — except for eleven places recorded in the Masorah to Genesis 38:25, in which היא is written. And these are the words of the Masorah there: "Eleven are written with yod in the Torah, and the mnemonic: היא צוער, the first; the second of הלא הוא אמר לי; והיא שלחה אל חמיה; וכי ימות מן הבהמה; והיא הפכה שער לבן; ואם יראנה הכהן, the first; שבת שבתון היא of Aharei Mot; ואיש כי יקח את אחותו בת אביו; היא מחללת, the first; ושכב איש אותה, the first in the verse; ועבר עליו רוח קנאה, the second in the verse", end quote. Now some of the moderns held that this spelling הוּא also for the feminine remained from ancient times, when they did not yet distinguish in the pronoun between masculine and feminine and said הוא for both, just as they said נער both for the masculine and for the feminine. But this opinion is hard to accept, for we have already seen that it is almost certain that the ancient Semitic language too distinguished between masculine and feminine in the pronoun; and besides this it is difficult why היא comes in the eleven places, and why this ancient spelling, הוא for the feminine, is not found also in the book of Joshua, which is without doubt of almost the same time as the Torah? Therefore some of the moderns hold that this spelling, הוא for the feminine, is simply the error of one ancient scribe, from whom the other scribes afterwards copied. But this opinion is stranger and more astonishing still, for how is such a scribal error possible, not in one place but in all two hundred places in the Torah in which הוא comes instead of היא? — And see further in the Introduction, in the grammar section. — The pronoun for the third person masculine, animate and inanimate, German er, French il, English he; and it serves: a) in place of the noun of the third person when it has already been mentioned once: "And Adah bore Jabal; he (הוּא) was the father of those who dwell in tents and have cattle. And his brother's name was Jubal; he (הוּא) was the father of all who handle the lyre and pipe" Genesis 4:20-21. "And Cush begot Nimrod; he (הוּא) began to be a mighty one in the earth. He (הוּא) was a mighty hunter before the Lord" ibid. 10:8-9. "And she called his name Moab; he (הוּא) is the father of Moab to this day" ibid. 19:37. — And almost *without need, only for further clarity: "He tied the ship with something that is able (שהוא יכול) to hold it" Oholot 8:5, like בדבר שיכול etc. "One who enters the synagogue and finds them standing and praying" Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:2, instead of זה שנכנס. "This teaches that Moses seized the Holy One, blessed be He, like a man who seizes (שהוא תופס) his fellow by his garment" Berakhot 32a, that is, כאדם שתופס. "A ditch that is (שהוא) ten deep and four wide, and likewise a fence that is (שהוא) ten high and four wide" Shabbat 6a, instead of חריץ עמוק י ורחב ד, and likewise גדר גבוה י ורחב ד. "Whoever accepts (שהוא מקבל) evil talk, even though you go and appease him and he is appeased, he still burns within" Genesis Rabbah 98, like כל מי שמקבל. — And in the sense of °who: "He (Abraham) said to him (Isaac): We know that after you our days will be few; He who (הוא ש) comforted us before you were born, He will comfort us from this day on" Midrash Vayosha 1. — And especially to emphasize and stress the third person and to exclude anyone else: "This one shall not be your heir, but one who comes forth from your own body, he (הוּא) shall be your heir" Genesis 15:4. "The Lord, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my birth etc., He (הוּא) will send His angel before you" ibid. 24:7. "The man in whose hand the goblet was found, he (הוּא) shall be my servant; and as for you, go up in peace to your father" ibid. 44:17. "And it shall be that of whom I say to you, This one shall go with you, he (הוּא) shall go with you; and of whomever I say to you, This one shall not go with you, he (הוּא) shall not go" Judges 7:4. "The Lord is our King; He (הוּא) will save us" Isaiah 33:22. "For my mouth, it (הוּא) has commanded, and His spirit, it (הוּא) has gathered them" ibid. 34:16. "Hillel says: Be of the disciples of Aaron etc. He (הוא) used to say: If I am not for myself, who will be for me?" Avot 1:12-14. — And likewise when something new is added to the third-person subject: "And Abram went up out of Egypt, he (הוּא) and his wife and all that he had" Genesis 13:1. "And he (Lot) dwelt in a cave, he (הוּא) and his two daughters" ibid. 19:30. "And they ate and drank, he (הוּא) (Abraham's servant, mentioned earlier) and the men who were with him" ibid. 24:54. "Then it (הוּא) (the offering) and its substitute shall be holy" Leviticus 27:10. — And with גַּם after the subject, to stress and add to what precedes: "And Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering to the Lord; and Abel, he too (גם הוּא) brought of the firstlings of his flock and of their fat" Genesis 4:3-4. — And in the sense of he himself: "Therefore the Lord Himself (הוּא) will give you a sign" Isaiah 7:14. — And also after אַתָּה: "Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup shall surely drink; and are you he (ואתה הוּא) who shall go altogether unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for you shall surely drink" Jeremiah 49:12. — And somewhat in the sense of *whereas in truth: "He shall not say to him, How much is this object? when he (והוא) does not want to buy" Bava Metzia 4:10. — And in the sense of *any person, everyone, German man, French on, English people: "Over fruits of the tree one (הוא) says 'Who creates the fruit of the tree', except for wine, for over wine one (הוא) says 'Who creates the fruit of the vine'; and over fruits of the earth one (הוא) says 'Who creates the fruit of the ground'" Berakhot 6:1. "One (הוא) may always give it as pe'ah and be exempt from tithes, until he has smoothed the pile" Pe'ah 1:6. — *And with כְּשֶׁ prefixed: "When he (כשהוא) relieves himself, he uncovers a handbreadth behind and two handbreadths in front" Berakhot 23b. "When he (כשהוא) bows, he bows at 'Blessed'; when he (כשהוא) straightens up, he straightens up at the Name" ibid. 12a. "For these waters are like nothing but a dry drug that one (שהוא) puts on live flesh, and it does not harm it" Numbers Rabbah 9. — *And to show the state in which a person is when he does something: "The attendant who ate an olive's bulk of matzah while reclining (כשהוא מיסב) has fulfilled his obligation" Pesachim 108a. "A person shall not eat on the eves of Sabbaths and festivals from the time of minhah onward, so that he may enter the Sabbath with an appetite (כשהוא תאוה)" ibid. 99b. "That he not enter the Sabbath while fasting (כשהוא מעונה)" Eruvin 41a. "Nakdimon entered the Temple in sadness (כשהוא עצב), wrapped himself and stood in prayer" Ta'anit 20a. "And according to Rabbi Meir, who says a person can transfer ownership of a thing that has not come into the world, why do I need 'he shall acknowledge' for property that fell to him while he was dying (כשהוא גוסס)?" Bava Batra 127b. "And they broke his eyes and made him an example, and he went weeping to his house, made an example (כשהוא עשוי דוגמא)" Tanhuma Kedoshim 8. — And it includes within it also the notion of the link between two nouns, in place of the needed verb: "Now therefore restore the man's wife, for he is (הוּא) a prophet, and he shall pray for you" Genesis 20:7. "And all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the Lord, for it is (הוּא) awesome" Exodus 34:10. "And the fourth river, it is (הוּא) the Euphrates" Genesis 2:14. "And whatever the man called every living creature, that was (הוּא) its name" ibid. 19. "You are He (אתה הוּא), my King" Psalms 44:5. "I, I am He (הוּא) who comforts you" Isaiah 51:12. "What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is (הוּא) not with us?" Job 15:9. "The order of inheritance is (הוא) thus: 'If a man dies and has no son, you shall pass his inheritance to his daughter' — a son precedes a daughter" Bava Batra 8:2. "I am He (אני הוא) who will exact punishment from one who hangs his money on a gentile and lends it to Israelites at interest" Bava Metzia 61b. "Samuel the Small stood up and said: I am the one (אני הוא) who came up without permission" Sanhedrin 11a. "Are you (אתה הוא) Hillel, whom they call Prince of Israel? He said to him: Yes. He said to him: If you are he (אתה הוא), may there not be many like you in Israel" Shabbat 31a. "Her husband came back home and found the Egyptian leaving his house; he asked her: Did he touch you? She said: Yes, and I thought that it was you (שאתה הוא)" Exodus Rabbah 1. — And in a question, after מי: "Who then is he (הוּא) that hunted game?" Genesis 27:33. "Who is he (הוּא) that will condemn me?" Isaiah 50:9. "Remember, I pray you, who (מי הוּא) ever perished being innocent?" Job 4:7. "Who is he (הוּא) that will contend with me?" ibid. 13:19. "Who is he (הוּא) that will strike hands with me?" ibid. 17:3. — And after כמה: "How much is (כמה הוא) its measure?" Eruvin 8:2. — And the word הוּא comes before a participle, to relate this action to the third-person subject mentioned before: "The name of the first (river) is Pishon; it is the one that (הוּא הסבב) encompasses the whole land of Havilah etc. And the name of the third river is Hiddekel; it is the one that (הוּא ההלך) goes east of Assyria" Genesis 2:11-14. — And the word הוּא comes with the definite ה prefixed, in the sense of that same known thing, whether because it was mentioned before, or because it is a thing known and famous in the world: "On that day (ביום הַהוּא) the Lord made a covenant with Abram" Genesis 15:18, that is, on that same day mentioned there earlier. "For the Lord of Hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, and against all that is lifted up, and it shall be brought low etc., and the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day (ביום הַהוּא) etc. On that day (ביום הַהוּא) a man shall cast away his idols of silver" Isaiah 2:12-20. "There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man (האיש הַהוּא) was blameless and upright" Job 1:1. — And before the noun referred to: "They said: That man (ההוא אדם) did not leave a donkey-driver or a camel-driver in the Land of Israel that he did not draw after him" Sifre, Vezot Haberakhah, שנה. "And that place (וההוא מקום), all their cooks are Israelites" Ve-Hizhir, Leviticus 8b. "That deed of gift (ההוא שטר מתנה) on which two robbers signed" ibid. 33a. "It is a ruling from Aristotle that that one (ההוא) is called perfect in essence which lacks nothing" Sha'ar ha-Shamayim by R. Abraham Herrera 3:2, translation of R. Isaac Aboab. — And some also say it in this manner of speech without the definite ה: "And he lay with her that night (בלילה הוּא) [note: In the Masorah: סבי' ההוא.]" Genesis 30:16. — And without יום, in the sense of from ancient times: "To a nation tall and smooth, to a people terrible from then (מן הוּא) onward" Isaiah 18:2. — And before אֲשֶׁר, in the sense of: this is the thing which, this is the man who, and the like: "And Joseph said to them: That is it (הוּא) which I spoke to you, saying, You are spies" Genesis 42:14. "And Moses said to Aaron: This is it (הוּא) which the Lord spoke, saying: Through those near to Me I will be sanctified" Leviticus 10:3. "But if you say to me: We trust in the Lord our God — is it not He (הוּא) whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed?" Isaiah 36:7. — *And somewhat in the sense of and therefore: "And if our father Jacob, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, promised and said to him, 'Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go', was afraid — we, how much more so! That is why (הוא ש) the prophet rebukes them and says to them: 'And you have forgotten the Lord your Maker'" Pesikta de-Rav Kahana, 'Anokhi Anokhi'. "And that is why (והוא ש) David said: For my father and my mother have forsaken me" Leviticus Rabbah 14. — *And in general in place of this thing: "That the shaving for leprosy overrides the shaving of the Nazirite when it (שהוא) is certain, but when it is doubtful it does not override" Nazir 8:2. "Rabbi Joshua stood on his feet and said: Is it (הוא) not a shame and a disgrace for us that we should decree uncleanness on the city of our fathers?" Zevachim 113a. "For just as He is merciful to man, so He has mercy on the beast. Know that it is (שהוא) so, for at the time when the Holy One, blessed be He, sought to destroy His world etc." Tanhuma Noah 8. — And in the sense of that same thing mentioned: "When (is a dice player or one who lends at interest disqualified from testifying)? When they have no occupation but it (אלא הוא); but if they have an occupation other than it (שלא הוא), they are fit" Sanhedrin 3:3. — And in the sense of: this thing holds only on this condition: "The three years that they spoke of (regarding presumptive ownership) — that is (הוא) when he enjoyed them consecutively" Bava Batra 29a. — And והוּא שֶׁ, in the sense of: what is said above holds only on condition: "A pool that drips water from an irrigated field — it is permitted to water another irrigated field from it etc. Abaye said: And that is provided (והוא ש) that the first spring has not ceased" Mo'ed Katan 4a. "Egyptian beans that took root before Rosh Hashanah, if he sowed them for seed, are tithed for the past year etc., provided (והוא ש) that he gathered from them before Rosh Hashanah" Rambam, Laws of Second Tithe and Fourth-Year Fruit 1:10. "An Israelite who had land in Syria and put a sharecropper on it, and the sharecropper sent him fruit — these are exempt, for I say he bought them from the market; provided (והוא ש) that that species is found in the market" the same author, Laws of Terumot 1:19. "If six (ribs) were broken on this side and six on that side, or eleven on this side and eleven on that side, it is terefah, provided (והוא ש) that they were broken in their half that faces the spine" the same author, Laws of Slaughter 10:1. — b) A designation for God: "I, I am He (אני הוּא) [note: Although it is possible to interpret the word הוא in all the following examples simply in the sense of the copula, nevertheless it seems that this combination was also a designation for the Godhead, and therefore perhaps the compounding of names with הוא at the end: Avihu, Elihu and others.] and there is no god with Me" Deuteronomy 32:39. "I am the Lord, that (הוּא) is My name, and My glory I will not give to another" Isaiah 42:8. "Listen to Me, O Jacob, and Israel My called: I am He (אני הוּא); I am the first, I also am the last" ibid. 48:12.

he: רק בעבר', ובארמ' הוי. בכנע' כמו בערב' ובאת' שמש למשמ' זו השרש כון. והנה סובר ברט, ES, 72, כי שני השרשים היה וכון היה עקר משמעתם ההכנה, ובחרו להן העברית והארמ' השרש היה במשמ' ההויה, והשרש כון במשמ' ההכנה, והכנענ' והערב' השרש כון לענין ההויה, והשרש הַיַא ھيَا במשמ' ההכנה והתכונה. אבל אעפ"י שקצת תמוה הדבר שבמושג קדום כל כך תבדלנה לשונות האחיות ולא תשתמשנה כלן בשרש אחד, מכל מקום קשה כמו"כ להניח כי למושג קדום ועקרי זה לא הניחו הלשונות שרשים לכתחלה במשמעה העקרית והשתמשו במשמעות מושאלות. ממנו א. הָיָה.
en: Only in Hebrew, and in Aramaic הוי. In Canaanite, as in Arabic and Ethiopic, the root כון served for this sense. Now Barth (ES, 72) holds that the basic meaning of both roots, היה and כון, was preparation, and Hebrew and Aramaic chose for themselves the root היה in the sense of being and the root כון in the sense of preparation, while Canaanite and Arabic chose the root כון for being and the root hayaʾa ھيَا in the sense of preparation and disposition. But although it is somewhat strange that for so primeval a concept the sister languages should differ and not all use one root, it is nevertheless equally difficult to assume that for this primeval and basic concept the languages did not set down roots from the start in its basic meaning, but used borrowed meanings. From it: א. הָיָה.

he:

המים המאררים למרים וצבתה בטנה וְנָפלה ירכה במד' ה כז, ואם אין מושיע אתנו וְיָצאנו אליך ש"א יא ג, ועתה  אראה פני המלך ואם יש בי עון וְהֱמִתִָנִי ש"ב יד לב, אם אמרנו נבוא העיר והרעב בעיר וּמַתנו שם מ"ב ז ד. — ואחרי כִּי, וְכִי: וכי ירק הזב בטהור וְכִבס בגדיו ויקר' יה ח, איש איש כי יקלל אלהיו וְנשא חטאו שם כד יה, וכי ימוך אחיך ומטה ידו עמך וְהֶחזקת בו שם כה לה, כי תקרב אל עיר להלחם עליה וְקָראת אליה לשלום דבר' כ י, כי תבנה בית חדש וְעָשית מעקה לגגך שם כב ח. — ולשאלה ותֵמה אחרי הסבה: בנשך נתן ותרבית לקח וָחָי לא יחיה יחזק' יח יג. — ואחרי הנחה אפשרית: לו איש הלך רוח ושקר כזב אטף לך ליין ולשכר וְהָיָה מטיף העם הזה מיכ' ב יא. — ואחרי הנחה מוחלטת: כי כל אכל חמץ וְנִכרתה הנפש ההוא מישראל שמות יב יה, מכה איש וָמֵת שם כא יב, והיה כל הנשוך וראה אותו וָחָי במד' כא ט. — ואחרי מקור של תנאי: בעברכם את ברית יי' אלהיכם וכו' וְחָרָה אף יי' בכם וַאֲבדתם מהרה יהוש' כג יו. — ואחרי מלת הסבה: יען כי גבהו בנות ציון ותלכנה נטוות גרון וכו' וְשִׂפַּח אדני קדקד בנות ציון ישע' ג יו-יז, לפני יי' אשר בחר בי מאביך ומכל ביתו לצות אתי נגיד על עם יי' על ישראל וְשִׂחקתי לפני יי' ש"ב ו כא. — ואחרי שמות כשהפעולה המצטרפת אליהם תפול בעתיד: וערל זכר אשר לא ימול בשר ערלתו וְנִכרתה הנפש ההוא מעמיה בראש' יז יד, כל האדם והבהמה אשר ימצא בשדה ולא יאסף הביתה וְיָרַד עליהם הברד וָמֵתוּ שמות ט יט, ואשר לא צדה והאלהים אנה לידו וְשַׂמתי לך מקום אשר ינוס שמה שם כא יג, איש אשר ירקח כמהו ואשר יתן ממנו על זר וְנִכרת מעמיו שם ל לג, ואשה אשר ישכב איש אתה שכבת זרע וְרָחצו במים וְטָמאו עד הערב ויקר' יה יח, והנפש אשר תפנה אל האבת ואל הידענים לזנת אחריהם וְנָתתי את פני בנפש ההוא וְהִכרתי אתו שם כ ו, והיה הטוב ההוא אשר ייטיב יי' עמנו וְהִטבנו לך במד' י לב, ודבר מה יראני וְהִגדתי לך שם כג ג, והאיש אשר יעשה בזדון וכו' וּמֵת האיש ההוא דבר' יז יב, הנביא אשר יזיד לדבר דבר בשמי וכו' וּמֵת הנביא ההוא שם יח כ, אשר יכה את קרית ספר ולכדה וְנָתתי לו את עכסה בתי לאשה יהוש' יה יו, הברכה הזאת אשר הביא שפחתך לאדני וְנִתנה לנערים ש"א כה כז, המדבר אליך וַהֲבאתו אלי ש"ב יד י, כל שמר שבת מחללו ומחזיקים בבריתי וַהֲביאותים אל הר קדשי וְשִׂמחתים בבית תפלתי ישע' נו ו-ז, והנביא והכהן והעם אשר יאמר משא יי' וּפָקדתי על האיש ההוא ירמ' כג לד, והגוי אשר יביא את צוארו בעל מלך בבל ועבדו וְהִנחתיו על אדמתו שם כז יא, חי אני אם לא אלתי בזה ובריתי אשר הפיר וּנְתתיו בראשו יחזק' יז יט, ואשר לא יתן על פיהם וְקִדשו עליו מלחמה מיכ' ג ה.

ו המהפכת העתיד לעבר תבוא אחרי עָבָר פשוט להמשך הסִפור בזמן העבר, ולהגיד מעשים ומאורעות ומעמד ענינים שהם המשך זמני או הגיוני למה שהוגד מקודם: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ והארץ היתה תהו ובהו וכו' ויאמר אלהים יהי אור וַיהי אור בראש' א א-ג.  והנחש היה ערום מכל חית השדה אשר עשה יי' אלהים וַיּאמר אל האשה אף כי אמר אלהים לא תאכלו מכל עץ הגן וַתּאמר האשה אל הנחש מפרי עץ הגן נאכל וכו' וַיּאמר הנחש אל האשה לא מות תמתון שם ג א-ד.  והאדם ידע את חוה אשתו וַתּהר וַתּלד את קין וַתּאמר קניתי איש את יי' שם ד א.  זכר ונקבה בראם וַיְברך אתם וַיִּקרא את שמם אדם שם ה ב.  כנמרד גבור ציד לפני יי' וַתּהי ראשית ממלכתו בבל שם י ט-י.  ובארבע עשרה שנה בא כדרלעמר במקור נדפס 'כדר-לעמר' והמלכים אשר אתו וַיַכּוּ את רפאים בעשתרת קרנים וכו' וַיָשֻׁבוּ וַיבאו אל עין משפט וכו' וַיצא מלך סדום וכו' וַיערכו אתם מלחמה שם יד ה-ח.  ואברהם זקן בא בימים ויי' ברך את אברהם בכל וַיאמר אברהם אל עבדו זקן ביתו המשל בכל אשר לו שים נא ידך תחת ירכי וכו' וַיאמר אליו העבד אולי לא תאבה האשה ללכת אחרי וכו' וַיאמר אליו אברהם השמר לך פן תשיב את בני שמה וכו' וַיקח העבד עשרה גמלים וכו' וַיַּבְרֵךְ את הגמלים מחוץ לעיר שם כד א-יא.  וכל הבארת אשר חפרו עבדי אביו בימי אברהם אביו סתמום פלשתים וַיְמלאום עפר שם כו יה.  אשר נתן יי' לנו וַיִּשמר אתנו וַיתן את הגדוד הבא עלינו בידנו ש"א ל כג.  הכו החצבם אש לקראת רעו גרזן על גרזן וילכו המים מן המוצא אל הברכה כתב' השלח, שורה ד-ה.  כאשר עזבתם אותי וַתַּעבדו אלהי נכר בארצכם כן תעבדו זרים בארץ לא לכם ירמ' ה יט.  לגבר אשר דרכו נסתרה וַיָּסָךְ אלוה בעדו איוב ג כג.  כציץ יצא וַיִּמָּל ויברח כצל שם יד ב.  ביום קראתי וַתַּענני תרהבני בנפשי עז תהל' קלח ג. — ואחרי הִנֵּה: הנה נא מצא עבדך חן בעיניך וַתַּגדל חסדך אשר  עשית עמדי בראש' יט יט, ונפתחה את אמתחתינו והנה כסף איש באמתחתו כספנו במשקלו וַנָּשֶב אתו בידנו שם מג כא, והנה רוח גדול באה מעבר המדבר וַיִּגַּע בארבע פנות הבית וַיִּפֹּל על הנערים וַיָּמוּתוּ איוב א יט.  — ואחרי בינוני: וגם אמנה אחתי בת אבי הוא אך לא בת אמי וַתְּהִי לי לאשה בראש' כ יב, מי אפוא הוא הצד ציד וַיָבֵא לי וָאֹכַל מכל בטרם תבוא שם כז לג, ולו שתי נשים שם אחת חנה ושם השנית פננה וַיהי לפננה ילדים ולחנה אין ילדים ש"א א ב, העם הרע הזה המאנים לשמוע את דברי ההלכים בשררות לבם וַיֵּלְכוּ אחרי אלהים אחרים ירמ' יג י, ואדני יי' הצבאות הנוגע בארץ וַתָּמוֹג עמו' ט ה, האל המאזרני חיל וַיִּתֵּן תמים דרכי תהל' יח לג, ובתו שארה וַתִּבֶן את בית חורון התחתון דהי"א ז כד. — ואחרי מקור: כשמע עשו את דברי אביו וַיּצעק צעקה גדלה בראש' כז לד, ויהי כהרימי קולי וָאקרא וַיעזב בגדו אצלי שם לט יח, בקרבתם לפני יי' וַימתו ויקר' יו א, ובבא משה אל אהל מועד לדבר אתו וַישמע את הקול מדבר אליו במד' ז פט, בצאתו מרחם אמו וַיאכל חצי בשרו שם יב יב, ובשלח יי' אתכם מקדש ברנע לאמר עלו ורשו את הארץ אשר נתתי לכם וַתּמרו את פי יי' אלהיכם דבר' ט כג, מכתב לחזקיהו מלך יהודה בחלֹתו וַיְחִי מחליו ישע' לח ט, כמרעיתם וַיִּשׂבעו הוש' יג ו, ובשוב רשע מרשעתו אשר עשה וַיעש משפט וצדקה יחזק' יח כז, יען עשות אדום בנקם נקם לבית יהודה וַיאשמו אשום שם כה יב, יען עשות פלשתים בנקמה וַינקמו נקם בשאט בנפש שם יה, בצאת האיש קדים וקו בידו וַיָּמָד אלף באמה וַיעברני במים שם מז ג, ולרשע אמר אלהים מה לך לספר חקי וַתשא בריתי עלי פיך תהל' נ יו. — ואחרי הגדת זמן המעשה: ביום  השלישי וַיִּשָׂא אברהם את עיניו וַירא את המקום מרחק בראש' כב ד, בשנת מות המלך עזיהו וָאראה את אדני יושב על כסא רם ונשא ישע' ו א, כי בעלותם ממצרים וַילך ישראל במדבר שופט' יא ו, ובעת מותה וַתְּדברנה הנצבות עליה ש"א ד כ, וכשוב דוד מהכות את הפלשתי וַיקח אתו אבנר וַיבאהו לפני שאול שם יז נז, בצאתי וַיהיו כלי הנערים קדש שם כא ו. — ואחרי עתיד בכונת עבר: ירכבהו על במותי ארץ וַיאכל תנובת שדי וַינקהו דבש מסלע דבר' לב יג, ויאמר אעלה אתכם ממצרים וָאביא אתכם אל הארץ אשר נשבעתי לאבתיכם וָאֹמר לא אפר בריתי אתכם לעולם שופט' ב א. — ואחרי לוּ: לוּא הקשבת למצותי וַיְהִי כנהר שלומך וצדקתך כגלי הים וַיְהי כחול זרעך וצאצאי מעיך כמעותיו ישע' מח יח-יט. — ואחרי הגדת סבה ומטרה: למען עבדי יעקב וישראל בחירי וָאקרא לך בשמך ישע' מה ד. — ובשני עתידים מהֻפכים שבא זה אח"ז יש שתבא הראשונה בכונה של סבה להשניה: וירא עשו כי רעות בנות כנען בעיני יצחק אביו וילך עשו אל ישמעאל ויקח את מחלת בת ישמעאל בראש' כח ח-ט, ויאמרו איש אל אחיו הנה בעל החלמות הלזה בא וכו' וַישמע ראובן וַיצלהו מידם שם לז יט-כא. —  וכמו פרוש להקודם, מפני שֶׁ:  ותקרא שמו משה וַתּאמר כי מן המים משיתהו שמות ב י. ר"ל מפני שאמרה.  ויקרא את שמה אבן העזר וַיאמר עד הנה עזרנו יי' ש"א ז יב. —  ואחרי עבר קצת במשמ' ואף-על-פי-כן:  כי ראיתי אלהים פנים אל פנים וַתִּנצל נפשי בראש' לב לא. ולא המציתך ביד דוד וַתִּפקד עלי עון האשה היום ש"ב ג ח, ידיך עצבוני ויעשוני יחד סביב וַתְּבלעני איוב י ח.  —  ואחרי שמות במשמ' ואעפי"כ, או לכן:  הנמלים עם לא עז וַיכינו בקיץ לחמם, שפנים עם לא עצום וַישימו בסלע ביתם, מלך אין לארבה וַיצא חצץ כלו משלי ל כה-כז. —  ומצוי הרבה במשמעה של לכן:  מבלתי יכלת יי' להביא את העם הזה אל הארץ אשר נשבע להם וַיִּשחטם במדבר במד' יד יו, יען מאסת את דבר יי' וַיִּמאסך ממלך ש"א יה כג, מדעתי כי קשה אתה וגיד ברזל ערפך ומצחך נחושה וָאגיד לך מאז ישע' מח ד-ה. —  ואחרי שם או פעל, במשמ' וּבנוגע לפלוני:  ופילגשו ושמה ראומה וַתֵּלֵד גם הוא את טבח בראש' כב כד, ואשר לא שם לבו אל דבר יי' וַיּעזֹב את עבדיו ואת מקנהו בשדה שמות ט כא, כל הזהב העשוי למלאכה בכל מלאכת הקדש וַיְהִי זהב התנופה תשע ועשרים ככר וכו' שם לח כד, והאנשים אשר שלח משה לתור את הארץ וַישבו וַילנו עליו את כל העדה במד' יד לו, וכל איש ישראל בראותם את האיש וַיָּנֻסו מפניו ש"א יז כד, כי המגיד לי לאמר הנה מת שאול והוא היה כמבשר בעיניו וָאֹחזה בו ואהרגהו בצקלג ש"ב ד י, בניהם אשר נֹתרו אחריהם בארץ אשר לא יכלו בני ישראל להחרימם וַיַּעלם שלמה למס עֹבד מ"א ט כא, ובני ישראל הישבים בערי יהודה וַיִּמלֹך עליהם רחבעם שם יב יז, והעם הנשאר בארץ יהודה אשר השאיר נבוכדנאצר מלך בבל וַיפקד עליהם את גדליהו מ"ב כה כב, כי על דברי לא הקשיבו ותורתי וַיִּמאסו בה ירמ' ו יט, שתי המשפחות אשר בחר יי' בהם וַיִּמאסם שם לג כד, והנשברת וַתַּעמֹדנה ארבע תחתיה דני' ח כב, ר"ל ומה שנוגע לקרן הנשברת הנה עמדו וכו'. —  ובסוף ספור המעשה כעין חתימת האמור קודם, קצת במשמ' וּבְכֵן:  ואחרי כן קבר אברהם את שרה אשתו אל מערת שדה המכפלה וכו' וַיָּקָם השדה והמערה אשר בו לאברהם לאחזת קבר בראש' כג יט-כ, וישלח דוד את ידו אל הכלי ויקח משם אבן ויקלע וכו' וַיֶּחזק דוד מן הפלשתי  בקלע ובאבן ש"א יז מט-נ, וידבקו פלשתים את שאול וכו' וירא נשא כליו כי מת שאול ויפל גם הוא על חרבו וימת עמו וַיָּמָת שאול ושלשת בניו וכו' שם לא ב-ו, ר"ל הנה ככה מת שאול עם בניו. —  וכמו תולדה להאמור קודם, קצת במשמ' אם-כן:  ויאמר יי' אל השטן השמת לבך אל עבדי איוב כי אין כמהו בארץ איש תם וישר ירא אלהים וסר מרע ועדנו מחזיק בתמתו וַתְּסיתני בו לבלעו חנם איוב ב ג, ר"ל אם-כן, מה שהסיתני בו היה חנם. —  ואחרי עבר בכונה לפעולה נכחית:  יען כי גבהו בנות ציון וַתֵּלכנה נטוות en:
The sixth letter [Note: See, concerning the order of the letters in the Hebrew alphabet, the notes to the letters א, ב, ג.]. In the laments of Lamentations and in those psalms arranged in alphabetical order, the verses after the verses of the letter ה begin with the letter ו: "Her adversaries are the chief, etc. And from the daughter of Zion all her beauty is departed" (Lamentations 1:5–6); "Behold, I have longed after thy precepts: quicken me in thy righteousness. Let thy mercies come also unto me, O Lord, even thy salvation, according to thy word" (Psalms 119:40–41), and more. In the Hebrew alphabet its name is *וָו, *ואו, *ויו, see the entry וָו.
This letter was set as the sign of a compound sound that is produced with a rounded opening of the lips, as in the sound אֻ, and by friction of the breath between fluttering lips [Note: Such is the sound of the letter و almost everywhere; only the Turks and the Persians pronounce it like the letter v in the European languages. Now, the most ancient testimony about the quality of the sound of the letter ו has been preserved for us from the days of the Mishnah, in the tradition of R. Judah (Sukkah 4:5) concerning the pronunciation of the Explicit Name, and perhaps in the testimony of R. Eliezer there (and see below, the note to the entry והו), and in the transcription of Jerome, who transcribed some Hebrew words as they are in Roman script, and these are they: וְלא ulo, וְרֹחב urob, ורְאיתי uraithi, וְאָשם vasam, חוה ava, אָוֶן aven, כַּוָּנִים chaunim, יִלָּוֶה illaue, שְׁוָרִים surim, אֵילָיו elau, פניו phanau, רַגְלָיו raglau, צַו לָצַו קַו לָקַו sau la sau cau la cau, בַּדָּיו baddau, כִּסְלֵו caslau, עֲוֹנָם onam (Siegfried, ZAW 1884, 34-83). From this transcription we see that in the days of Jerome, that is, close to the sealing of the Talmud, the Jews pronounced the letter ו for the most part as its sound is now in the mouths of most Jews before a vocal sheva and the letters במפ, or something like it, and Jerome transcribed this sound as far as possible in the letters of the Latin language. And R. Simeon ben Tzemach Duran already spoke of the changes in the pronunciation of this letter in the mouths of the Jews; he said, and these are his words: "For the Arabs pronounce the vavs with great softness, and so the Israelites who dwell among them learned from them; and the Europeans pronounce it with a strong joining of the lips, and so do the Israelites who dwell in their lands" (Magen Avot, ח"י ד). And the moderns have discussed this question a great deal, especially Philippi (ZDMG, 1817), who decided that the two letters ו י were originally vowel signs in the Semitic language, and König disputed him in his books. And the matter will be explained further in the Introduction, in the part on grammar.], and so the Yemenite Jews pronounce it even now. But the rest of the Jews, Sephardim and Ashkenazim, now pronounce it at the beginning of a syllable and at its end [Note: Nöldeke already condemned this pronunciation and protested against it, and decided that this pronunciation must be abandoned: Die barbare Gewohnheit silbenauslautendes wie deutsch. w oder gar f auszusprechen atatt rein vokalisch sollte auch im Hebr. aufgegeben werden (Nö. syr. Gram. 26). But there is a kind of proof for the matter that even in the days when the language was alive, its sound in the mouth of the people, especially at the end of words, tended somewhat toward the sound of a soft פ (see the note to the entry והו); and besides this, in the matter of the pronunciation of letters in languages, the decree of the scholars has no force.] as a simple sound with friction of fluttering lips, except when it comes before a letter with a vocal sheva, where they pronounce it like אֻ [Note: R. Judah Hayyuj said, and these are his words: "That we read (like אֻ) this prefix, vowelled with shuruk, which is at the head of the word and is followed by one of the letters במ"ף as a sign, whether one of them is vowelled with one of the seven kings or quiescent with a sheva, or whether after the vav there comes one of the other letters quiescent with a sheva only. And the example of the latter: שמרתם וקראתם; and of the former: ובאו שמה, ומפתח אהל מועד, ופתח אהל מעד, ובה', ומה', ומאלהים, ופרו ורבו — you shall not read a vav at all. And the reason for this matter appears to be that the articulation of the vav in these words is heavy on the tongue; and this matter is a tradition in our hands from our first fathers, and we have received it from our ancient elders" (Sefer Otiyot ha-Nach, the gate of אהוי). And so in Ibn Ezra's translation: "And so our reading of the conjunctive vav, which is vowelled with shuruk, when one of במ"ף comes after it, whether vowelled or quiescent, is read like an alef vowelled with kubutz, as in וּשמרתם וּקראתם and as in ובה' ואלהיכם ומאלוהי' ומה ופתח אהל מועד ופרו ורבו — they are never read as vav; and the reason is known, because the vav is heavy [on the tongue]; so they inherited it from our ancients, generation after generation" (ibid.). And so Ibn Ezra in his commentary: "And if a vav, they say shuruk instead of hiriq, as though the vav were read as א, as in וזבולן, for the word appears as though read with an alef, אוּזבולן" (Exodus 1:2).]: וקְחו like אֻקְחו, ודְעו like אֻדְעו, and likewise before the labial letters במפ: ובֵין like אֻבֵין, ומֶשך like אֻמֶשך, and ופִי like אֻפִי; and as a sign of this sound a dot serves in the heart of the letter: וּ.

In Hebrew roots the letter ו is now not found at the beginning of the root or at its end, for already in early times the sound of the vav — with which some roots in the ancient Semitic language began or ended — became heavy for the Hebrews, and they exchanged it for the sound of yod, which was easier for them; and of them there remained only a few roots with first ו and with final ו in which the sound of the vav remained as a pronounced consonant, such as וָו, וָזָר, וָלָד, and in the verbs with first נ or first י in the Hitpa'el: הִתְוַדָּה, הִתְוַכֵּחַ, הִתְוָעֵד; and in a later period more words were added: *וִדּוּי, *וִכּוּחַ, *וַעַד, *וִעוּד, *ורד, *ושט, *וִתֵּר, *וַתְרָן, and more; and at the end: גֵּו, סְתָו, עָנָו, קַו, שָׁלֵו, שְׂלָו, תָּו. And likewise few are the roots with a pronounced middle ו: אָוֶן, גָוַע, דָּוֶה, חִוָּה, חָוַר, כַּוָּן, עִוְעִים, עָוֶל, צִוָּה, צָוַח, קִוָּה, שִׁוַּע, רָוָה, רָוַח, תָּוָה. In contrast, many are the roots with a quiescent middle ו, in which the sound is not pronounced but quiescent and serves only to make the vowel before it long, such as those with holam: אוֹר, בּוֹשׁ, and those with shuruk: קוּם, שׁוּב, and the like. And afterward they began to use the letter וּ as a sign of the long vowel of shuruk and the letter ו for the long vowel of holam, as in גְּבוּל, גִּבֹּור and the like; and the custom spread, especially in unvocalized texts, of using the letter vav for the vowels shuruk and holam even when they are short by nature.

The letter ו is one of the servile letters, and it is joined at the ends of nouns to indicate relation and possession of the third person, and it is quiescent with the vowel holam ו: בֵּיתוֹ, סִפְרוֹ, and pronounced after hiriq and kamatz: אָבִיו, אָחִיו, פִּיו, בָּנָיו, עֲבָדָיו; and likewise at the ends of verbs to indicate the third-person object: דַבְּרוֹ, שְׁפָטוֹ, שְׁמַרְתִּיו; and quiescent with shuruk וּ at the ends of verbs in the past and future to indicate the action of third-person plurals: כָּתַב-כִּתְבוּ, יִכְתֹּב-יִכְתְּבוּ.
It serves further to join [Note: In Arabic two letters serve this use in all its shades, the letter و and the letter ف, and in Hebrew all the shades of the uses of conjunction and coordination were joined in the letter ו alone. — And Ibn Ezra said: "The vav in ולא עליהם יהיה הגשם is like a soft פ in the language of Ishmael and in the holy tongue" (Ibn Ezra, Zechariah 17:14). And so R. Samuel ibn Tibbon: "The ו in והארץ is like a soft פ in the language of Ishmael, whose way is to place them at the heads of sayings and at the heads of genealogies, not in the sense of coordination and not in the sense of a beginning" (R. Samuel ibn Tibbon, Yikkavu ha-Mayim 126).] nouns and verbs and sayings to what was said before them, and in this use it is joined at the beginning of nouns and verbs with varying vowels according to the nature of the letters and vowels to which the vav is joined: for the most part וְ; before a hataf patach וַ; before a hataf segol וֶ; before a word stressed on the penult וֶ; before a yod וִ; before a letter with sheva and before במף וּ; and it is called the conjunctive vav, the coordinating vav, the accompanying vav, — and it indicates:

a) simple joining and connection between two nouns, verbs or sayings, German und; French et; English and: "the heavens and the earth," "Judah and Jerusalem," "male and female created he them" (Genesis 1:27), "Now Abraham and Sarah were old" (ibid. 18:11), "the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah" (ibid. 4:19), "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" (ibid. 1:1), "thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field" (ibid. 3:14), "ill favoured and leanfleshed" (ibid. 41:4), "well favoured and fatfleshed" (ibid.), "take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow" (ibid. 27:3), "Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands" (ibid. 16:9), "Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly" (ibid. 17:20), "Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee" (ibid. 26:28), "Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee" (ibid. 27:29). — And if more than two words must be joined together, sometimes the conjunctive ו is added to each one of the words being joined: "The sons of Japheth; Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras" (Genesis 10:2), "the Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Rephaims" (ibid. 15:19–20), "and he hath given him flocks, and herds, and silver, and gold, and menservants, and maidservants, and camels, and asses" (ibid. 24:35), "the eagle, and the ossifrage [Note: in the printed source: 'והפרץ'], and the ospray, etc. and the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind" (Deuteronomy 14:12–15), "and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats" (Isaiah 1:11), — and sometimes it is added only to one of them, to the last, or to several of them: "And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold" (Genesis 13:2), "Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations" (ibid. 14:1), "ringstraked, speckled, and spotted" (ibid. 30:39). — And if the word to which the vav is joined is stressed on the penult, and for the most part if it is itself marked with a disjunctive accent or adjacent to a disjunctive, the vav is vowelled with kamatz: בני נח שם חם וָיָפֶת, "The sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth" (Genesis 10:1); פן תדבקני הרעה וָמַתִּי, "lest some evil take me, and I die" (ibid. 19:19); הנה רבקה לפניך קח וָלֵךְ, "Behold, Rebekah is before thee, take her, and go" (ibid. 24:51); ודפקום יום אחד וָמֵתוּ כל הצאן, "and if men should overdrive them one day, all the flock will die" (ibid. 33:13); אשר ימצא אותו מעבדיך וָמֵת, "With whomsoever of thy servants it be found, both let him die" (ibid. 44:9); וירד עליהם הברד וָמֵתוּ, "the hail shall come down upon them, and they shall die" (Exodus 9:19); ואת משפטי אשר יעשה אתם האדם וָחַי בהם, "and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them" (Leviticus 18:5); והחזקת בו גר ותושב וָחַי עמך, "then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee" (ibid. 25:35); וסקלוה אנשי עירה באבנים וָמֵתָה, "and the men of her city shall stone her with stones that she die" (Deuteronomy 22:21); רבה צבאך וָצֵאָה, "Increase thine army, and come out" (Judges 9:29); ויעברו בארץ שעלים וָאַיִן, "then they passed through the land of Shalim, and there they were not" (1 Samuel 9:4); ואם ישבנו פה וָמָתְנוּ, "and if we sit still here, we die also" (2 Kings 7:4); האספי אל תערך הרגעי ודָמִּי, "put up thyself into thy scabbard, rest, and be still" (Jeremiah 47:6); היֹרה זקים חצים וָמָוֶת, "who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death" (Proverbs 26:18); ורחצת וָסַכְתְּ ושמת שמלתך עליך, "Wash thyself therefore, and anoint thee, and put thy raiment upon thee" (Ruth 3:3). — And not at a pause the vav is vowelled with other vowels even if the word is stressed on the penult: וכי יכה איש את עבדו וכו' בשבט וּמֵת תחת ידו, "And if a man smite his servant, etc. with a rod, and he die under his hand" (Exodus 21:20). — And also in a word that is itself a complete sentence: ויאמר אבשלום וָלא ילך נא אתנו אמנון אחי, "Then said Absalom, If not, I pray thee, let my brother Amnon go with us" (2 Samuel 13:26), that is, if you will not go. ויאמר נעמן וָלא יֻתן נא לעבדיך משא וכו', "And Naaman said, Shall there not then, I pray thee, be given to thy servant two mules' burden, etc." (2 Kings 5:17), that is, if you will not take the gift. — And especially if the two words joined are a natural pair, for instance if the same word itself is repeated: כֹּה וָכֹה (Exodus 2:12), מי וָמי (ibid. 10:8), אֶלֶף וָאָלֶף (Numbers 26:51), הנה וָהנה (Joshua 8:20), אָנֶה וָאָנָה (1 Kings 2:36 and elsewhere), לְדֹר וָדֹר (Psalms 10:6 and elsewhere), בלב וָלב (ibid. 12:3), אבן וָאבן (Proverbs 20:23 and elsewhere), לשער וָשער (1 Chronicles 26:13), עיר וָעיר (ibid. 11:12), איש וָאיש (Esther 1:8). יוֹם וָיוֹם (ibid. 2:11 and elsewhere), עַם וָעָם (ibid. 3:12 and elsewhere). — Or they are close to each other in meaning: תהוּ וָבֹהו (Genesis 1:2), נע ונָד (ibid. 4:12), אימתה וָפחד (Exodus 15:16), שמחה וָגיל (Isaiah 16:10), עון וָפשע (Exodus 34:7), עצום וָרב (Deuteronomy 26:5), רעה וָפשע (1 Samuel 24:12), ונין וָנכד (Isaiah 14:22), מושיע וָרב (ibid. 19:20), וחתו וָבשו (ibid. 20:5), הפלא וָפלא (ibid. 29:14), הבל וָריק (ibid. 30:7), מסלול וָדרך (ibid. 35:8), מאפס וָתהו (ibid. 40:17), שרב וָשמש (ibid. 49:10), יד וָשֵׁם (ibid. 56:5), רפש וָטיט (ibid. 56:20), שׁד וָשבר (ibid. 59:7), רע וָמר (Jeremiah 2:19), חמס וָשׁד (ibid. 20:8 and elsewhere), עני וָדל (Zephaniah 3:12), לעולם וָעד (Psalms 9:6 and elsewhere), עמל וָאָוֶן (ibid. 10:7), טוב וָחסד (ibid. 23:6), תֹּם וָישׁר (ibid. 25:21), כבוד וָעֹז (ibid. 29:1 and elsewhere), כסיל ובָער (ibid. 49:11), חלב וָדשן (ibid. 63:6), עני וָרש (ibid. 82:3), אֹהֵב וָרֵעַ (ibid. 88:19), הון וָעשר (ibid. 112:3), חרפה וָבוז (ibid. 119:22), משפט וָצדק (ibid. ibid. 121), אבדון וָמות (Job 28:22), נער וָרך (1 Chronicles 22:5), מכאֹבים וָכעס (Ecclesiastes 2:23), בזיון וָקצף (Esther 1:18). — Or they are opposites of each other: בהמה וָרמש (Genesis 1:24), טוב וָרע (ibid. 2:9 and elsewhere), וקֹר וָחֹם (ibid. 8:22), וקיץ וָחרף (ibid.), שמים וָארץ (ibid. 14:19 and elsewhere), שור וָשה (Exodus 34:19 and elsewhere), b) joining in the sense of עִם, German mit; French avec; English with: "I will let you go, and your little ones" (Exodus 10:10), that is, with your little ones. "roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it" (ibid. 12:8), that is, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. "For they came up with their cattle and their tents" (Judges 6:5), that is, with their cattle and with their tents. "For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture" (Psalms 75:9), that is, a cup with wine. — And in the sense of אוֹ, German oder; French ou; English or: "And he that smiteth his father, and his mother, shall be surely put to death" (Exodus 21:15), that is, his father or his mother. "And he that curseth his father, and his mother, shall surely be put to death" (ibid. 17), "Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?" (Genesis 17:17), "But if the priest's daughter be a widow, and divorced" (Leviticus 22:13). — And the vav is repeated twice or more in the sense of all one, this or that: "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, and he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death" (Exodus 21:17), "If a man be found stealing any of his brethren, and maketh merchandise of him, and selleth him" (Deuteronomy 24:7), that is, he maltreated him or sold him. — And for addition and surpassing what came before, somewhat in the sense of אַף גַּם, still more, even: "And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also" (1 Kings 2:22), "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided" (2 Samuel 1:23), and even in their death they were not divided. "And though they say, The Lord liveth; surely they swear falsely" (Jeremiah 5:2), and even though they say "The Lord liveth." "So much did the children of Ammon pay unto him, both the second year, and the third" (2 Chronicles 27:5). — And in the sense of אֶלָּא, אֲבָל: "Nay, my lord (we have not come to see the nakedness of the land), but to buy food are thy servants come" (Genesis 42:10), that is, but we have come to buy food. "But for Adam there was not found an help meet for him" (ibid. 2:20), "for in Isaac shall thy seed be called. And also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation" (ibid. 21:12–13), that is, but also the son of the bondwoman, etc. "choose you this day whom ye will serve, etc. or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord" (Joshua 24:15), that is, but I and my house. "And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I" (Ruth 3:12), "For all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God" (Micah 4:5), "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" (Proverbs 11:13). — And for the consequent of a condition, if so, then so: "separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left" (Genesis 13:9), "When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned and enquired early after God" (Psalms 78:33), "But if they had stood in my counsel, and had caused my people to hear my words" (Jeremiah 23:22). — And somewhat in the sense of אֲשֶׁר, שֶׁ: "and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, and her name was Hagar" (Genesis 16:1), that is, whose name was Hagar. "And his concubine, and her name was Reumah [Note: in the printed source: 'רעומה']" (ibid. 22:24), "And Rebekah had a brother, and his name was Laban" (ibid. 24:29), "a virgin, and no man had known her" (ibid. 16), "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered for multitude" (ibid. 16:10), that is, until it cannot be numbered. "Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, and it shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom" (Jeremiah 7:32), that is, when it shall no more be called. "Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and he had none to help him" (Job 29:12), who has none to help him. — And it indicates the state of the matter and its circumstance [Note: In Arabic واو الحال, ואו אלחאל.]: "and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward" (Genesis 9:23), that is, while their faces were backward. "(God appeared to him) and he sat in the tent door" (ibid. 18:1), "And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel" (ibid. 25:26), "(he came to the woman) and she sat in the field" (Judges 13:9), "which speak peace to their neighbours, and mischief is in their hearts" (Psalms 28:3). — And in the sense of after, since, although, nevertheless: "Lord God, what wilt thou give me, and I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?" (Genesis 15:2), since I go childless. "Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, and I am but dust and ashes" (ibid. 18:27), although I am dust and ashes. "(he laid his hand upon Ephraim's head) and he was the younger" (ibid. 48:14), although he was the younger. — And in the sense of הֲלֹא: "Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; and she is a man's wife" (Genesis 20:3), "How canst thou say, I love thee, and thine heart is not with me?" (Judges 16:15), "The Lord will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof: and ye have eaten up the vineyard" (Isaiah 3:14), "Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?" (Job 6:26). — And for wonder: "Shall I of a surety bear a child, and I am old?" (Genesis 18:13), "Wherefore come ye to me, and ye hate me" (ibid. 26:27), "What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, etc. and thou hatest instruction" (Psalms 50:16–17). — And somewhat in the sense of and if so, and therefore: "And they said, An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, etc. And he said unto his daughters, And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man?" (Exodus 2:19–20), "they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof. But he said, And bring meal" (2 Kings 4:40–41), that is, if so, bring meal. "Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: and these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood" (Isaiah 47:8–9). — And in the sense of כְּמוֹ, to compare the two matters joined by the vav, and it is called וָו הַהַשְׁוָאָה [Note: In Arabic too ו serves this use.], waw adaequationis: "As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25), that is, good news from a far country is like and equal to cold waters to a weary soul. "As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart" (ibid. 20), "The legs of the lame are not equal: so is a parable in the mouth of fools" (ibid. 26:7), "As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up: so man lieth down, and riseth not" (Job 14:11–12), that is, and so if a man lies down and does not rise. "The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man" (ibid. 19), that is, and so You destroy the hope of man. — And the thing compared comes before the thing to which it is compared: "Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?" (Job 12:11), as the palate tastes the food. — And in the sense of אֵיפוֹא: "Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north" (Zechariah 2:10), like "flee, then." — And to indicate the purpose, the aim and the manner, in the sense of לְמַעַן, כְּדֵי שֶׁ, in such a way: "Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles" (Isaiah 13:2), "To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal?" (ibid. 40:25), "Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, He is righteous?" (ibid. 41:26), "For who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath perceived and heard his word?" (Jeremiah 23:18), "Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought? neither do ye kindle fire on mine altar for nought" (Malachi 1:10), "For it was not [Note: Some read לוּא, and then ואשא will be in the sense of "then I would bear it."] an enemy that reproached me, that I might bear it: neither was it [Note: Some read לוּא, and then ואשא will be in the sense of "then I would bear it."] he that hated me that did magnify himself against me, that I might hide myself from him" (Psalms 55:13), "and to him shall be given of the gold of Sheba: and prayer also shall be made for him continually" (ibid. 72:15). — And in the sense of in this way: "This do, and live" (Genesis 42:18), that is, in this way you will live.

c) The vav serves to indicate the joining of two actions that occurred or will occur one after the other in varying relations; and the letter ו is joined to a past verb and the meaning of the verb is turned to the future, and to a future verb the letter ו is joined and the meaning of the verb is turned to the past [Note: This distinctive property has no parallel in the other languages, not even in the Semitic languages, except that in the Canaanite and Moabite language, which are almost Hebrew, something resembling it is found; and it gives the narrative style of Hebrew diction a delightful original character. But until now the scholars have not succeeded in finding a sufficient explanation of how this property arose in Hebrew, and by what natural path the Hebrew language came to this strange and foreign usage, contrary to natural logic. The ancients did not seek reasons for this, and only at the beginning of the eighteenth century of the Western peoples did some Christian scholars, II Sholze, 1735, and afterward Ch. Windheim 1744, begin to investigate the nature and reason of this ו, and they arrived at the conjecture that the וַ that converts the future to the past is a contraction of the verb וְהָיָה, and where they later said וַיֹּאמֶר they earlier said וְהָיָה יֹאמַר, somewhat like the usage of the Arabic language כאן יפעל کان يفعل; and most scholars held this opinion for a long time, until the moderns came and showed how far this conjecture is from the natural course of the development of language, and most of them inclined after another conjecture: that the two forms of the past and the future customary in the Semitic languages did not, in the ancient Semitic language, serve with a fixed meaning for past and future, but served indiscriminately for both tenses according to additional signs, such as the place of the stress, penultimate or ultimate, and the like; and therefore the Hebrew language could use both of them for past and for future (Lambert, REJ, Bö, § 969 ff, and others). But all this is not an explanation of this strange property of the Hebrew language, but only a change of name in other words; for in the end the temporal meaning of the two forms was fixed in the languages already in very ancient times, even before they separated from one another, since their form is similar in almost all the sister languages except Akkadian; and it is hard to understand what Hebrew alone saw to choose this strange path in using its two tenses in a reversed meaning in this way. And see further in the Introduction, in the part on grammar.], and the vav in this use is called וָו הַהִפּוּךְ, וָו הַמְּהַפֶּכֶת [Note: This distinctive property has no parallel in the other languages, not even in the Semitic languages, except that in the Canaanite and Moabite language, which are almost Hebrew, something resembling it is found; and it gives the narrative style of Hebrew diction a delightful original character. But until now the scholars have not succeeded in finding a sufficient explanation of how this property arose in Hebrew, and by what natural path the Hebrew language came to this strange and foreign usage, contrary to natural logic. The ancients did not seek reasons for this, and only at the beginning of the eighteenth century of the Western peoples did some Christian scholars, II Sholze, 1735, and afterward Ch. Windheim 1744, begin to investigate the nature and reason of this ו, and they arrived at the conjecture that the וַ that converts the future to the past is a contraction of the verb וְהָיָה, and where they later said וַיֹּאמֶר they earlier said וְהָיָה יֹאמַר, somewhat like the usage of the Arabic language כאן יפעל کان يفعل; and most scholars held this opinion for a long time, until the moderns came and showed how far this conjecture is from the natural course of the development of language, and most of them inclined after another conjecture: that the two forms of the past and the future customary in the Semitic languages did not, in the ancient Semitic language, serve with a fixed meaning for past and future, but served indiscriminately for both tenses according to additional signs, such as the place of the stress, penultimate or ultimate, and the like; and therefore the Hebrew language could use both of them for past and for future (Lambert, REJ, Bö, § 969 ff, and others). But all this is not an explanation of this strange property of the Hebrew language, but only a change of name in other words; for in the end the temporal meaning of the two forms was fixed in the languages already in very ancient times, even before they separated from one another, since their form is similar in almost all the sister languages except Akkadian; and it is hard to understand what Hebrew alone saw to choose this strange path in using its two tenses in a reversed meaning in this way. And see further in the Introduction, in the part on grammar.], waw conversivum, waw consectivum.
The ו that converts the past to the future has a vowel like the vowel of the conjunctive vav in its simple form: וְ, וּ, וַ, וָ, according to the nature of the letters and vowels after it: וְהָיה, וּבָאת, וַהֲסירת, וָמָתנו; and besides this, for the most part the stress is pushed forward from the penult to the ultima, as in שָׁבה-וְשׁבָה [Note: In all the following examples the stress is after the vowel that is explicitly marked.], כתַבת-וְכתבתָּ: וְירשתָּ אתם וְישבתָּ בארצם, "When the Lord thy God shall cut off the nations from before thee, whither thou goest to possess them, and thou succeedest them, and dwellest in their land" (Deuteronomy 12:29); וְשׁבָה אל בית אביה, "But if the priest's daughter be a widow, or divorced, and have no child, and is returned unto her father's house" (Leviticus 22:13); אשר שַׂמתי בידך, "all those wonders which I have put in thine hand" (Exodus 4:21), past. וְשׂמתִּי פדת בין עמי ובין עמך, "And I will put a division between my people and thy people" (ibid. 8:19), future. סכֹּתה באף ותרדפנו, "Thou hast covered with anger, and persecuted us" (Lamentations 3:43), past. וְסכֹּתָ על הארן את הפרכת, "and cover the ark with the vail" (Exodus 40:3), future. — But before a pause the stress always stays in its place, even with the converting vav: וְנָתתִּי עשב בשדך לבהמתך ואָכלתָּ ושבעת, "And I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle, that thou mayest eat and be full" (Deuteronomy 11:15); אם תלכי עמי וְהלָכתי, "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go" (Judges 4:8), as against: וְהלכתִּי גם אני אתך בגורלך, "and I likewise will go with thee into thy lot" (ibid. 1:3). כרמים תטע וְעבָדת ויין לא תשתה, "Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine" (Deuteronomy 28:39), as against: וְעבדתָּ את איביך, "Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies" (ibid. 48). — And before a stressed syllable: וְישַׁבתה בה, "and shalt dwell therein" (Deuteronomy 17:14), וְנתַתי לו, "to him will I give" (Judges 1:12), וְשלַחתי אש בחומת עזה, "But I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza" (Amos 1:7), וְשבַרתי לה מטה לחם, "and will break the staff of the bread thereof" (Ezekiel 14:13), וְלקַחתי אָני מצמרת הארז, "I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar" (ibid. 17:22); but as against this: וְחָשקתָּ בה וְלָקחתָּ לך לאשה, "and hast a desire unto her, that thou wouldest have her to thy wife" (Deuteronomy 21:11). — And likewise the stress is kept in its place in verbs with final quiescent א and final ה, almost always in those with final א in the first person singular: וְנלאֵיתי כלכל, "and I was weary with forbearing" (Jeremiah 20:9), וְנמצֵאתי לכם נאם יי' וְשבתִּי את שביתכם וְקבצתִּי אתכם מכל הגוים, "And I will be found of you, saith the Lord: and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations" (ibid. 29:14). — And in verbs with final י when the second radical has hiriq: הנני עמד לפניך שם על הצור בחרב וְהכִּית בצור, "Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock" (Exodus 17:6), וְעשִׂית ללאת תכלת, "And thou shalt make loops of blue" (ibid. 26:4), ואת האשרה אשר עליו תכרת וּבנִית מזבח ליי' אלהיך, "and cut down the grove that is by it: and build an altar unto the Lord thy God" (Judges 6:25–26). — But if the second radical has tzere, the stress moves down, in those with final א as in those with final י: וְהֵבאתָ לאביך ואכל, "And thou shalt bring it to thy father, that he may eat" (Genesis 27:10), וְהכיתִי אתכם גם אני, "and I, even I, will punish you" (Leviticus 26:24), וְגליתִי להם עתרת שלום, "and will reveal unto them the abundance of peace" (Jeremiah 33:6), וְכסיתִי בכבותך שמים, "And when I shall put thee out, I will cover the heaven" (Ezekiel 32:7). — But as against this [Note: The scholars hold that the source of these variations is in differing opinions of the Masoretes, none of which entirely tipped the scale to its side.]: וְירֵאת מאלהיך, "but shalt fear thy God" (Leviticus 19:14), וְנקֵּיתי דמם, "For I will cleanse their blood" (Joel 4:21), אז איתם וְנקֵּיתי מפשע רב, "then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression" (Psalms 19:14), — And if after the verb with final א or final י there comes a word beginning with alef, the stress moves down: וּבאתָ אל התבה, "and thou shalt come into the ark" (Genesis 7:8), וּבאתָ אתה וזקני ישראל, "and thou shalt come, thou and the elders of Israel" (Exodus 3:18). — And as against this [Note: The scholars hold that the source of these variations is in differing opinions of the Masoretes, none of which entirely tipped the scale to its side.]: וְקרָאת את שמו יצחק, "and thou shalt call his name Isaac" (Genesis 17:19), וְקרָאת אליהם ולא יענוכה, "thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee" (Jeremiah 7:26), וְקרָאתי אל הדגן, "and I will call for the corn" (Ezekiel 36:29). — כי אהיה עמך וְהכיתָ את מדין, "Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites" (Judges 6:16), וְצפיתָ אתו זהב טהור, "And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold" (Exodus 25:11), ולקחת סלת וְאפיתָ אתה שתים עשר חלות, "And thou shalt take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes thereof" (Leviticus 24:5). — And as against this [Note: See the previous note.]: וְצוִּיתי את ברכתי לכם, "Then I will command my blessing upon you" (ibid. 25:21). — And before ה: וְהבאתִי השמש בצהרים, "that I will cause the sun to go down at noon" (Amos 8:9). — And before ע: וְהבאתָ עלינו אשם, "and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us" (Genesis 26:10), וְהבאתִי עלי קללה, "and I shall bring a curse upon me" (ibid. 27:12), וְהבאתִי עליכם חרב, "And I will bring a sword upon you" (Leviticus 26:25). — And as against this [Note: See the previous note.]: וְקרָאתי עליו לכל הרי חרב, "And I will call for a sword against him throughout all my mountains" (Ezekiel 38:21). — In the Hif'il, the second radical with hiriq keeps the stress even with the converting vav, except before ה and before א: וְהבאתָ שמה מבית לפרכת את ארון העדות וְהבדילָה הפרכת, "that thou mayest bring in thither within the vail the ark of the testimony: and the vail shall divide" (Exodus 26:33), תקח לה שני תרים או שני בני יונה וְהביאָה אותם אל הכהן, "she shall take unto her two turtles, or two young pigeons, and bring them unto the priest" (Leviticus 15:29). — And the ה of the stem before guttural letters has segol in the past, הֶאֱזִין (Deuteronomy 1:45), past, and as against it וְהַאֲזִין: קולי אל אלהים וְהַאֲזִין אלי, "I cried unto God with my voice, and he gave ear unto me" (Psalms 77:2). הֶעביר (Genesis 47:21), past. And as against it: וְהַעברתָּ כל פטר רחם ליי', "That thou shalt set apart unto the Lord all that openeth the matrix" (Exodus 13:12). הֶעמיד (1 Chronicles 6:16), past, and as against it: וְהַעמדתָּ אתו לפני אהרן, "and present them before Aaron" (Numbers 3:6). הֶעתיר, past, and as against it: הנה אנכי יוצא מעמך וְהַעתרתִּי אל יי', "Behold, I go out from thee, and I will intreat the Lord" (Exodus 8:25); and likewise hataf patach in place of hataf segol: הֱשיבות מחרון אפך, "thou hast turned thyself from the fierceness of thine anger" (Psalms 85:4), past, and as against it: וידעת היום וַהֲשֵׁבֹתָ אל לבבך, "Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart" (Deuteronomy 4:29).

The ו that converts the future to the past is vowelled with patach followed by a dagesh: וַיּפְעַל; and before א of the first person singular it has kamatz: וָאֹמַר, וָאָקוּם, וָאַשמיד, וָאֲשברה, וָאֶשקלה, וָאֱהי, וָאֵרא, except: וַאֲכסך [Note: Diqduqei ha-Te'amim, section 71: "סדר קמצות כל העבר על הפקודים ענינו עין מצרי בר מן וַאכסך משי." End quote. And Radak said: "ואכסך משי — the vav has patach, although the sense indicates the past; and like it ואעמוד עליו ואמותתהו."] משי (Ezekiel 16:10), וַאֲמתתהו (2 Samuel 1:10). — If a yod with sheva follows it, the dagesh drops: וַיְדבר, וַיְהי, וַיְבקש, וַיְפיצם, and the like. Its effect also is a shortening of the vowel of the second radical, and together with the shortening a change of the vowel: future יַפְעִיל, and with the converting ו וַיַּפְעֵל: יבדִיל וַיַּבדֵל, יצמִיח וַיַּצמַח, יוצִיא וַיּוצֵא, יבִיא וַיַּבֵא, יָמוּת וַיָּמָת. In some verbs they continued to vowel with the ancient vowel, only shortened: יָקוּם, and with the converting ו וַיָּקֻם, וַיָּקִם; but at a later time they replaced it: ויקָם, ויקֶם, ויסָב, ויסֶך, ויבֶן, ותיטֶב. In the first person singular this shortening is not much practised: ואקוּם, ואקִים, ואשִׁיב, ואוצִיא. In verbs with final ה, for the most part after the converting ו the shortened future is used, with the dropping of the final radical: ויעַש, ויעַל, ויבֶן, ויפֶן, ואשְׁתְּ, ותרֶב, ויתכַּס, וימַּח, ותכַהּ, ויחַר, ויוֹר, ויִיף, וירְא, וידָא, and the like. In the first person singular a הָ is for the most part added at the end: ואתאבלָה, ואבקשָׁה, ואדברָה, ואיחלָה, ואֹכְלָה, ואעברָה, ואקחָה, ואשמרָה, ואשוֵּעָה, ואתנָה, and the like.

The ו that converts the past to the future comes after a verb in the true future: "Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly; twelve princes shall he beget" (Genesis 17:20), "For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have brought down all their nobles" (Isaiah 43:14), "For the tidings; because it cometh: and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be feeble, and every spirit shall faint" (Ezekiel 21:12). — And likewise where the past speaks of an action in the future: "But think on me when it shall be well with thee, and shew kindness, I pray thee, unto me, and make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house" (Genesis 40:14), "But the olive tree said unto them, Should I leave my fatness, wherewith by me they honour God and man, and go to be promoted over the trees?" (Judges 9:9), "as the Lord liveth, I will run after him (that is, I will run), and take somewhat of him" (2 Kings 5:20). — And after the future יִפְעַל: "But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground" (Genesis 2:6), "And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp" (Exodus 33:7), "And that I also have walked contrary unto them, and have brought them into the land of their enemies" (Leviticus 26:41), "And so it was, when the cloud abode from even unto the morning, and that the cloud was taken up in the morning, then they journeyed" (Numbers 9:21), "until the child be weaned, and then I will bring him, that he may appear before the Lord, and there abide for ever" (1 Samuel 1:22), "Moreover his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year" (ibid. 2:19), "yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread" (Isaiah 44:15). — And after יפעל in the sense of the present: "and from thence it (the river) was parted, and became into four heads" (Genesis 2:10), "She put her hand to the nail, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer; and with the hammer she smote Sisera" (Judges 5:26). — And likewise after יפעל in the sense of the imperative: "it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the even" (Leviticus 11:32). — And likewise after an infinitive and a participle: "And when the cloud tarried long upon the tabernacle many days, then the children of Israel kept the charge of the Lord, and journeyed not" (Numbers 9:19), "when any man came nigh to him to do him obeisance, he put forth his hand, and took him, and kissed him" (2 Samuel 15:5), "that cometh into the house of the Lord: and the priests that kept the door put therein all the money that was brought into the house of the Lord" (2 Kings 12:10), "And the priest's custom with the people was, that, when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant came, etc. and he struck it into the pan" (1 Samuel 2:13–14), "Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by En-rogel; and a wench went and told them" (2 Samuel 17:17). — And likewise if the יִפעל itself is omitted: "To morrow is the new moon: and thou shalt be missed" (1 Samuel 20:18), "In the morning, when it is day, we shall kill him" (Judges 16:2), "Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed" (Daniel 8:14). — And likewise after עוֹד מְעַט: "they be almost ready to stone me" (Exodus 17:4), "For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease" (Isaiah 10:25), "Is it not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field" (ibid. 29:17), "yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come" (Jeremiah 51:33), "for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel" (Hosea 1:4). — And after אוּלַי: "if so be the Lord will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out" (Joshua 14:12). — And after פֶּן: "and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever" (Genesis 3:22), "lest some evil take me, and I die" (ibid. 19:19), "Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me" (1 Samuel 31:4). — And after לְמַעַן: "that ye may live, and go in and possess the land" (Deuteronomy 4:1), "and that they may learn, and fear the Lord your God, and observe to do all the words of this law" (ibid. 31:12). — And after a wish: "Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!" (2 Samuel 15:4). — And after an exclamation of anger and curse: "Woe to the rebellious children, saith the Lord, etc. That walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt! Therefore shall the strength of Pharaoh be your shame" (Isaiah 30:1–3), "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm" (Jeremiah 13:5), "Cursed be the man who brought tidings to my father, saying, A man child is born unto thee; making him very glad. And let that man be as the cities which the Lord overthrew" (ibid. 20:15–16). — And likewise after אַשְׁרֵי: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, etc. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Psalms 1:1–3). — And it is found after urging: "Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou; and let it be for a witness between me and thee" (Genesis 31:44), "Come, and let us draw near to one of these places to lodge all night, in Gibeah" (Judges 19:13). — And likewise after an imperative: "And take thou unto thee of all food that is eaten, and thou shalt gather it to thee; and it shall be for food for thee, and for them" (Genesis 6:21), "Now therefore, my son, obey my voice; and arise, flee thou to Laban my brother to Haran; and tarry with him a few days" (ibid. 27:43–44), "Up, follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say unto them, Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?" (ibid. 44:4), "Haste ye, and go up to my father, and say unto him" (ibid. 45:9), "Go, and gather the elders of Israel together" (Exodus 3:16), "Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men" (Judges 4:6), "Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead: and when thou comest thither, look out there Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brethren, and carry him to an inner chamber; then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the Lord, I have anointed thee king over Israel. Then open the door, and flee, and tarry not" (2 Kings 9:1–3). — And so after a future in the sense of an imperative: "And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: and let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven" (Genesis 1:14–15). — And also after an infinitive in the sense of an imperative: "Every man child among you shall be circumcised. And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you" (Genesis 17:10–11), "Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee" (Deuteronomy 31:26), "Go, and say to Hezekiah" (Isaiah 38:5), "Go and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, Return, thou backsliding Israel" (Jeremiah 3:12), "Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah, etc. Then take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them upon the head of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest" (Zechariah 6:10–11). — And after an infinitive in the sense of the future: "Until thy brother's anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him" (Genesis 27:45), "When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools" (Exodus 1:16), "Depart not hence, I pray thee, until I come unto thee, and bring forth my present, and set it before thee" (Judges 6:18), "Until I come and take you away to a land like your own land" (2 Kings 18:32), "But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity" (Ezekiel 18:24), "until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him" (ibid. 21:32). — And very frequently after הִנֵּה: "And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land" (Genesis 28:15), "Behold, there is a place by me, and thou shalt stand upon a rock" (Exodus 33:21), "Behold, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz Zadok's son, and Jonathan Abiathar's son; and by them ye shall send unto me every thing that ye can hear" (2 Samuel 16:36), "Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it" (Amos 8:8). — And with a participle after it with the intent of the future: "And, behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, etc. But with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark" (Genesis 6:17–18), "Behold, I stand here by the well of water; and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water: and let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink" (ibid. 24:13–14), "behold, he cometh forth to meet thee: and when he seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart" (Exodus 4:14), "Behold, the days come, that I will cut off thine arm" (1 Samuel 2:31), "Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house shall be carried" (2 Kings 20:17), "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14), "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised" (Jeremiah 9:24), "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch" (ibid. 23:5), "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah" (ibid. 31:31), "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her" (Hosea 2:16), "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord God, that I will send a famine in the land" (Amos 8:11). — And after הִנְנִי אֶל: "Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, etc. and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand" (Ezekiel 30:22). — And in general after a participle with the intent of the future: "For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy" (Genesis 7:4), "Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed; and thou shalt call his name Isaac: and I will establish my covenant with him" (ibid. 17:19), "I will shake the heavens and the earth; and I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, and I will destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the heathen; and I will overthrow the chariots, and those that ride in them; and the horses and their riders shall come down" (Haggai 2:21–22). — And sometimes after a participle the past with the converting ו has the intent of the present: "shall I cause to bring forth, and shut the womb? saith thy God" (Isaiah 66:9), "These waters issue out toward the east country, and go down into the desert, and go into the sea" (Ezekiel 47:8). — And further, after other words, the past with the converting ו has the intent of present or future: "for the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion" (Genesis 47:22), "And Pharaoh said, Behold, the people of the land now are many, and ye make them rest from their burdens" (Exodus 5:5), "Only the Lord had a delight in thy fathers to love them, etc. Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:15–16), "behold, I have therewith sent Naaman my servant to thee, that thou mayest recover him of his leprosy" (2 Kings 5:6). — And after an oath: "I am the Lord, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you" (Exodus 6:6), "Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the Lord;
