en: [Note: This word, which is called in the Talmud and Midrash the four-letter name, the unique name and the explicit name (see the entry שֵׁםׂ), is pointed in the Bible with two pointings: the one, which is the majority, יְהֹוָה, and the second, with אדני next to it, יְהֶוִֹה. Now the very fact of two alternating pointings for one word gives room to doubt the genuineness of both, and the second pointing testifies of itself that it is not the true pointing of this word, since this is a pointing that is altogether impossible in the grammar of the language. And the tradition handed down for generations, from mouth to mouth, concerning the reading of this word in each of the two pointings confirms and verifies this assumption. For all Jews, without any distinction, read this word not with the letters with which it is written but with the letters of two other words: in the first pointing with the letters of the word אֲדֹנָי, and in its second pointing with the letters of the word אֱלֹהִים. And this reading is ancient, and the masters of the Talmud already mentioned the reading אדני in place of the unique name, and said: “Rabbi Yaakov bar Aḥa said: It is written (the name of God) with yod he and read with alef dalet” (Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 10, 28b); “Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Not like this world is the world to come. In this world it (the name of God) is written with yod he and read with alef dalet, but in the world to come it is all one: it is read with yod he and written with yod he, etc. Rabbi Avina raised a contradiction: It is written ‘This is My name forever (לעלם), and this is My memorial to all generations’ — said the Holy One, blessed be He: Not as I am written am I read; I am written with yod he and I am read with alef dalet” (Babylonian Talmud Pesachim 50a). And the words testify of themselves that R. Yaakov bar Aḥa and ר"ג בר"י and R. Avina are speaking of a thing known and long customary, and not of something that was newly introduced in their time. And earlier still, the Mishnah testifies that the witnesses who testified before a court against a man who had reviled and blasphemed the name of God did not utter the unique name explicitly from their mouths as it is written, but testified with a substitute name: “The blasphemer is not liable until he pronounces the Name explicitly. Said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥah: All day long the witnesses are examined with a substitute name: ‘May Yosi smite Yosi’” (Sanhedrin 7:5); and see the entry כנוי. But here one may perhaps say that because of the blasphemy the witnesses were not permitted to utter the unique name from their mouths. And likewise in the saying of Abba Shaul (Sanhedrin 10:1): “One who pronounces the Name with its letters has no share in the world to come,” there is some room for doubt, because of the differences of opinion of the commentators about the intent of the word ההוגה, about which Rashi and the Tosafot disagreed; and there is likewise room for this doubt in what is said about Rabbi Ḥananiah ben Teradion, upon whom a sentence of burning was decreed because he used to pronounce the Name with its letters (Avodah Zarah 7b). But there is an explicit tradition that only in the Temple did the high priest read the Name as it is written, and only in a low voice, and that the manner of reading the unique name was transmitted only to select individuals: “Ten times the high priest would mention the Name on the Day of Atonement: six with the bull, and three with the goat, and one at the lots. Those near would fall on their faces; those far off would say: Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever. These and those would not move from there until it was concealed from them. ‘This is My name forever (לעולם)’ — ‘This is My name to be hidden (לעלם).’ At first he would say it in a loud voice; when the dissolute increased, he would say it in a low voice. Said Rabbi Tarfon: I was standing among my brothers the priests in the row, and I inclined my ear toward the high priest, and I heard him swallowing it in the chant of the priests. At first it was transmitted to every person; when the dissolute increased, it was transmitted only to the worthy. Shmuel was passing by and heard a Persian cursing his son with it, and he died. He said: The man has gone, and whoever heard, heard. Rabbi Inyani bar Susi went up to Rabbi Ḥanina in Sepphoris. He said: Come, and I will transmit it to you. He brought his son in under the bed, sneezed, and heard his voice. He said: Is this how you behave among yourselves, with trickery? Go — not for you and not for him. A certain physician in Sepphoris said to Rabbi Pinḥas bar Ḥama: Come, and I will transmit it to you. He said to him: I cannot. He said: Why? He said to him: Because I eat tithe, and one who is accustomed to it cannot eat anything from a person” (Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 3, 40d). There is therefore no doubt at all of the genuineness of the tradition itself, that the Jews, already in the time before the Mishnah, ceased to read the explicit name in its form, and read in its place אדני or אלהים. Now the scholars have argued at length about the cause of this strange practice, and the place and time in which this custom began among the Jews. Some of them said that the cause of it was simply the feeling of the holiness of the explicit name and an error in the interpretation of the verse “And he that blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death” (Leviticus 24:16); and some of them said that the original cause was that the gentiles among whom the Jews lived used to blaspheme the name of the God of Israel, and therefore some scholars held that the custom of refraining from pronouncing the explicit name as it is written began outside the Land of Israel, perhaps about four hundred years before the second destruction. In any case, this custom spread everywhere among the Jews. And in the Septuagint translation, where at first they wrote it in some places in Hebrew letters, they afterwards put in its place the Greek word χύρις, that is, lord. Now, as long as the Temple stood and the people heard at least once a year the reading of the unique name when it came out explicitly from the mouth of the high priest, its reading was known among the people, and perhaps for several generations after that in the Land of Israel, perhaps also among non-Jews who had heard it, perhaps from the mouth of the Samaritans, of whom Rabbi Mana testified that when they swore they mentioned the Name as it is written: “Rabbi Mana said: (One who pronounces the Name with its letters is) like those Cutheans who swear” (Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 10, 28b), that is, like these Cutheans who swear. And in Babylonia at any rate the Jews still knew the reading of the Name, as appears from the discussion in the Gemara (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 60a): “For Rabbi Ḥiyya said: One who hears a mention of the Name in this time is not obligated to tear his garment, for if you do not say so, the whole garment would be filled with tears. From whom? If you say from a Jew — are they so unrestrained? Rather, it is obvious, from an idolater; and if it is the unique name, do they know it?” End quote, that is: and if the mention is the unique name, do the idolaters know it? It is evident that Jews still knew the pronunciation at that time. But, with the passing of time, the true reading of this name in its entirety was certainly forgotten, and we have no tradition about it and no valid testimony fit to be relied upon without doubt. Only for the reading of one part of it is there a reading handed down in the mouths of the Jews, and some external hints from foreigners, on the basis of which we can establish its original form with some certainty. For it is a known thing that many personal names are compounded at their beginning or their end with a part of this name, namely the letters יהו, pointed יְהוֹ at the beginning of the name and pointed יָהוּ at its end; and it has already been said above, in the note to these two entries, that there are indications that the original pointing has a yod with sheva. And as for the pointing of the he in this combination in all these compound names, the traditional reading of the Jews and the transcription of these names in Assyrian and Greek agree that it is ḥolam or shuruk, which are one and the same. And there is no doubt that this was the reading of this part also in the complete combination of the holy name of God; for one cannot object and say that in secular names they read this combination with a different pointing in order not to utter the pronunciation of the holy name, for this conjecture is refuted from two sides. First, because these names were current in the mouth of the whole people, by tradition from mouth to mouth, from the time when everyone still pronounced the unique name in its form, and it is impossible to change a received reading of names. And second, because there is no doubt that it was only the four-letter name in its entirety that they refrained from pronouncing as it is written, and not half the name; and this feeling was still alive in the minds of the masters of the Talmud, and they said explicitly: “Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov said: He is not liable until he blesses (that is, blasphemes) the four-letter name, to exclude the two-letter one” (Sanhedrin 60a). We can therefore conclude with almost complete certainty that the first part of the four-letter name was truly read with the pointing יְהוֹ or יְהוּ, both of which are really one reading. What we do not know is: what was the reading of the end of the four-letter name. In its usual pointing in the Bible the vav is vocalized sometimes with kamatz and sometimes with ḥirik, and this alternation itself testifies, as was mentioned at the beginning of this note, that this is not the true pointing of the unique name, but the pointing of the two other words that are read in its place, namely אדני and אלהים, as most scholars have already sensed; and we do not know whether in the true reading of the unique name the vav was vocalized or quiescent, and likewise we do not know whether the final he was weak and quiescent, as it is now in the usual pointing, or was sounded with a mappiq and vocalized with one of the vowels. And the scholars of the nations of the world have already disagreed for hundreds of years about the reading of the unique name, and have debated and argued much over this question. In the second century of the Christian era, the church father Irenaeus (Irenaios) wrote the unique name in Greek ιαου. In the third century of their era Clement (Clemens) wrote ιαουε. Epiphanius, and especially Theodoret (Theodoret) in the fifth century, testified that the Samaritans say Ιαβε. In the book of the apostate rabbi, the Christian priest Raymond Martini (Raymon Martini), called Pugio fidei (The Dagger of Faith), which was composed in the year 1278, the name יהוה is found transcribed from Hebrew into Roman script in this form: Jehova, and it is a transcription of the Hebrew form in the usual pointing. However, it has not been established whether the author himself transcribed it thus, or one of the copyists afterwards. In particular the priest Petrus Galatinus used this form in his book of hostility against the Jews, which he published in the year 1528 in Rome, and since then this use spread in the books of the nations of the world, and Luther and others also used it; and in the dictionaries of the Hebrew language in Latin the name Jehova appears in Forster's dictionary in the year 1556, and close to the year 1700 this use also entered the hymns of the Christian church in German (Dir, dir Jehova will ich singen). In German (Dir, dir Jehova will ich singen). The first who challenged this reading was the Frenchman Le Mercier (Le Mercier, 1570), afterwards especially Drusius (J. Drusius 1604) and others; and in the year 1696 came Le Clerc (le Clerc, Comm. Ex. VI, 3), and after him Reland (Reland de ver. prop. nom. 1707), and they invented out of their own heads a new reading for the unique name, in Hebrew יַהְוֶה and in a foreign tongue Jahveh; and although at first the Christian scholars paid no attention to this conjecture, most of the Christian scholars have held to it with all their strength, especially since the time of Gesenius (Gesenius) and Ewald (E. Ewakd); and they set two principal foundations for this conclusion, namely: the testimony of Theodoret concerning the Samaritans' reading Ιαβε, mentioned above, and grammatical necessity. Now, how far the testimony of Theodoret about the reading of the Samaritans is trustworthy I have not been able to establish. The Samaritans in our time are also very careful not to pronounce the unique name as it is written, and they are very strict about this; and the researcher of the pronunciation of sounds in Hebrew, Mr. Abraham Zvi, took great pains over this, to induce them to pronounce the Name as it is written in his hearing, and they would not; and in their prayer and also in their reading of the Torah they say, in place of the written combination, the word שימא, meaning “the Name.” Only their high priest, at the time of prayer, when he is pure, utters the Name explicitly from his mouth as it is written and in their traditional reading, and Mr. Abraham Zvi has not heard the reading of the high priest to this day. And likewise Mr. David Yellin, the researcher and expert in Samaritan matters, has never heard the reading of the explicit name from the mouth of their high priest. However, in essence the opinion of Mr. Abraham Zvi is that the testimony of Theodoret has a foundation, and nevertheless this reading is no proof at all for the reading that Le Clerc invented and that almost all the moderns have held to. For the Samaritans have no vocal sheva, and they read a vocal sheva at the beginning of a word like pataḥ, and the pronunciation of the letter ה in their mouths is similar to the pronunciation of א, and in some words they pronounce ו like בּ, as the name לוי they pronounce לַבִּי; and although the pronunciation of the ḥolam is preserved among them, and they read it like shuruk, it is possible that this sound was somewhat lightened in the mouth of the high priest and he says יַאבה instead of יַאֹבה. And the scholar Joseph Halévy, in the French journal of Jewish studies (J. Halévy, REJ, IX, 161), already sought to find support for the reading of the Samaritans in the Mishnah itself (Sanhedrin 7:5), in the saying “May Yosi smite (יכה) Yosi,” for the aforementioned scholar conjectured that instead of יכה one should read יבה, and that this is the reading of the Samaritans to which Theodoret testified. But this conjecture cannot explain this obscure saying for us. In any case, this reading of the Samaritans, even if the testimony of Theodoret is trustworthy, cannot decide anything about the reading of the unique name in the mouths of the Jews in the first part of the name, for which there are conclusive proofs that the pointing יְהוֹ is genuine, as brought above. And the segol of the bet in the Samaritans' reading, even if the testimony of Theodoret is trustworthy in this too, proves nothing regarding the Jews' reading of the second part of the unique name, for the Samaritans have no clear and pure pataḥ sound; rather every pataḥ among them tends somewhat toward the sound of segol (testimony of Abraham Zvi and David Yellin); and since they read everything with penultimate stress and the pronunciation of the he has been effaced among them, it is possible that Theodoret heard them reading the combination — וה in the second part of the unique name as בֶּ, even if the Jews read the vav with a pataḥ vowel, or even if the Jews sounded the final he with a mappiq. From all that has been said above we have therefore seen that the first foundation on which the moderns established the reading that Le Clerc invented, namely the reading of the Samaritans according to the testimony of Theodoret, has been shaken and destroyed. There now remains the grammatical foundation. But it too is not as strong as most of the moderns decide. These scholars saw in the name יהוה a verb in the future tense, and relied in this on the name אֶהְיֶה that God revealed to Moses in answer to Moses' question what he should say to the children of Israel when they asked him the name of the God who had sent him to them. And the scholars said that יהוה is a future of the Aramaic root הוה, in place of the Hebrew root היה, and in the grammar of the Hebrew language there is no future verb of the ל"י verbs like the form יְהֹוָה. But even if we assume as a certainty that the unique name is derived from this verb, the form יְהֹוָה is not among the impossibilities; for is it not possible that it is of the פוֹעַל conjugation, whose future is יְפוֹעַל, from which comes משופטי, and perhaps this is also the conjugation of the name יְהֹדָה, from הדה, although Scripture derived it from ידה, perhaps by way of popular word-midrash. And for the kamatz עה"פ too one can find an analogy, as the form תִּכְלָה (1 Kings 17:14). But the whole basis of the assumption that the unique name is derived from the root היה or הוה in this sense is still in doubt, as many researchers have already cast a stone at this assumption. For Scripture itself indeed testified that this name was not known at all to Israel before Moses, and there is also proof of this, that among all the Hebrew personal names before Moses there are no names compounded with the name יהו, except Jochebed, Moses' mother, which is perhaps a different compound. Nevertheless, had the name יהוה itself been newly created then in the sense of the name אהיה, there would have been no reason to change the yod in it to a vav, and its form would have been יהיה. Rather, certainly the name is ancient, and the fact that Israel and the patriarchs did not know it gives room to doubt its Hebrew origin; and some researchers have already said that this was the name of the god of the Midianites and the Kenites, the people of the tribe of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law. And if the origin of this name is not in the Hebrew language, there is no wonder at its form even if it is not exactly according to the grammar of the Hebrew language. And even if we say that its origin is in the Hebrew language or in another language similar to Hebrew, it is hard to suppose that in very ancient times people called God by a name as abstract as the concept of אהיה אשר אהיה. Primitive man called his god by a more concrete, coarser name, and it is close to certain that in the name יהוה too there was at first a concept of some perceptible action of nature, such as a mighty and strong sound and the like, and Moses raised it to the level of the great and lofty concept of אהיה אשר אהיה and sanctified it with the holiness of this abstract idea, but the ancient form itself did not move from its place. And some researchers have already attributed to the name יהוה concepts similar to the aforementioned concept, the hurler of thunder and lightning and the like, and derived it from the Arabic root הויهرى, which is used also in the sense of hurling. And perhaps it is an imitative word for the roaring sound of wind and the like, and the yod at its beginning is not servile at all but radical; and there is in Arabic a quadriliteral verb and noun exactly similar to the four-letter name, namely וַהוַה رٙهرٙۑ, in the sense of a mighty sound like the roar of the lion and the like, and we can posit the pointing יְהֹוָה on the pattern of בְּדֹלַח, חֲנָמָל, סְמָדַר, and the like. And perhaps one can learn the true reading of the end of the name יהוה by analogy with the general name that exists in the Hebrew language for this very concept, namely the name אֱלוֹהַּ. For if we consider these two words we will see that the reading of the first part in both is exactly the same, יְהוֹ like אֱלוֹ, and the final letter in both is ה, and this similarity gives room for the conjecture that the nature and pointing of this final letter were also the same in both; and just as in the one name it is a letter sounded in pronunciation and its vowel is pataḥ, so too in the second name: they read יְהוֹהַּ like אֱלוֹהַּ, and in a foreign transcription Jehoha; and just as the alef of אֱלוֹהַּ is radical, so too the yod of יְהוֹהַּ is perhaps radical. This was the four-letter name, the unique, the explicit, which the Jews refrained from pronouncing in its entirety as it is written and in its true reading. But its first half they pronounced in the composition of secular personal names, at their beginning and at their end; and also as a holy name of God they pronounced this name once a year in the Temple, in the days of the festival of Sukkot, at the time of the circuits with the willows; and concerning the manner of reading the Name in the Temple on that day there has been preserved for us in the Mishnah an almost certain tradition, namely the tradition that Rav Yehudah transmitted (Mishnah Sukkah 1:2), which was cited in the entry והו; and as I proved in the note there, the true explanation of the words of Rabbi Yehudah is according to the nature of the pronunciation of the letter yod and the reading of the vocal sheva before the guttural letters. For although from the transcription of the names compounded with the name יהו in Assyrian and Greek it appears that the yod of יהו in most of these names was read soft and not like א, nevertheless there is no doubt that in essence the yod was read in some words like א, as was explained in the note to the entry י; and likewise there is no doubt that what the early grammarians said about the vocal sheva before guttural letters, that it is pronounced with the sound of the vowel of the guttural letter after it, is not something invented or artificial, for this inclination of the vocal sheva toward the vowel after it existed also in the Canaanite language, even not before guttural letters, and likewise in the pronunciation of Hebrew names in Greek, as סְדוֹם Sodom, and the like (Schr. Phön. Spr. 38). And although in the reading of secular names in the ordinary speech of the Hebrews this inclination of the vocal sheva was not customary in the name יְהוֹ, it appears that in the chanted and drawn-out reading, in holy splendor, the vocal sheva of the yod inclined toward the ḥolam of the he; and since even in the Temple they did not pronounce the whole four-letter name in its entirety except the high priest on the Day of Atonement, therefore the reading of the name יהוה in the verse “Please, יהוה, save us now,” which the congregation recited on that day, was heard as וּהוּ. And see the note to that entry. And the outcome of all this long investigation is: in the pointing יְהֹוָה only the kamatz under the vav is not the true pointing of this letter, but the pointing יְהוֹ is without doubt the ancient, original pointing, like the pointing of אֱלוֹ in the name אֱלוֹהַּ, and there are indications that the whole name יהוה too was read יְהוֹהַּ, Jehoha. The origin of the name has not been established with certainty, but in any case it is a very ancient name, perhaps an imitative word and echo of a roaring sound and the like, of the movements occurring in nature; and Moses made it known to Israel and raised and sanctified it in the abstract and lofty concept אהיה אשר אהיה, and from then on it became for the Jews the personal name of the God of Israel, and afterwards the name of the Maker and Creator of all and the Ruler over all; and they used an abbreviation of it for the composition of personal names. Because of the holiness of this name, the feeling of fear of profaning the holy name by constant use of it began to grow stronger little by little among the people, and therefore more and more they began to be careful about pronouncing it in its entirety as it is written and in its form, until a time came when they did not pronounce it as it is written at all, and said in its place אדני or אלהים; only the high priest in the Temple on the Day of Atonement uttered it explicitly from his mouth in a low voice, and they transmitted it only to the discreet; and in the days of the festival of Sukkot the whole people in the Temple read its first part in a festive, chanted reading, and it sounded as if they were reading וּהוּ.], (יְהֹוָה, יְהֶוִֹה, and with prefixes בַּיהֹוָה, לַיהֹוָה, מֵיהֹוָה), — the personal name of the God of Israel, the Shield of Israel, Maker of all and Ruler over all, German Eigenname des Gottes Israels, French n. pr. du dieu d'Israel, English pr. n. of the supreme god of Israel: “And God spoke to Moses and said to him: I am יְהֹוָה; and I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob as El Shaddai, but by My name יְהֹוָה I was not known to them” (Exodus 6:2). “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: יְהֹוָה, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you” (ibid. 3:15). “Say to the children of Israel: I am יְהֹוָה, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, and I will deliver you from their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments; and I will take you to Me for a people, and I will be to you a God, and you shall know that I am יְהֹוָה your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt; and I will bring you into the land which I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob, and I will give it to you for a heritage: I am יְהֹוָה” (ibid. 6:6–8). “And you shall come, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: יְהֹוָה, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now let us go, we pray you, three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice לַיהֹוָה our God” (ibid. 3:18). “And afterward Moses and Aaron came and said to Pharaoh: Thus says יְהֹוָה, the God of Israel: Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness. And Pharaoh said: Who is יְהֹוָה, that I should hearken to his voice to let Israel go? I do not know יְהֹוָה, and moreover I will not let Israel go” (ibid. 5:1–2). “And יְהֹוָה said to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says יְהֹוָה: Let My people go, that they may serve Me” (ibid. 7:26). “And יְהֹוָה said to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh and speak to him: Thus says יְהֹוָה, the God of the Hebrews: Let My people go” (ibid. 9:1). “And Pharaoh's servants said to him: How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve יְהֹוָה their God, etc. And he (Pharaoh to Moses and Aaron) said to them: Go, serve יְהֹוָה your God” (ibid. 10:7–8). “For thus says יְהֹוָה, the God of Israel: There is a devoted thing in your midst, O Israel” (Joshua 7:13). “Then Joshua built an altar לַיהֹוָה, the God of Israel” (ibid. 8:30). “Because the princes of the congregation had sworn to them בַּיהֹוָה, the God of Israel” (ibid. 9:18). “So now יְהֹוָה, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites from before His people Israel, and should you possess them? Will you not possess that which Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So whomsoever יְהֹוָה our God has dispossessed from before us, them will we possess” (Judges 11:23–24). “Yet I am יְהֹוָה your God from the land of Egypt, and you know no God but Me” (Hosea 13:4). — And Maker of all: “These are the generations of the heaven and of the earth when they were created, in the day that יְהֹוָה God made earth and heaven” (Genesis 2:4). “Then יְהֹוָה God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (ibid. 7). — And the God of lovingkindness, justice and righteousness: “For I am יְהֹוָה who exercises lovingkindness, justice and righteousness in the earth, for in these things I delight, says יְהֹוָה” (Jeremiah 9:23). — And Almighty and Ruler over all: “I יְהֹוָה have spoken it, and will do it” (Ezekiel 22:14). “And I will execute great vengeance upon them (upon the Philistines) with furious rebukes, and they shall know that I am יְהֹוָה, when I lay My vengeance upon them” (ibid. 25:17). “So shall the heavens praise Your wonders, O יְהֹוָה, Your faithfulness also in the assembly of the holy ones” (Psalms 89:6). — יְהֹוָה God of hosts: “I have been very jealous לַיהֹוָה, the God of hosts” (1 Kings 19:10). “But יְהֹוָה, the God of hosts, יְהֹוָה is His memorial” (Hosea 12:6). “For behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel, says יְהֹוָה the God of hosts, and they shall afflict you” (Amos 6:14). “It may be that יְהֹוָה, the God of hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph” (ibid. 5:15). “יְהֹוָה, the God of hosts, is His name” (ibid. 27). “Therefore thus says יְהֹוָה, the God of hosts: Because you speak this word, behold, I will make My words in your mouth fire” (Jeremiah 5:14). “O יְהֹוָה God of hosts, who is a mighty one like You, O Yah?” (Psalms 89:9). — אדני יְהֶוִֹה: “And he (Abraham) said: אדני יְהֶוִֹה, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?” (Genesis 15:8). “אדני יְהֶוִֹה, You have begun to show Your servant Your greatness” (Deuteronomy 3:24). “Who am I, אדני יְהֶוִֹה, and what is my house, that You have brought me thus far?” (2 Samuel 7:18). “Therefore thus says אדני יְהֶוִֹה: Behold, I lay in Zion a stone” (Isaiah 28:16). “אדני יְהֶוִֹה has given me the tongue of them that are taught, that I should know” (ibid. 50:4). “Therefore thus says אדני יְהֶוִֹה: An adversary, even round about the land” (Amos 3:11). “Ah, אדני יְהֶוִֹה! Behold, You have made the heaven and the earth by Your great power” (Jeremiah 32:17). “Thus says אדני יְהֶוִֹה: This is Jerusalem; I have set her in the midst of the nations” (Ezekiel 5:5). “As I live, says אדני יְהֶוִֹה, you shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel” (ibid. 18:3). — ואדני יְהֶוִֹה: “For ואדני יְהֶוִֹה of hosts is He that touches the land and it melts” (Amos 9:5). “For ואדני יְהֶוִֹה will help me; therefore I have not been confounded” (Isaiah 50:7). “And ואדני יְהֶוִֹה will blow the horn, and will go with whirlwinds of the south” (Zechariah 9:14). — שֶׁיְהֹוָה: “Happy is the people that is in such a case; happy is the people שֶׁיְהֹוָה is their God” (Psalms 144:15). — And with מ before יְהֹוָה, מֵיְהֹוָה: “Is anything too hard מֵיְהֹוָה? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah shall have a son” (Genesis 18:14). “My way is hid מֵיְהֹוָה, and my right is passed over from my God” (Isaiah 40:27). “Yea, her prophets find no vision מֵיְהֹוָה” (Lamentations 2:9). — And בגד כפת after it have dagesh, as is the rule after the syllable -נָי: “Behold, there is the feast of יְהֹוָה בּשלו” (Judges 21:19). “So יְהֹוָה sent דּבר in Israel” (2 Samuel 24:15). “Therefore is the anger of יְהֹוָה kindled בּעמו” (Isaiah 5:25). — And the drawing back of the accent from the final syllable before it, as is the rule before a guttural letter[Note: R. Elijah Baḥur in his notes to the Mikhlol, שדה"פ, the verb שוב.]: “קומָֽה יְהֹוָה, and let Your enemies be scattered” (Numbers 10:35). “קומָה יְהֹוָה; save me, O my God” (Psalms 3:8). “קומָה יְהֹוָה in Your anger; lift up Yourself against the rage of my adversaries” (ibid. 7:7). “קומָה יְהֹוָה; let not man prevail” (ibid. 9:20). “שובָה יְהֹוָה to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel” (Numbers 10:36). “שובָה יְהֹוָה, deliver my soul” (Psalms 6:5). “שׁוּבָה יְהֹוָה; how long?” (ibid. 90:13). “שׁוּבָה יְהֹוָה our captivity” (ibid. 126:4). — *And in construct with another word, used like אֱלֹהֵי, יהוה משפט, יהוה תשלומות: “Give to the Most High according as He has given to you, and with a good eye, as your hand has found; for He is יהוה תשלומות, and He will repay you sevenfold. Do not offer a bribe, for He will not take it, and do not trust in a sacrifice of oppression, for He is יהוה משפט, and with Him there is no respect of persons” (Ben Sira, Genizah, 32:12–14).

he: בכנענ' יובל-איל. וכבר אמרו בגמ' (ר"ה כו.): מאי משמע דהאי יובלא לישנא דדכרא הוא דתניא אמר ר' עקיבא כשהלכתי לערביא היו קורין לדכרא יובלא. ע"כ. והנה בערב' העתיקה והחדשה אין שם זה להאיל. אבל, שם זה היה נהוג אצל הפונים באפריקה כמו שנראה ברור בהכתבת הפונית על לוח אבן השמורה בבית הנכת במרשליה שרשומים בה כמה צריך אדם לתת להכהן אם רוצה האדם להעלות קרבן או מנחה, וכתוב שם בשורה ז בזה הלשון: ביבל אם בעז כלל אם צועת אם שלם כלל לכהנם כסף שקל, ע"כ, ובעבר': בעד יובל (ר"ל איל) או עז אם עולה או זבח או שלמים להכהנים כסף שקל. ואולי הגרסה האמתית היא במקום שהלכתי לערביא, כשהלכתי לכרכי הים, עי' ד"ס, והכונה היא לקרתא חדתא, וכדומה. לפי דעת קניג (Kö. 2,105) יובל פרושו המוליך, ההולך בראש. וקצת קשה למה דוקא בענין השופר השתמשו בהשם יובל ולא בשמות אחרים, אם לא שהיובל הוא מין איל מיוחד שיש לו קרנים מיוחדות עלולות לכלי תקיעה., יֹבֵל, ש"ז, מ"ר יוֹבְלִים, — א) אַיִל, Widder; bélier; ram: וביום השביעי תסבו את העיר שבע פעמים והכהנים יתקעו בשופרות והיה במשך בקרן הַיּוֹבֵל בשמעכם את קול השופר יריעו כל העם תרועה גדולה (יהוש' ו ד-ה).  ושבעה כהנים ישאו שבעה שופרות יוֹבְלִים לפני ארון יי' (שס ו).  ושבעה הכהנים נשאים שבעה שופרות הַיּוֹבְלִים לפני יי' עברו ותקעו בשופרות (שס ה).  — ובהרחבה, עצם קרן היובל, ונרדף עם שופר: במשך הַיֹּבֵל המה יעלו בהר (שמות יח יג).  — ב) שנת היּוֹבֵל, שנת החמשים של עבודה בשדה בארץ ישראל שנועדה להיות שנת שבתון ודרור לכל העם, והיו מכריזים את תחלת השנה הזאת בתקיעה בשופר של יוֹבֵל, Jubeljahr; jubilé; -lee: וספרת לך שבע שבתת שנים שבע פעמים והיו לך ימי שבע שבתת השנים תשע וארבעים שנה והעברת שופר תרועה בחדש השבעי בעשר לחדש וכו' וקדשתם את שנת החמשים שנה וקראתם דרור בארץ לכל ישביה יוֹבֵל הוא תהיה לכם ושבתם איש אל אחזתו ואיש אל משפחתו תשבו יוֹבֵל הוא שנת החמשים שנה תהיה לכם לא תזרעו ולא תקצרו את ספיחיה ולא תבצרו את נזריה כי יוֹבֵל הוא קדש תהיה לכם (ויקר' כה ח-יב).  ואם לא יגאל באלה ויצא בשנת הַיֹּבֵל הוא ובניו עמו (שס נד).  — ובתו"מ: שוה היובל לראש השנה לתקיעה ולברכות (ר"ה ג ה).  — ומ"ר * יוֹבְלוֹת: באחד בתשרי ראש השנה לשנים ולשמיטין וליובלות לנטיעה ולירקות (ר"ה א א).  ר' יהודה אומר בר"ה תוקעין בשל זכרים וביובלות בשל יעלים (שס ג ה). שבעה עשר יובלות מנו ישראל משנכנסו לארץ ועד שיצאו (ערכ' יב:).  מאימתי פסקו היובלות משעלה פול מלך אשור ותגלת פלנאסר מלך אשור והגלה לראובני ולגדי ולחצי שבט המנשי (מס' עבדים א).  — ואמר המשורר: אהי כעבד לא חֻפש לא אשאלה עוד יובלי, עד מה יריבו תבעיו מאס לבבי מוסרי (ר"י הלוי, לבי שני אורים).
en: [Note: In Canaanite/Phoenician יובל = ram. And they already said in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 26a): “How do we know that this יובלא is a word for a ram? For it was taught: Rabbi Akiva said, When I went to Arabia they called a ram יובלא.” End quote. Now in Arabic, ancient and modern, there is no such name for the ram. But this name was in use among the Phoenicians in Africa, as is clearly seen in the Punic inscription on a stone tablet kept in the museum in Marseille, on which is recorded how much a person must give the priest if he wishes to offer a sacrifice or a meal-offering, and it is written there in line 7 in these words: ביבל אם בעז כלל אם צועת אם שלם כלל לכהנם כסף שקל, end quote, and in Hebrew: “for a יובל (that is, a ram) or a goat, whether a burnt-offering or a sacrifice or peace-offerings, to the priests a shekel of silver.” And perhaps the true reading, instead of “when I went to Arabia,” is “when I went to the cities by the sea,” see Dikdukei Soferim, and the meaning is Carthage (קרתא חדתא), and the like. According to König (Kö. 2,105) יובל means the one who leads, the one who goes at the head. And it is somewhat difficult why specifically in connection with the shofar they used the name יובל and not other names, unless the יובל is a special kind of ram that has special horns suited to a blowing instrument.] יֹבֵל, masculine noun, plural יוֹבְלִים, — a) ram, German Widder; French bélier; English ram: “And on the seventh day you shall go around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow with the shofars. And it shall be, when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the shofar, all the people shall shout with a great shout” (Joshua 6:4-5). “And let seven priests bear seven shofars of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD” (ibid. 6). “And the seven priests bearing the seven shofars of rams' horns before the LORD passed on and blew with the shofars” (ibid. 5). — And by extension, the ram's horn itself, synonymous with shofar: “When the ram's horn sounds long, they shall come up to the mount” (Exodus 18:13). — b) the Jubilee year (שנת היּוֹבֵל), the fiftieth year of working the fields in the Land of Israel, which was designated to be a year of solemn rest and liberty for all the people, and they would proclaim the beginning of this year with the blowing of a shofar of יוֹבֵל, German Jubeljahr; French jubilé; English -lee: “And you shall count for yourself seven sabbaths of years, seven times seven years, and the days of the seven sabbaths of years shall be to you forty-nine years. Then you shall sound the shofar of blasting in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month, etc. And you shall hallow the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants; it shall be a jubilee to you, and you shall return every man to his possession, and every man to his family you shall return. A jubilee shall that fiftieth year be to you; you shall not sow, nor reap what grows of itself in it, nor gather the grapes of its untended vines. For it is a jubilee; it shall be holy to you” (Leviticus 25:8-12). “And if he is not redeemed by these, he shall go out in the year of the jubilee, he and his children with him” (ibid. 54). — And in the Talmud and Midrash: “The Jubilee is like Rosh Hashanah with regard to the blowing and the blessings” (Rosh Hashanah 3:5). — And plural *יוֹבְלוֹת: “On the first of Tishri is the new year for years, for sabbatical years and for Jubilees, for planting and for vegetables” (Rosh Hashanah 1:1). “Rabbi Judah says: On Rosh Hashanah they blow with those of males, and on the Jubilees with those of ibexes” (ibid. 3:5). “Seventeen Jubilees Israel counted from when they entered the land until they went out” (Arakhin 12b). “From when did the Jubilees cease? From when Pul king of Assyria and Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came up and exiled the Reubenites and the Gadites and half the tribe of Manasseh” (Tractate Avadim 1). — And the poet said: “Shall I be like a slave not set free — shall I no longer ask for my jubilee? How long will its claimants contend? My heart has spurned my chastisement” (Rabbi Judah Halevi, Libbi Shenei Orim).

he: *קריאת הספרדים, וסמך לקריאה זו שמה של אות זו ביונית yota. והאשכנזים קוראים יוּּד, וכן הסורים (Nö. Syr. Gram. §9). והנה החליטו רוב החדשים כי משמ' השם הזה הוא יָד, ואמרו כי צורתה של אות זו בכתב העברי הקדום היא כצורת יד, ונשתנה קול הפתח הארוך לקול חולם, כנהוג. אך קצת קשה, יען ברוב שמות אותיות האלף בית ראינו כי השם נשאר בפי כל היהודים בצורתו הקדומה וגם הברת התנועה נשארה בקדמותה, עי' הערה לשם אות אַלף, בֵּית, ובפרט בשם כל כך רגיל בפי העם כמו יד, קשה להניח, כי הוא נשתנה דוקא בשם האות, אעפ"י שהשם כף נשתנה בפי האשכנז' וכמו"כ בפי הסורים לקול החולם (נלד' שם). ואולי היו לפנים שני משקלים גם לשם אבר האחיזה, יָד ויוֹד, כמו שאין ספק בדבר שמלבד השם יוֹם היה עוד שם יָם שממנו מ"ר יָמִים, עי' זה הערך, ופשט השמוש בהשם יד ונשאר השם יוד רק בשם האות., ש"נ, מ"ר יוֹדִים, יוֹדִין, —  שֵׁם האות העשירית באלף בית העברית:  חמורים העריות שהוא פותח בהן ביוד הא וחותם ביוד הא (ספרא, אחרי קלז).  מה להלן שבועה אף כאן שבועה מה להלן ביוד הא אף כאן ביוד הא (מכי' משפט' טו).  מם יוד מם מים (ירוש' שביע' א לג:).  בשתי אותיות נבראו שתי עולמות העולם הזה והעולם הבא אחד בהא ואחד ביוד וכו' מה יוד כפוף כך יהיו כל באי העולם כפופין (שם חגי' ב עז ג).  העולם הזה נכתב (שמו של אלהים) ביוד הי ונקרא באלף דלת אבל לעולם הבא כולו אחד נקרא ביוד הא ונכתב ביוד הא (פסח' נ.).  יוד שנטלתי משרי עומד וצווח כמה שנים עד שבא יהושע והוספתי לו (סנה' קז.).  אין אנו יודעין אם העוה"ז נברא בהא והעוה"ב ביוד או אם העוה"ז נברא ביוד והעוה"ב בהא (מד"ר בראש' יב).  אמר ר"י בן קרחה יוד שנטל הקב"ה משרי נחלקו חציו לשרה וחציו לאברהם (שם מז).  באותה שעה עלה יוד שבירבה ונשתטחה לפני הקב"ה ואומר רבון העולם לא כך אמרת אין אות בטלה מן התורה לעולם (שם שמות ו).  שלמה בטל ומאה כיוצא בו ויוד ממך אינה בטילה לעולם (שם ויקר' יט).  אם מתכנשין כל באי עולם לעקור יוד שהוא קטן האותיות שבתורה אינן יכולין (שם שה"ש, ראשו כתם).  שכן דרכו של נער להיות כותב יוד (שם איכ', לא האמינו). —  ובכנ':  ולא נאמר שיתכן היותו כמו ויבשהו מן ולא ייחל לבני אדם בעבור שהיוד ממנו קמוצה כי אלו היה משפטו מה שזכר ר' יהודה היתה יודו פתוחה כמו שהוא ולא ייחל לבני אדם (השרש' לריב"ג, חול). —  ומ"ר:  כתב לאלפים עיינים וכו' לווים יודים וליודים ווין לזיינין נונים ולנונים זיינים (ספרי ואתחנן לו).  שלא יכתוב אלפין עיינין וכו' ווין יודין יודין ווין (שבת קג:). —  ומצוי מאד בספרות, ואמר המליץ:  והחביר יוד יקר, ויגע עיקר, ולו היטב חקר, מצאם נעדרים, בנאמני עדים, אשר הם מגידים, שניהם היודים, לעת מקרה סרים (תשו' תלמ' דונש 82). —  ומ"ר יודות:  יא יודות שבתורה (אדר"נ נוסח' ב לח).  יהיה בה שלש יודות יוד העתיד ויוד הפעל ויוד המשיכה (הור' הקור' 24). —  °וראשי האלף:  כגון שנגעו יודי הא' בגוף האלף בין אותם שלמעלה בין אותם שלמטה (הלבוש או"ח לב כה).
en: [Note: *The pronunciation of the Sephardim, and a support for this pronunciation is the name of this letter in Greek, yota. And the Ashkenazim pronounce it יוּּד, and so do the Syrians (Nö. Syr. Gram. §9). Now most of the moderns have decided that the meaning of this name is יָד "hand", and they said that the shape of this letter in the ancient Hebrew script is like the shape of a hand, and the sound of the long patach changed to the sound of cholam, as is usual. But it is somewhat difficult, since in most of the names of the letters of the alphabet we have seen that the name remained in the mouth of all Jews in its ancient form, and the pronunciation of the vowel also remained in its original state, see the note to the name of the letter אַלף, בֵּית; and in particular, with a name so common in the mouth of the people as יד, it is hard to assume that it changed precisely in the name of the letter, even though the name כף changed in the mouth of the Ashkenazim, and likewise in the mouth of the Syrians, to the sound of cholam (Nöldeke, ibid.). And perhaps there were formerly two patterns also for the name of the limb of grasping, יָד and יוֹד, just as there is no doubt that besides the noun יוֹם there was also a noun יָם, from which the plural יָמִים, see that entry; and the use of the noun יד spread, and the noun יוד remained only in the name of the letter.], feminine noun, plural יוֹדִים, יוֹדִין, — the name of the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet: "Grave are the forbidden relations, for He opens them with yod-he and closes them with yod-he" (Sifra, Acharei 137). "Just as there it is an oath, so here it is an oath; just as there it is with yod-he, so here it is with yod-he" (Mekhilta, Mishpatim 15). "mem yod mem — מים" (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 1, 33b). "With two letters two worlds were created, this world and the world to come, one with he and one with yod, etc. Just as the yod is bent, so all who come into the world will be bent" (ibid. Chagigah 2, 77, col. 3). "In this world (the name of God) is written with yod-he and read with aleph-dalet, but in the world to come it will be entirely one: read with yod-he and written with yod-he" (Pesachim 50a). "The yod that I took from Sarai stood and cried out for many years, until Joshua came and I added it to him" (Sanhedrin 107a). "We do not know whether this world was created with he and the world to come with yod, or whether this world was created with yod and the world to come with he" (Genesis Rabbah 12). "R. Joshua ben Korcha said: The yod that the Holy One, blessed be He, took from Sarai was divided — half of it to Sarah and half of it to Abraham" (ibid. 47). "At that moment the yod of ירבה went up and prostrated itself before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said: Master of the world, did You not say thus, no letter shall ever be abolished from the Torah?" (ibid., Exodus Rabbah 6). "Solomon and a hundred like him will be abolished, but a yod of yours will never be abolished" (ibid., Leviticus Rabbah 19). "If all who come into the world gathered to uproot a yod, which is the smallest of the letters in the Torah, they would not be able" (ibid., Song of Songs Rabbah, "ראשו כתם"). "For such is the way of a youth, to write a yod" (ibid., Lamentations Rabbah, "לא האמינו"). — And with suffixes: "And we shall not say that it could be like ויבשהו from ולא ייחל לבני אדם, because its yod has kamatz; for if its rule were what R. Judah mentioned, its yod would have patach, as in ולא ייחל לבני אדם" (Sefer ha-Shorashim by Ibn Janach, חול). — And the plural: "If he wrote alephs as ayins, etc., vavs as yods and yods as vavs, zayins as nuns and nuns as zayins" (Sifre, Va-etchanan 36). "that he should not write alephs as ayins, etc., vavs as yods, yods as vavs" (Shabbat 103b). — And it is very frequent in the literature, and the writer said: "And he joined a precious yod, and labored over a root; had he investigated well, he would have found them missing, by trustworthy witnesses, who declare that both yods depart at times" (Responses of the Students of Dunash 82). — And the plural יודות: "eleven yods that are in the Torah" (Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version B, 38). "It will have three yods: the yod of the future, and the yod of the verb, and the yod of prolongation" (Horayat ha-Kore 24). — °And the tips of the aleph: "such as when the yods of the aleph touched the body of the aleph, whether those above or those below" (Ha-Levush, Orach Chayim 32:25).

הסתכל בו ענה לו לא אוכל א"ל השֶׁמש שהוא אחד משמשיו העומדים לפני הקב"ה אינך יכול להסתכל בו שכינה לא כש"כ, — ועוד: לשייפיה מישחא ולוקמיה להדי יומא שבת קלד., ר"ל ויעמידו נגד השֶׁמֶשׁ. והגשמים והנפש בשעה שהיא יוצאה מן הגוף היום מנין א"ר יהודה את סבור שהוא שף ברקיע ואינו אלא כמסר הזה שהוא נוסר בעץ מד"ר בראש' ו.

אוֹר. — בין השׁמָשׁות. — בֹּקֶר. — חֹדֶשׁ. — חַמָּה. — יוֹם, יום הראשון בשבוע, יום השני, וכו', יום א', יום ב', וכו', שבת, הוא יום השביעי בכל שבוע. — °יוֹמִי. — יוֹמָם.  — יָמִים. — יֶרַח.  — *לוּח, שרשומים בו הימים לפי השבועות והשנים. — לָיִל, עי"ש. — מחר, תמול, שִׁלְשֹׁם.  — נָטָה, נטה היום.  — עֶרֶב, ערב החג וכדומה. — ערבָים, בין הערבָים.  — *ערבית.  — עת, *מעת לעת.  — צהרים.  — °צפר.  — *צַפְרָה.  — שָׁבוּעַ.  — *שחרית. שׁכם, הִשְׁכִּים.  — שֶׁמֶשׁ.  — שָׁנָה.
en: [Note: A word common to all the Semitic languages. In Canaanite ים, in Aramaic יום, in Arabic יומ يوم, in South Arabian יומ and also ימ. In Assyrian אִמֻּ in the sense of the time when the sun shines on the earth, in contrast to the night, and אוּמֻ in the general sense of the measure of time. The early authorities already found difficulty in the matter of the plural and the construct, which do not follow the singular. Ibn Janah said, and these are his words: ואו יום אנקלבת אלפא לינה פי ימים פי אללפט' וד'לב אנ אלאצל פי יום אנ יכונ עלי זנה חדש שרש ישי בקר אערך לך ותגזר אמר פאלאנוא אלואו מנה אשתת'קאלא מנהמ לתחריכהא פלמא אלאנוהא אג'תמע שאכנאנ לינאנ ואו אלמדּ וואו אלאצל פחד'פוא ואו אלמדּ ובקי ואו אלאצל וכאן אלאצל פי ימים איצ'א אנ יכונ יומים עלי אלאצל בתחריב אלואו בקמץ גדול עלי זנה לבקרים אצמית פלמא אלאנוה פי אלואחד אלאנוה איצ'א פי אלג'מע לא שׂימא אנ אלג'מע את'קל מנ אלואחד פלמא לאנ ואו יומים נקלת חרכתה והי אלקמצות אלי אליא' ללדאלה עליה פאנקלב אלואו אללינ אלפא וצאר ימים וכו' ולמא אצ'אפוא ימים אלא אלאשמא' אלט'אהרה ח'אלפוא בה הד'ה אלאלפאט' פאשקטוא מנה אלאלפ אללינה, וקאלוא ימי יעקב כל ימי היות דוד במצודה פאג'חפוא בה כמא תרי ולמ יפעלוא בד'לב פי ראשים ולא פי בתים אד' קאלוא ראשי אלפי ישראל ובתי החצרים וע'ירה, end of quote, and in Hebrew: "The vav of יום changed into a quiescent alef in ימים in pronunciation, and their original form was to be on the pattern of חדש שרש ישי בקר אערך לך ותגזר אמר; and they made the vav in it quiescent because it was heavy for them to vocalize it, and when they made it quiescent two quiescent letters came together, the vav of the root and the vav of prolongation, and they dropped the vav of prolongation and the vav of the root remained. And the original form of ימים too was to be יומים according to the root, with the vav vocalized with kamatz gadol, on the pattern of לבקרים אצמית כל רשעי ארץ; and when they made it quiescent in the singular they made it quiescent also in the plural, all the more so since its plural is heavier than the singular. And since the vav of יומים became quiescent, its vowel, which is the kamatz, was moved to the yod to indicate it, and the quiescent vav changed into an alef and it became ימים, etc. And when ימים is put in construct with explicit nouns its usage changes and the quiescent alef drops from it, as they said ימי יעקב, כל ימי היות דוד במצודה; and they did not do so with ראשים nor with בתים, as they said ראשי אלפי ישראל and בתי החצרים, and others." And likewise Radak: "And the plural is ימים, plural, and the quiescent letter that was with the cholam in the word יום became kamatz gadol in the plural, and likewise ראש ראשים; but in construct the quiescent letter is lost, which is not so with ראשים, for the quiescent letter is written in it: כל ימי אשר ישכון הענן." End of quote. But most of the moderns agreed that there were two patterns: יום, and from it was the plural יומים, as in Aramaic, and perhaps it was preserved from it also in Hebrew in the Midrash, in the expression מה יום מיומים (see below), but in general this plural form went out of use; and also ים, and from it the plural ימים, and it is this that prevailed and spread in the language, perhaps because of the similarity with שנים; and perhaps there was also the pattern ימם in the singular, and so in Canaanite: בימם ו' לירח בל ("on day 6 of the month Bul") (CIS No 10), בימם יד לירח מרפא ("on day 14 of the month Marpe") (ibid., No 88), בימם ז' לירח י' ("on day 7 of the month י'") (ibid., No 93); and some say that from this also in Hebrew יומם, see that entry. In any case the construct plural ימי is from the singular ים. And there are indications that there was yet a third form ימה, and from it the plural and construct יְמות.], masculine noun, plural יָמִים, יָמִין, construct יְמֵי, יְמוֹת, with suffixes יוֹמִי, יוֹמְךָ,יוֹמוֹ, יָמַי, יָמָי, יָמֶיךָ, יָמַיִךְ, יָמֵינוּ, יְמֵיכֶם, dual יוֹמַיִם, — The time when the sun shines on the earth and on those who dwell on it, the opposite of night, Tag; jour; day: "And God called the light day, and the darkness He called night" (Genesis 1:5). "And God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars" (ibid. 16). "And summer and winter and day and night shall not cease" (ibid. 8:22). "Whether stolen by day or stolen by night" (ibid. 31:39). "And the Lord drove an east wind over the land all that day and all the night" (Exodus 10:13). "They were by Jebus, and the day was far spent" (Judges 19:11). "That Your eyes may be open toward this house night and day" (I Kings 8:29). "A day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness" (Joel 2:2). "I the Lord guard it, I water it every moment; lest any harm it, I guard it night and day" (Isaiah 27:3). "That in the night they may be a guard to us, and labor in the day" (Nehemiah 4:16). "Yours is the day, Yours also the night; You have established the light and the sun" (Psalms 74:16). "And the night shines as the day" (ibid. 139:12). — And the measure of time of the day alone, or of day and night together: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day" (Genesis 1:5). "And there was evening and there was morning, a second day" (ibid. 8). "The children are tender, and the flocks and herds giving suck are a care to me; and if they overdrive them one day, all the flocks will die" (ibid. 33:13). "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes" (ibid. 22:4). "But the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:10). — מַחֲצִית היום, midday: "And he read in it (in the book of the Torah), etc., from early morning until midday" (Nehemiah 8:3). "And they read in the book of the Torah of the Lord their God a fourth part of the day" (ibid. 9:3). — יוֹם יוֹם, that is to say, every day: "And as she spoke to Joseph day by day, he did not listen to her" (Genesis 39:10). "And on the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather day by day" (Exodus 16:5). "Yet they seek Me daily, and delight to know My ways" (Isaiah 58:2). "Blessed is the Lord, day by day He bears our burden" (Psalms 68:20). "Then I was by Him as a nursling, and I was daily His delight, playing always before Him" (Proverbs 8:30). "Happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors" (ibid. 34). — יוֹם וָיוֹם, likewise in this sense: "And every day Mordecai walked before the court of the women's house" (Esther 2:11). "Now when they spoke to him day by day, and he did not listen to them" (ibid. 3:4). — And יום בְּיוֹם: "And they kept the feast of Tabernacles, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt-offerings by number" (Ezra 3:4). "And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read in the book of the Torah of God" (Nehemiah 8:18). "And the children of Israel that were present at Jerusalem kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness, and the Levites and the priests praised the Lord day by day" (II Chronicles 30:21). "Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance" (ibid. 24:11). — כְּיוֹם בְּיוֹם, as on every day: "And David played with his hand, as day by day; and Saul had his spear in his hand" (I Samuel 18:10). — יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ, on each fixed day, according to what was fixed for that day: "And the taskmasters were urgent, saying: Fulfill your work, each day's task in its day, as when there was straw" (Exodus 5:13). "You shall not diminish anything from your bricks, each day's task in its day" (ibid. 19). "To bring an offering made by fire to the Lord, a burnt-offering and a meal-offering, a sacrifice and drink-offerings, each on its own day" (Leviticus 23:37). "That He maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as each day may require" (I Kings 8:59). "And for his allowance there was a continual allowance given him by the king, every day a portion, all the days of his life" (II Kings 25:30). "And a settled provision for the singers, as every day required" (Nehemiah 11:23). "And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah gave the portions of the singers and the porters, as every day required" (ibid. 12:47). "And the king appointed for them a daily portion of the king's food" (Daniel 1:5). "To praise and to minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required" (II Chronicles 8:14). — יוֹם אחד, on one of the days, one day: "And David said in his heart: I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul; there is nothing better for me than that I should escape into the land of the Philistines" (I Samuel 27:1). — And in construct with other nouns, to define the nature of the day spoken of; יום השבת, the Sabbath day: "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy" (Exodus 20:8). — יום כפֻרים, Day of Atonement: "For it is a day of atonement, to make atonement for you" (Leviticus 23:28). — יום תרועה, day of blowing the horn: "You shall do no manner of servile work; it is a day of blowing the horn to you" (Numbers 29:1). — יום השֶׁלג, day of snow: "And he went down and slew the lion in the midst of the pit on the day of snow" (II Samuel 23:20). — יום הקציר, day of harvest: "As the cold of snow on the day of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him" (Proverbs 25:13). — יום קרה, cold day: "As one who takes off a garment on a cold day" (ibid. 20). — יום צרה, day of trouble: "Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of trouble and of rebuke and of contempt" (II Kings 19:3). — And in the sense of the time when something happened: "Behold now, I am old, I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). "But if the cloud was not taken up, then they did not journey until the day that it was taken up" (Exodus 40:37). "You shall not shout nor let your voice be heard, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth, until the day I tell you: Shout; then you shall shout" (Joshua 10:10). "He and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day [Note: The vav is missing in the printed source. Note of Project Ben-Yehuda.] of the captivity of the land" (Judges 18:30). "So Jeremiah abode in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken" (Jeremiah 38:28). "A very grievous hail, such as has not been in Egypt since the day it was founded until now" (Exodus 9:18). "Since the day that God created man upon the earth" (Deuteronomy 4:32). "From the day that you went out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place" (ibid. 9:7). "On the day that the Lord God made earth and heaven" (Genesis 2:4). "On the day that I smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt" (Numbers 3:13). "On the day we came forth to go to you" (Joshua 9:12). "For You have been my high tower and a refuge in the day of my distress" (Psalms 59:17). — יוֹם of so-and-so, on which so-and-so did or will do some thing: "Howl, for the day of the Lord is at hand; as destruction from the Almighty shall it come" (Isaiah 13:6), the day on which God will reveal His power and His might, on which He will do miracles and wonders, and the like. "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, and with wrath and fierce anger, to make the earth a desolation" (ibid. 9). "Woe to you who desire the day of the Lord! Why would you have the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light" (Amos 5:18). "Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the Lord comes, for it is near" (Joel 2:1). "Hold your peace at the presence of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is at hand; for the Lord has prepared a sacrifice, He has consecrated His guests" (Zephaniah 1:7). "To stand in the battle on the day of the Lord" (Ezekiel 13:5). "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord" (Malachi 3:23). — יום מִדְיָן, the day on which there was the war with Midian: "For the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, You have broken as in the day of Midian" (Isaiah 9:3). — יוֹם יזרעאל, the day on which the people will gather in this place: "And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint themselves one head, and shall go up out of the land; for great shall be the day of Jezreel" (Hosea 2:2). — יוֹם ירושלם: "Remember, O Lord, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said: Raze it, raze it, even to its foundation" (Psalms 137:7), that is, the day of its destruction, in which they took part. — And יוֹם alone, in the sense of a day of trouble: "But you should not have gazed on the day of your brother, on the day of his disaster, neither should you have rejoiced over the children of Judah on the day of their destruction, neither should you have spoken proudly on the day of distress" (Obadiah 1:12). "He shall have neither son nor grandson among his people (the wicked), nor any remaining in his dwellings. They that come after shall be astonished at his day, as they that went before were seized with horror" (Job 18:19-20). — And in the sense of the day fixed for his death, or for his being punished with some punishment: "For the day of their calamity is at hand" (Deuteronomy 32:35). "And David said: As the Lord lives, the Lord shall smite him, or his day shall come to die" (I Samuel 26:10). "They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the Lord was a stay to me" (II Samuel 22:19). "Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their visitation" (Jeremiah 50:27). "And you, O wicked one, that are to be slain, the prince of Israel, whose day has come, in the time of the iniquity of the end" (Ezekiel 21:30). "The slain wicked, whose day has come, in the time of the iniquity of the end" (ibid. 34). "The Lord laughs at him, for He sees that his day is coming" (Psalms 57:13). — And Ben Sira said: "Do not envy a wicked man, for you do not know what his day will be" (Ben Sira, Genizah 9:11). — בְּלֹא יוֹמוֹ, before the fixed, proper and usual time to die, and the like: "It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green" (Job 15:32). — And in the sense of the day of a person's birth, and in general his birth, his fate, his life, and the like: "After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day. And Job spoke and said: Let the day perish on which I was born" (ibid. 3:1-3). — And יוֹם in the sense of fortune: "Did I not weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy?" (ibid. 30:25). — הַיּוֹם, instead of "this day", the present one, heute; aujourd'hui; to day : "Behold, You have driven me out this day from the face of the land" (Genesis 4:14). "Neither did I hear of it until today" (ibid. 21:26). "And I came this day to the fountain" (ibid. 24:42). "I will pass through all your flock today, removing from there every speckled and spotted sheep" (ibid. 30:32). "This heap is witness between me and you this day" (ibid. 31:48). "Why do you look so sad today?" (ibid. 40:7). "I make mention of my faults this day" (ibid. 41:9). "One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father" (ibid. 42:32). "Behold, I have bought you this day and your land for Pharaoh" (ibid. 47:23). "And he said: How is it that you have come so soon today?" (Exodus 2:18). "Why have you not fulfilled your appointed task in making brick both yesterday and today, as before?" (ibid. 5:14). "This day you go forth in the month Aviv" (ibid. 13:4). "Stand still and see the salvation of the Lord, which He will work for you today; for the Egyptians whom you have seen today, you shall see them again no more forever" (ibid. 14:13). "And Moses said: Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord; today you shall not find it in the field" (ibid. 16:25). "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow" (ibid. 19:10). "For today the Lord appears to you" (Leviticus 9:4). "Behold, this day they have offered their sin-offering" (ibid. 10:19). "The Lord your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude" (Deuteronomy 1:10). "You are this day to pass over the border of Moab" (ibid. 2:18). "I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day" (ibid. 4:26). "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the ordinances which I speak in your ears this day" (ibid. 5:1). "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse" (ibid. 11:26). "You draw near this day to battle against your enemies" (ibid. 20:3). "You are standing this day all of you before the Lord your God" (ibid. 29:9). "See, I have set before you this day life and good, and death and evil" (ibid. 30:15). "And the Lord said to Joshua: This day I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you" (Joshua 5:9). "And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old; I am still strong this day as I was on the day that Moses sent me" (ibid. 14:10-11). "That you must turn away this day from following the Lord? And it will be, seeing you rebel today against the Lord, that tomorrow He will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel" (ibid. 22:18). "And behold, I am going this day the way of all the earth" (ibid. 23:14). "Why has the Lord smitten us today before the Philistines?" (I Samuel 4:3). "For he has come today into the city, for the people have a sacrifice today on the high place" (ibid. 9:12). "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?" (ibid. 20:27). "And Joab said: Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight" (II Samuel 14:22). "I am this day eighty years old; can I discern between good and bad?" (ibid. 19:36). "As the Lord lives, etc., Adonijah shall be put to death this day" (I Kings 2:24). "Do you know that the Lord will take away your master from over your head today?" (II Kings 2:3). "This very day he shall halt at Nob" (Isaiah 10:32). "For behold, I have made you this day a fortified city" (Jeremiah 1:18). "Behold, I release you this day from the chains which are upon your hand" (ibid. 40:4). "And her mother-in-law said to her (to Ruth): Where did you glean today? etc. And she (Ruth) said: The name of the man with whom I worked today is Boaz" (Ruth 2:19). "Sacrifices of peace-offerings were due from me; this day I have paid my vows" (Proverbs 7:14). "And prosper, I pray You, Your servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man" (Nehemiah 1:11). "Let the king and Haman come this day to the banquet that I have prepared for him" (Esther 5:4). — And הַיּוֹם in the sense of the time in which we live: "For he who is now called a prophet was beforetime called a seer" (I Samuel 9:9). "Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants nowadays who break away every man from his master" (ibid. 25:10). — כְּהַיּוֹם, now, shortly [Note: In the source, printed 'טעם'.]: "As soon as you come into the city you shall find him, etc., for he blesses the sacrifice, and afterwards those who are invited eat; now therefore go up, for at this time you shall find him" (I Samuel 9:13). — כַּיּוֹם, in this sense: "And Esau said to Jacob: Let me swallow, I pray you, etc. And Jacob said: Sell me first your birthright, etc. And Jacob said: Swear to me first; and he swore to him, and he sold his birthright to Jacob" (Genesis 25:30-33). "Even before they burnt the fat, the priest's servant came and said to the man who sacrificed: Give flesh to roast for the priest, etc. And if the man said to him: Let them first burn the fat, and then take as much as your soul desires, then he would say: No, but you shall give it now" (I Samuel 2:15-16). "But you stand still now, that I may cause you to hear the word of God" (ibid. 9:27). "Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not slay his servant with the sword" (I Kings 1:51). "And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel: Inquire, I pray you, at the word of the Lord today" (ibid. 22:5). "Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to smite with the fist of wickedness; you do not fast this day so as to make your voice heard on high" (Isaiah 58:4). — כַּיּוֹם הזה, as it is now: "And as for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive" (Genesis 50:20). "For the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into your hand, as it is this day" (Deuteronomy 2:30). "But you the Lord has taken and brought forth out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be to Him a people of inheritance, as you are this day" (ibid. 4:20). "That my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day" (ibid. 22:8). "And You have kept for him (for David) this great kindness, that You have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day" (I Kings 3:6). "To give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day" (Jeremiah 11:5). "To make them a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing and a curse, as it is this day" (ibid. 25:18). "To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us shamefacedness, as at this day" (Daniel 9:7). — כְּהַיּוֹם הזה: "For our good always, that He might preserve us alive, as it is this day" (Deuteronomy 6:24). "Therefore your land has become a desolation and an astonishment and a curse, without an inhabitant, as at this day" (Jeremiah 44:22). "And for our iniquities we, our kings and our priests, have been delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, and to spoiling, and to shamefacedness, as it is this day" (Ezra 9:7). — And also in the sense of "on that day, at that time": "And it came to pass on a certain day, when he went into the house to do his work" (Genesis 39:11). — עד הַיּוֹם הזה, until the time of the speaker or the writer: "And Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth" (Genesis 47:26). "And they succeeded them and dwelt in their stead, to this day" (Deuteronomy 2:22). "And called them, even Bashan, after his own name, Havvoth-jair, to this day" (ibid. 3:14). "But Rahab the harlot and her father's household, etc., Joshua saved alive, and she dwelt in the midst of Israel to this day" (Joshua 6:25). "And they raised over him a great heap of stones, to this day, and the Lord turned from the fierceness of His anger; therefore the name of that place was called the valley of Achor, to this day" (ibid. 7:26). "And he made it a heap forever, a desolation, to this day" (ibid. 8:28). "And the Canaanites dwelt in the midst of Ephraim to this day" (ibid. 16:10). "And he called its name Luz, which is its name to this day" (Judges 1:26). "Therefore its name was called En-hakkore, which is in Lehi, to this day" (ibid. 15:19). "Therefore Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day" (I Samuel 27:6). "And he (David) made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day" (ibid. 30:25). "And it is called Absalom's monument to this day" (II Samuel 18:18). "And there they are to this day" (I Kings 8:8). "Of them did Solomon raise a levy of bondservants, to this day" (ibid. 9:21). "And the Edomites came to Elath and dwelt there, to this day" (II Kings 16:6). "As their fathers did, so do they to this day" (ibid. 17:41). "The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, which he commanded his sons, not to drink wine, are performed, and to this day they drink none, for they obey their father's commandment" (Jeremiah 35:14). "So its name is called Bamah to this day" (Ezekiel 20:29). — כָּל הַיּוֹם, all day: "I have set watchmen upon your walls, O Jerusalem; they shall never hold their peace day nor night" (Isaiah 62:6). "When I kept silence, my bones wore away through my groaning all the day long" (Psalms 32:3). — And in the sense of always, without interruption: "Does the plowman plow all the day to sow? Does he open and harrow his ground? When he has made its face even, does he not scatter the black cummin, etc." (Isaiah 28:24-25). "These are a smoke in My nose, a fire that burns all the day" (ibid. 65:5). "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The mercy of God endures all the day" (Psalms 52:3). "Be gracious to me, O God, for man would swallow me up; all the day he, fighting, oppresses me. My watchful foes would swallow me up all the day, for they are many that fight against me" (ibid. 56:2-3). — וַיְהִי הַיּוֹם, in the sense of: there came one of the days, suddenly, on one day not specified which: "And this man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice to the Lord, etc. And it came to pass on the day that Elkanah sacrificed" (I Samuel 1:3-4). On one of the days. "And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash. And it came to pass on a certain day that Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who bore his armor: Come and let us go over to the Philistines' garrison" (ibid. 13:23-14:1). "And it fell on a day that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a great woman, and she constrained him to eat bread, etc. And she said to her husband: Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually. Let us make, I pray you, a little chamber on the wall, etc., and it shall be, when he comes to us, that he shall turn in there. And it fell on a day that he came there, and he turned into the upper chamber" (II Kings 4:8-11). "And when the child was grown, it fell on a day that he went out to his father to the reapers" (ibid. 18). "Thus did Job continually. Now it fell upon a day that the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord" (Job 1:5-6). "So Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord. And it fell on a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house, that there came a messenger to Job" (ibid. 12-14). — And the dual יוֹמַיִם, יֹמַיִם, two days: "See that the Lord has given you the Sabbath; therefore He gives you on the sixth day the bread of two days" (Exodus 16:29). "But if he continues a day or two days, he shall not be punished" (ibid. 21:21). "You shall not eat (meat) one day, nor two days, nor five days" (Numbers 11:19). "Or two days [Note: Some doubt the correctness of this vocalization, and conjecture that one should read יָמים, with kamatz under the yod.] or a month" (ibid. 9:22). "For He has torn, and He will heal us; He has smitten, and He will bind us up. After two days [Note: Some doubt the correctness of this vocalization, and conjecture that one should read יָמים, with kamatz under the yod.] He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His sight" (Hosea 6:1-2). — And the plural יָמִים [Note: See the note above.], for the time when the sun shines on the earth: "For he had eaten no bread nor drunk any water three days and three nights" (I Samuel 30:12). "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights" (Job 2:13). — And the measure of time of the days and nights together: "And he stayed yet another seven days" (Genesis 8:10). "And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every male" (ibid. 17:12). "And stay with him a few days" (ibid. 27:44). "And he mourned for his son many days" (ibid. 37:34). "Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread" (Exodus 12:15). "Six days you shall labor and do all your work" (ibid. 20:9). — And the construct יְמֵי [Note: Like בְּנֵי from בָּנִים.]: "And forty days were fulfilled for him, for so are fulfilled the days of embalming; and the Egyptians wept for him seventy days. And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the house of Pharaoh" (Genesis 50:3-4). "She shall touch no hallowed thing, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are fulfilled" (Leviticus 12:4). "The seven days of the feast" (Judges 14:12). "And the seven days of the feast" (Ezekiel 45:23). "The six working days" (ibid. 46:1). "As in the days of the impurity of her sickness she shall be unclean" (Leviticus 12:2). "As the time of a hired servant shall he be with him" (ibid. 25:50). — And יָמִים alone in the sense of "a few days": "Let the damsel abide with us days, or ten; after that she shall go" (Genesis 24:55). — עוּל יָמִים, of a few days: "There shall be no more from there an infant of days, nor an old man who has not filled his days" (Isaiah 65:20). — And in the sense of "some time": "And he (Pharaoh) put them (the chief butler and the chief baker) in ward, etc., and they continued days in ward" (Genesis 40:3-4). "Whether it be two days, or a month, or days" (Numbers 9:22). "And she, and he, and her house, ate many days" (I Kings 17:15). "I sat down and wept and mourned days, and I fasted and prayed" (Nehemiah 1:4). "And I Daniel fainted and was sick days; then I rose up and did the king's business" (Daniel 8:27). — קץ יָמִים, after some time: "And in process of time it came to pass that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering to the Lord" (Genesis 4:3). "And it came to pass after a while that the brook dried up" (I Kings 17:7). "In the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I went to the king, and after certain days I asked leave of the king" (Nehemiah 13:6). — מלאו יָמָיו, the fixed time was completed: "And Jacob said to Laban: Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her" (Genesis 29:21). "And when her days to be delivered were fulfilled" (ibid. 25:24). "And the days were not expired; and David arose and went, he and his men, and slew of the Philistines" (I Samuel 18:26-27). — And יָמִין, like יָמִים: "But go your way till the end be; and you shall rest, and shall stand up to your lot at the end of the days" (Daniel 12:13). — מִיָּמִים, after days, more or fewer: "And it came to pass after a time that the children of Ammon made war against Israel" (Judges 11:4). "And after a time he returned to take her" (ibid. 14:8). "But it came to pass after a while, in the time of wheat harvest, that Samson visited his wife" (ibid. 15:1). — And מִיָּמִים רבים: "And it came to pass after many days, when the Lord had given rest to Israel, etc., that Joshua called for all Israel" (Joshua 23:1-2). — לְיָמִים: "And it came to pass, in process of time, at the end of two years, his bowels fell out" (II Chronicles 21:19). — לְמִיָּמִים: "And as from the days that I commanded judges to be over My people" (I Chronicles 17:10). — יָמִים in the sense of a year, and מִיָּמִים יָמָימָה, see the entry יָמִים. — And with חדש, שנה, ירח, שבוע, מוֹעֵד, תקופה: "And he abode with him a month of days" (Genesis 29:14). "At the end of two full years" (ibid. 41:1). "And bewail her father and her mother a full month" (Deuteronomy 21:13). "And you did not come within the days appointed" (I Samuel 13:11). "And it came to pass, when the time was come about, that Hannah conceived and bore a son" (ibid. 1:20). "I Daniel was mourning three whole weeks" (Daniel 10:2). — And in general יָמִים in the sense of time; בַּיָּמִים ההם, at that time: "The Nephilim were in the earth in those days" (Genesis 6:4). "And it came to pass in those days, when Moses was grown up, that he went out to his brethren" (Exodus 2:11). "And you shall come to the priests the Levites and to the judge that shall be in those days" (Deuteronomy 17:9). "In those days there was no king in Israel" (Judges 17:6). "In those days Hezekiah was sick unto death" (Isaiah 38:1). "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar" (Genesis 14:1). "The first famine that was in the days of Abraham" (ibid. 26:1). "In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways ceased" (Judges 5:6). "And the man was an old man in the days of Saul" (I Samuel 17:12). "Silver was nothing accounted of in the days of Solomon" (I Kings 10:21). "In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah" (Isaiah 1:1). "In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, etc., and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel" (Hosea 1:1). "For there was not kept such a Passover from the days of the judges" (II Kings 23:22). "From the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel" (Hosea 10:9). "From the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day" (Jeremiah 36:2). "All her treasures that she had from the days of old" (Lamentations 1:7). "Have you not heard how I have done it long ago, from ancient times?" (II Kings 19:25). "From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from My statutes" (Malachi 3:7). "For there shall be peace and truth in my days" (Isaiah 39:8). "Nevertheless in your days I will not do it" (I Kings 11:12). "For in his days was the earth divided" (Genesis 10:25). "In his days Pharaoh-necoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria" (II Kings 23:29). "In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely" (Jeremiah 23:6). "Has this been in your days, or in the days of your fathers?" (Joel 1:2). "Look among the nations, and behold, and wonder marvelously; for, behold, a work shall be wrought in your days which you will not believe though it be told you" (Habakkuk 1:5). "Our fathers have told us a work You did in their days, in the days of old" (Psalms 44:2). — יָמָיו of so-and-so, the time of his life: "That my days should be consumed in shame" (Jeremiah 20:18). "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope" (Job 7:6). "To drink no wine all our days" (Jeremiah 35:8). "For our days upon earth are a shadow" (Job 8:9). "You shall not seek their peace nor their prosperity all your days forever" (Deuteronomy 23:7). "Are Your days as the days of man, or Your years as a man's days?" (Job 10:5). — קרבו יָמָיו, מלאו יָמָיו, he reached the days of old age, his time to die arrived: "And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, your days approach that you must die" (Deuteronomy 31:14). "When your days are fulfilled and you shall sleep with your fathers" (II Samuel 7:12).
