en: , masculine noun, with suffixes כֹּחִי, כֹּחֲךָ, כֹּחֶךָ, כֹּחֶכָה, כֹּחֲכֶם, כֹּחוֹ, כֹּחָהּ, כֹּחָם, plural * כֹּחוֹת. — a) A natural property that gives the body of a living creature the ability to do hard, great deeds, to carry a very heavy load, to break something very strong, and the like; German Kraft; French force; English strength, — of man: “And Samson took hold of the two middle pillars upon which the house rested, and leaned upon them etc.; and he bent with all his might (בְּכֹחַ), and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people that were in it” (Judges 16:29–30). “And the lords of the Philistines came up to her (to Delilah, Samson's wife) and said to her: Entice him, and see wherein his great strength (כֹּחוֹ) lies etc. And Delilah said to Samson: Tell me, I pray you, wherein your great strength (כֹּחֲךָ) lies etc. If I be shaven, then my strength (כֹחִי) will go from me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man etc. And she began to afflict him, and his strength (כֹּּחוֹ) went from him” (ibid. 5–19). “The glory of young men is their strength (כֹּחָם), and the beauty of old men is the hoary head” (Proverbs 20:29). — Of the ox: “But much increase is by the strength (בְּכֹחַ) of the ox” (Proverbs 14:4). — Of the wild ox: “Can you bind the wild ox with his band in the furrow? Or will he harrow the valleys after you? Will you trust him because his strength (כֹּחוֹ) is great? Or will you leave your labor to him?” (Job 39:10–11). — Of the behemoth mentioned there: “Behold now behemoth, which I made with you; he eats grass as an ox. Lo now, his strength (כֹחוֹ) is in his loins, and his force is in the muscles of his belly” (Job 40:15–16). — The strength (כֹּחַ) of the hands for work: “But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I disdained to set with the dogs of my flock. Yea, the strength (כֹּחַ) of their hands, whereto should it profit me? Men in whom ripe age is perished” (Job 30:1–2). — There was no strength (כֹּחַ) in him, because of fasting and the like: “And there was no strength (כֹּחַ) in him, for he had eaten no bread all the day nor all the night” (1 Samuel 28:20). “Yea, he is hungry, and his strength (כֹּחַ) fails; he drinks no water, and is faint” (Isaiah 44:12). — And eating gave him strength (כֹּחַ): “And let me set a morsel of bread before you, and eat, that you may have strength (כֹּחַ) when you go on your way” (1 Samuel 28:22). “And he arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength (בְּכֹחַ) of that meal forty days and forty nights” (1 Kings 19:8). — And strength (כֹחַ) to make war, to overcome the enemy and the like: “I am still as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me; as my strength (כְּכֹחִי) was then, so is my strength (וּכְכֹחִי) now, for war, and to go out and to come in” (Joshua 14:11). “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor etc. Go in this your might (בְּכֹחֲךָ), and save Israel from the hand of Midian” (Judges 6:12–14). “For not by strength (בְכֹחַ) shall man prevail” (1 Samuel 2:9). “And flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not exert his strength (כֹּחוֹ), neither shall the mighty deliver himself” (Amos 2:14). “Her princes are become like harts that find no pasture, and they are gone without strength (כֹחַ) before the pursuer” (Lamentations 1:6). — And of a people, an army: “You are a great people, and have great power (וְכֹחַ) etc.; for you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron” (Joshua 17:17–18). “And under their hand was an army etc., that made war with mighty power (בְּכֹחַ חיל), to help the king against the enemy” (2 Chronicles 26:13). — And physical and spiritual strength to succeed in a matter: “And you say in your heart: My power (כֹּחִי) and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth. But you shall remember the LORD your God, for it is He that gives you power (כֹּחַ) to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17–18). “For he has said: By the strength (בְּכֹחַ) of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I am prudent” (Isaiah 10:13). “Not by might, nor by power (בְכֹחַ) (will he succeed and do all that is needed), but by My spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). “Whatsoever your hand finds to do by your strength (בְּכֹחֲךָ), that do” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). — And in relation to God and His great works: “But in very deed for this cause have I made you stand, to show you My power (כֹּחִי)” (Exodus 9:16). “LORD, why does Your wrath wax hot against Your people, whom You have brought forth out of the land of Egypt with great power (בְּכֹחַ) and with a mighty hand?” (ibid. 32:11). “For You brought up this people in Your might (בְכֹחֲךָ) from among them” (Numbers 14:13). “He that has made the earth by His power (בְּכֹחו), that has established the world by His wisdom” (Jeremiah 10:12). “Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, You have made the heaven and the earth by Your great power (בְּכֹחֲךָ) and by Your outstretched arm” (ibid. 32:17). “Is My hand shortened at all, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power (כֹחַ) to deliver? Behold, at My rebuke I dry up the sea” (Isaiah 50:2). “Who by His strength (בְּכֹּחוֹ) sets fast the mountains, who is girded about with might” (Psalms 65:7). “He has declared to His people the power (כֹּחַ) of His works, in giving them the heritage of the nations” (ibid. 111:6). “He stirs up the sea with His power (בְּכֹחוֹ), and by His understanding He smites through Rahab” (Job 26:12). — And joined with adjectives אַמִּיץ, גָּדוֹל, רַב, שַׂגִּיא and the like: “He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength (ואמיץ כֹּחַ); who has hardened himself against Him and prospered?” (Job 9:4). “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power (וגדול כֹּחַ)” (Nahum 1:3). “Great is our Lord, and mighty in power (ורב כֹּחַ)” (Psalms 147:5). “The Almighty, we cannot find Him out; He is excellent in power (שגיא כֹּחַ) and in justice” (Job 37:23). — And strength for various actions: to weep: “Then David and the people that were with him lifted up their voice and wept, until they had no more strength (כֹּחַ) to weep” (1 Samuel 30:4). — And to raise the voice: “O you that tells good tidings to Zion, get you up into the high mountain; O you that tells good tidings to Jerusalem, lift up your voice with strength (בַכֹּחַ)” (Isaiah 40:9). “The voice of the LORD is powerful (בַּכֹּחַ); the voice of the LORD is full of majesty” (Psalms 29:4). — And to give birth: “For the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength (וְכֹחַ) to bring forth” (Isaiah 37:3). — And of exertion of strength (הַכֹּחַ) and toil for work, and the work itself: “And you know that with all my power (כֹּחִי) I have served your father” (Genesis 31:6). “And I will make your heaven as iron and your earth as brass; and your strength (כֹּחֲכֶם) shall be spent in vain, for your land shall not yield her produce, neither shall the trees of the land yield their fruit” (Leviticus 26:19–20). “But I said: I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength (כֹּחִי) for nought and vanity” (Isaiah 49:4). — And physical and spiritual strength to stand in a great place: “Youths in whom was no blemish etc., and understanding science, and such as had ability (כֹּחַ) to stand in the king's palace” (Daniel 1:4). — And strength to bear and endure something, sufferings and the like: “What is my strength (כֹֹּחִִי), that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength (כֹֹּחַ) the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of brass?” (Job 6:11–12). “But the people are many, and it is a time of much rain, and we are not able (ואין כֹּחַ) to stand outside” (Ezra 10:13). “If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength (כֹּחֶכָה) is small” (Proverbs 24:10). — כֹּחַ הסבל, see סַבָּל. — החליף כֹּחַ, see חָלַף. — עצר כֹּחַ, see עָצַר. — כָּלָה הַכֹּחַ, see כלה. כשל כֹּחַ, הכשיל כֹּחוֹ, see כָּשַׁל. — יְגִיעַ כֹּחַ, see יָגִיעַ. — עמד מִכֹּחַ, see עמד. * סמך כֹּחַ, see סמך. — His strength (כֹּחוֹ) forsook him: “My heart flutters, my strength (כֹחִי) fails me” (Psalms 38:11). — And in the sense of the power of violence: “And he (the wicked) draws away the mighty by his power (בְּכֹחוֹ)” (Job 24:22). “And behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power (כֹּחַ), but they had no comforter” (Ecclesiastes 4:1). — b) Figuratively, a man's strength (כֹּחוֹ), his seed, and especially the first child: “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might (כֹּחִי), and the first-fruits of my strength” (Genesis 49:3). — כֹּחָהּ of the ground, its fruit and its produce: “When you till the ground, it shall not henceforth yield its strength (כֹּחָהּ) to you” (Genesis 4:12). “If my land cry out against me, and the furrows thereof weep together; if I have eaten its strength (כֹּחָהּ) without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life” (Job 31:38–39). — c) In general, wealth and property and the like: “Did I say: Give to me? Or: Offer a bribe for me of your substance (וּמִכֹּחֲכֶם)?” (Job 6:22). “Lest strangers be filled with your strength (כֹּחֶךָ), and your labors be in the house of a stranger” (Proverbs 5:10). “They gave after their ability (כְּכֹחָם) into the treasury of the work” (Ezra 2:69). — And in the Talmud and Midrash, as in the Bible: “And how many voices there were (at Mount Sinai), and how many torches there were! But they made each person hear according to his strength (כחו)” (Mekhilta Yitro, Bahodesh 9). “‘Stand still and see the salvation of the LORD.’ They said to him: When? He said to them: Tomorrow. They said to him: Moses our teacher, we have no strength (כח) to endure” (ibid. Beshallach 2:2). “I have kept my strength (כחי) for my old age” (Jerusalem Talmud Betzah 1, 60c). “Except for Elisha ben Abuyah, who knew My power (כחי) and rebelled against Me” (ibid. Hagigah 2, 77b). “If you arrange your prayer, there will be no begrudging eye for you from Above, but all will strengthen your power (כחך)” (ibid. Ta'anit 3, 66d). “Moses said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Now the nations of the world will say: His (the God of Israel's) strength (כחו) has weakened, and He cannot save” (Berakhot 32a). “Whoever slackens himself from words of Torah has no strength (כח) to stand on the day of trouble” (ibid. 63a). “R. Eleazar said: He blows with his hand and with all his strength (כחו)” (Betzah 14a). “For it (the Torah) weakens the strength (כחו) of a person” (Sanhedrin 26b). “Three things weaken the strength (כחו) of a person, and these are they: fear, travel and sin” (Gittin 70a). “Come and see how great is the strength (כחן) of the priests: for there is nothing among birds lighter than the crop and the feathers, and sometimes the priest throws them more than thirty cubits” (Zevachim 64a). “Greater than his brothers in beauty, in strength (בכח), in wisdom and in wealth” (Horayot 9a). “R. Simeon ben Halafta, who was confident in his strength (כוחו), went out at midnight to go to his town” (Deuteronomy Rabbah 9). “In the seven-year period in which the son of David comes, they bring beams of iron and put them on his neck until his stature is bent, and he cries and weeps, and his voice rises on high; he says before Him: Master of the universe, how much can my strength (כוחי) be, and how much can my spirit be, and how much can my soul be, and how much can my limbs be? Am I not flesh and blood?” (Pesikta Rabbati 36). — And the strength (כֹחוֹ) of an ox and the like: “An ox, its strength (כחו) is hard, and its horns are not handsome” (Sifre Deuteronomy 33). — * יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ, a blessing and an exclamation of gratitude to a person for a good deed; see ישר. — And of things that are not living creatures: “All the days that Simeon the Righteous was alive, the fire of the altar pile grew strong and rose up; once they had put two logs of wood on it in the morning, they would not put any more all day. When Simeon the Righteous died, the strength (כוחה) of the altar pile weakened, and they did not refrain from putting wood on it all day” (Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 6, 43c). “Whether a barren tree or a fruit tree: up to this point the cutting thickens it; from here on it weakens its strength (כוחו)” (ibid. Shevi'it 1, 33a). — כֹּחַ of the loaf, its quantity; and a proverb: “The master of the house knows the strength (כחו) of his loaf” (Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 8, 12a). — And figuratively, כֹּחָהּ of the eye and the like, the natural ability: “Any new moon that was born before six hours, the eye has no power (כח) to see the old one” (Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 2, 58b). — And in the sense of the quality of a thing: “One who walks in a beit ha-peras on stones that he cannot move, on a man or on a beast whose strength (שכחן) is good etc.; on stones that he can move, on a man or on a beast whose strength (שכחן) [Note: And they said in the Gemara, Bava Metzia 105b: What is the case of a man whose strength is poor? Resh Lakish said: Anyone whose knees knock together when he rides. What is the case of a beast whose strength is poor? In the school of R. Yannai they said: Any that drops dung when it is ridden.] is poor” (Oholot 18:6). “Like a householder who had two cows, one whose strength (כוחה) was good and one whose strength (כוחה) was poor: upon which does he put the yoke? Is it not upon the one whose strength is good?” (Genesis Rabbah 55). — And also of things that are not living creatures: “If they climbed up a tree whose strength (שכחו) is poor, or on a branch whose strength (שכחה) [Note: And they said in the Gemara, Bava Metzia 105b: What is the case of a tree whose strength is poor? In the school of R. Yannai they said: Any whose base is not thick enough to hollow out a quarter-kav. What is the case of a branch whose strength is poor? Resh Lakish said: Any that is נחבאת בחזיונה.] is poor” (Zavim 3:1). — And in spiritual matters, the spiritual strength (כֹּחוֹ) of a person, his greatness and importance: “R. Meir sat down first; the face of R. Simeon turned pale. R. Akiva said to him: By your life, it is enough that I and your Creator know your strength (כוחך)” (Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 1, 19a). “Rav said: From the day that the Book of Genealogies was hidden away, the strength (כוחן) of the Sages weakened and the light of their eyes grew dim” (Pesachim 62b). “R. Johanan said: When that righteous man came as far as Dan, his strength (כחו) weakened; he saw his descendants, who were destined to worship idols in Dan” (Sanhedrin 96a). “Like a king who had two sons, one older and one younger. He said to the younger: Walk with me; and he said to the older: Come and walk before me. So Abraham, whose strength (כחו) was good — (it was said of him): ‘Walk before Me and be wholehearted’” (Genesis Rabbah 30). “To Abraham, whose strength (כוחו) was good, they (the angels) appeared in the form of men; but to Lot, because his strength (כוחו) was poor, they appeared in the form of angels” (ibid. 50). — כֹּחוֹ of someone in opinions and the like, how far he goes in an opinion, in a legal ruling and the like: “Rabban Gamaliel declares him liable: it comes to inform you of the strength (כח) of Rabban Gamaliel, how far he declares liable” (Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot 6, 37a). — d) * כֹּחוֹ of a thing, what the thing can effect and cause: “Come and see how severe is the power (כח) of transgression: before they put forth their hands in transgression, there were no zavim and lepers among them; and once they put forth their hands in transgression, there were zavim and lepers among them” (Sifre Numbers 1). “At first he (the priest) informs her (the sotah) of the power (כוחן) of the bitter waters” (ibid. 12). “One through whom the name of Heaven was profaned: repentance has no power (כח) to suspend, nor the Day of Atonement to atone” (Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot 1, 33b). “He (Cain) went out (from before the LORD) rejoicing etc. Adam met him and said to him: What was done in your judgment? He said to him: I repented and was reconciled. Adam began to beat his face, saying: Such is the power (כחה) of repentance, and I did not know!” (Genesis Rabbah 22). “When Zipporah saw that it had swallowed him only up to the circumcision, she recognized that he was being harmed on account of the circumcision, and she knew how great is the power (כח) of circumcision, that it could not swallow him any further” (ibid. Exodus 5). “See how severe is the power (כחו) of evil speech: for they were commanded to build the Temple, and because the generation were people of evil speech, it was not built in their days” (ibid. Deuteronomy 5). — And in the sense of the importance and value of a thing: “Come and see how great is the power (כח) of work: for an ox, which he took away from its work, five; a sheep, which he did not take away from its work, four” (Bava Kamma 79b). — e) * Legal and judicial force (כֹּחַ): “If the judges' assessment was a sixth less or a sixth more, their sale is void. Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel says: Their sale stands. If so (if their sale is void), what force (כח) does the court have?” (Ketubot 11:5), that is, what legal force does the court have. “He should not separate terumah; if he transgressed and separated it, R. Berekhiah says: His power (כחו) is effective; R. Mana says: His power (כחו) is not effective” (Jerusalem Talmud Ma'aser Sheni 4, 51d). “An ordinary son (not a firstborn), whose power (כחו) is stronger, in that he takes what is due as what is possessed” (Bava Batra 130b). — And the expression is customary גדול or יפה כֹּחוֹ of so-and-so than that of so-and-so, so-and-so has more legal and judicial force than so-and-so: “A priest who had intercourse with an Israelite's daughter: she may not eat terumah; if she became pregnant, she may not eat; if she gave birth, she may eat. It turns out that the power (כחו) of the son is greater than that of the father” (Yevamot 7:5), for by virtue of the father she does not eat, and by virtue of the son she eats. “If two acquit and two convict and one says: I do not know, the judges should be added. The power (כח) of the one who says ‘liable’ is stronger than the power (מכח) of the one who says ‘I do not know’” (Tosefta Sanhedrin 6:3). “In this the power (כח) of the son is stronger than the power of the father: for the son collects without an oath, and the father collects only with an oath” (Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 9, 33b). “If one says: I heard it from the mouth of two, and two say: We heard it from the mouth of one, the power (כח) of the one who heard from the mouth of two is stronger than the power of the two who heard from the mouth of one” (ibid. Niddah 1, 49a). “For whoever spoke within his own domain, his power (כוחו) is stronger than his fellow's” (Teshuvot ha-Geonim, Harkavy 526). — And of a thing that is not a living creature: “R. Simeon says: The power (כח) of the altar is stronger than the power of the priests, and the power of the priests is stronger than the power of the altar. The power of the altar is stronger with the handful and with the frankincense etc.” (Tosefta Zevachim 5:3). “Just as judgment is by three, so compromise is by three. The power (כח) of compromise is stronger than the power of judgment: for two who judged may retract, and two who made a compromise may not retract” (ibid. Sanhedrin 1:9). — יִפָּה את כֹּחוֹ, made it so that he has more legal force: “And what does he (the buyer to the seller) return to him? Money; and if he wishes, he returns land to him. And why did they say he returns money to him? To strengthen the power (כוחו) of the seller” (Bava Batra 7:2). “Why did they say that a widow may sell without a court? To strengthen the power (כוחן) of the orphans, so as not to squander their property” (Tosefta Ketubot 11:1). “A gourd among the gourds (מוקשה מן המוקשיות), whose power you strengthened (שיפיתה כוחו) to save with eight” (Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 3, 28d). “A son, whose power you strengthened (שייפיתה כוחו) in the property of the father — is it not logical that we should strengthen his power (שנייפה כוחו) in the property of the mother?” (ibid. Bava Kamma 7, 16a). “He wished to give it to him as a gift; and why did he write it for him in the language of sale? In order to strengthen his power (כחו)” (Bava Batra 51a). “A dying person who said: Write and give a maneh to so-and-so, and he died: we consider; if it is as though he were strengthening his power (כוחו), they write it” (ibid. 135b). — הורע כֹּחוֹ, he does not have so much power and right in this matter: “Rabban Gamaliel said: Is the power (כח) of the householder made stronger or is his power (כחו) made weaker because of the multitude of sheaves (that he forgot in the field)?” (Pe'ah 6:6). “Standing grain in which the power (כח) of the poor man is weakened (for the poor man does not have in it the right of the forgotten sheaf)” (Tosefta ibid. 3:6). “If he borrowed a thousand dinars from him with a document and repaid him, and he seeks to borrow from him a second time, he should not give him back his first document, because he weakens the power (כוח) of the buyers” (ibid. Gittin 2:9). “A gourd among the onions, whose power you weakened (שהורעת כוחו) to save with twelve” (Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 3, 28d). “A predated prozbul is valid, because it weakens his power (כוחו), and a postdated one is invalid, because it strengthens his power (כוחו)” (ibid. Shevi'it 10, 39d). “A man and a woman, since their power (כחם) is weakened in damages, you did not distinguish in it between a tam and a mu'ad” (Bava Kamma 44a). “And if, in a place where your power (כחך) is stronger, in your sin offering, I excluded you from the sin offering of Israel, then in a place where your power (כחך) is weaker, in your meal offering, is it not logical that I should exclude you from the meal offering of Israel?” (Zevachim 102b). — גרע כחו: “One is not to diminish the power (כח) of the first one because she has no children” (Tur Even ha-Ezer 154). — *בָּא מִכֹּחוֹ of so-and-so, he has the right and the legal claim to request something, to do something, because this belonged to so-and-so and it came to him from so-and-so in a natural or legal way, or with the consent of so-and-so, who authorized him for this: “The father (inherits) the son (by a fortiori reasoning): if the son, who comes only by virtue (מכוח) of the father, inherits him, then the father, by virtue (מכוחו) of whom alone the son comes — is it not logical that he should inherit him?” (Jerusalem Talmud Bava Batra 8, 16a). — And in the medieval literature: “That this lender shall have power etc. to sell them or to pledge them to the amount of the money of the bond of debt that he produced before us, and to eat their fruits and their yields, he and those who come by his power (מכחו), until the said borrower so-and-so repays the debt” (Sefer ha-Shetarot of R. Judah al-Barceloni 1). “And any bribe and hire that he gives on account of my refusal or on account of the refusal of one who comes by my power (מכחי), he shall collect from me and from one who comes by my power (מכחי); all of it I pay” (ibid. 55). “I come by the power (מכח) [Note: In the Gemara, in Aramaic: קאתינא מכח גברא דלא מצית אשתעיה דיא בהדיא (Bekhorot 11b).] of a man from whom you cannot take anything” (Rambam, Terumot 1:11). “For the renter says to him: Your power (כחך) is no greater than the power (מכח) of this one, for you acquired this house through him” (ibid., Sekhirut 6:11). “And it was written in that document: Behold, I pledge myself to you and to all who come by your power (מכחך) etc.; for at the moment they sold that debt to this one, at once the borrower became pledged to the buyer, for he is called one who comes by his power (מכחו) after his purchase” (Sefer ha-Terumot 51:7). “And the author of the Terumot wrote that if he wrote in it trustworthiness concerning him and concerning those who come by his power (באי כחו), the court is included among those who come by his power (באי כחו)” (Tur, Gevi'at Hov 106). — And also of things that are not living creatures: “A negative commandment that comes by the force (מכח) of a positive commandment is a positive commandment” (Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin 4, 66b). “And he sent a letter with a greeting, and wrote in it: If I have not come from today until such-and-such a day, behold, you are permitted to any man; and the bill of divorce was inside the letter. And he did not come by the time he had set for her, and by the force (ומכח) of the letter she went and married another man” (Teshuvot ha-Geonim, חברון 101). “A widow who is to share with the heirs of her husband by the force (בכח) of the enactment” (Tur Even ha-Ezer 154). “That the borrower sold or pledged by the law of the Gemara or also by the force (מכח) of custom” (ibid. Hoshen Mishpat 60, in the name of the Rosh). — °And כֹּחוֹ of so-and-so, in the sense of his domain and his right: “It (the field) has gone out of the power (מכחו) of the seller and stands in the power (בכחו) of the buyer” (Rashi, Leviticus 25:29). “The lender has no power (כח) to challenge the agent and say: You caused me to lose my money, for you handed it to someone from whom I cannot get it back” (Tur Hoshen Mishpat 125:5). “For Reuben reserved for himself a power (כח) in this land etc.; and that power (כח) which Reuben reserved for himself in the land, when Reuben dies and leaves only that son, the son acquires that power (כח) which his father reserved for himself” (Levush, Hoshen Mishpat 111:4). — f) *כֹּחַ in the sense of that which causes some action: “This is the rule: whatever is by the force (מכח) of moving are unclean, and by the force (ומכח) of trembling are clean” (Tosefta Zavim 4:6). “If it was moved by reason of his force (כחו) (that he himself moved the thing), it is unclean; by reason of trembling, it is clean etc.; in trembling by reason of his force (כחו)” (Eruvin 35a). “(For the gentile emptied the wine out of the jars, and so the pouring of the wine is) his force (כחו) without intention (to touch the wine), and regarding anything that is his force (כחו) without intention, the Rabbis did not decree” (Avodah Zarah 58b). “R. Johanan (asked): If he threw an object and he himself moved from his place and went back and caught it, what is the law? etc. Two forces (כחות) [Note: And Rabbenu Hananel explained there: these two forces of his — that he threw, and that he moved and caught.] (the throwing and the going back to catch it) in one man — are they (comparable) to one man, and he is liable, or (perhaps) are they (comparable) to two men, and he is exempt?” (Shabbat 5a). — כֹּחוֹ and כֹחַ כֹּחוֹ, what is done by his own action, and what is done by an action that was born of his action: “(Symmachus distinguishes) between damage by his force (כחו) and by the force of his force (כח כחו) [Note: And Rashi explained: A bucket that rolled (and the bucket broke) is his force (for he set up the bucket); and the other, which was broken by the pebbles of the bucket, is the force of his force.]” (Bava Kamma 18a). “If the iron slipped off the wood that was being split (and killed someone), he is not exiled, because this does not come from his force (מכחו) but from the force of his force (מכח כחו)” (Rambam, Rotze'ach 6:15). “If a gentile took a vessel of wine and lifted it, and the wine came out, even though he did not stir it, it is forbidden for drinking, for the wine came out by his force (מכחו) etc. The force of his force (כח כחו) is considered like his force; and if it is the force of the force of his force (כח כח כחו), such as the beam of the winepress that a gentile rolled, in which there are three forces (כחות) — the boards, the wheel and the beam” (Tur Yoreh De'ah 125). — כֹּחַ ראשון, that which comes immediately after the action, and כֹחַ שני, that which comes after an interruption in between: “(One who bound his fellow and caused a stream of water to flood over him — its half is his, and he is liable; and these things are only) by the first force (בכח ראשון), but by the second force (בכח שני) (it is an indirect cause)” (Sanhedrin 77b). — כֹּחַ כחוּש, one that has weakened somewhat: “And Rav Papa said: If he threw a pebble upward and it went off to the sides, he is liable etc.; it is a weakened force (כח כחוש)” (ibid.). — g) *Like סִבָּה (cause): “Their odor (of the garments) was bad because (מכח) of the sweat” (Deuteronomy Rabbah 7). — And in abstract matters: “I thought that I had been rejected because (מכח) of that deed, and He counts me with my brothers” (Genesis Rabbah 84). “And they would leave the needs of the community and busy themselves with their own needs; and because (ומכח) of that deed Scripture accounts it as though they took a bribe” (ibid. 85). “All these (which the tribes merited) were by virtue (מכחו) of Jacob, who amassed commandments and good deeds and merited to raise up twelve tribes” (ibid. Exodus 1). “Because the exile of Media came only by force (מכח) of the exile of Babylon” (ibid. Numbers 7). h) °That which compels us to think such and such: “So we received from our fathers (to read ירושלם with a yod after the lamed, even though it is not in the written text); and moreover, we would not have known this by force (מכח) of the language and the way of reasoning, were it not for the tradition, what the reason for the yod is” (Ibn Ezra, Tzahot 4a). “Indeed, we have hinted how the intelligent person can be aroused to it by force (מכח) of our remarks in the preceding gates” (R. Judah ibn Natif, שעה"ש 3:2). “We must say, by force (מכח) of weighing the reasoning of the plain meaning, that (Tophel and Laban) are places, and likewise Di-zahab” (Hizkuni, Deuteronomy 1:1). “And first we will bring the opinions of the philosophers, and say that they decreed by force (בכח) of their inquiry and their speculation that no attributes at all are to be found in God, blessed be He” (Minhat Kena'ot of R. Jehiel of Pisa 22). “And they could not derive by force (מכח) of inquiry the matters of the soul and its reward and its punishment” (ibid. 73). — i) °כֹּחַ אֲנָשִׁים, °גבורת אנשים [Note: This expression, in the sense recorded in the text, is found in the Tosafot and in the responsa of the early authorities, and it was omitted in the entry גבורה, and it will be brought in the Supplements.], a term for the erection of the member: “Such as when she (the wife) claims that he (the husband) keeps apart from her and has no relations with her at all, or that he has no virility (כח אנשים) to lean on his house and does not stand” (Responsa of the Rivash 127). — °And כח גברא [Note: This expression is customary in the mouth of the common people, but in the early books only גבורת אנשים is customary, and in another place כח אנשים.] in this sense: “One who has no virility (כח גברא) at all and no erection of the member” (Ma'aseh Tuviyyah, Ma'yan Hatum 5). “And it once happened with one who smeared an ointment containing quicksilver on the flesh of his private parts and around it, and his virility (כח גברא) was taken from him etc.; and it is good for the erection of the member; and so he did, and his strength (כחו) returned as at first” (ibid. 1). — j) °The strength (כחו) of a herb and the like, its essence: “Let him gather every hot herb whose smell is good, and pound them well while fresh, and cook them well in a cauldron in water over the fire until all the strength (כח) of the herbs has come out into the water, and then let him take it off the fire” (Shabbetai Donnolo, Sefer ha-Merkahot, section 17). — And in the language of philosophical inquiry, in general °a material or spiritual property in a body that causes some action, German Eigenschaft; French propriété; English property: “And they throw some of it (of what is inside the cabbage) into wine and into beer, for it has a property (כוח) that prevents drunkenness; and this is written in the books of medicine, that cabbage has a property (כוח) that prevents drunkenness” (Rav Hai Gaon, Teshuvot ha-Geonim, Harkavy 379). “And the placing of these properties (הכחות) in the essence of the things found in nature is grasped by examination of the drugs and foods known to the sages of medicine, or in a specific nature that examination will not grasp etc.; for in each one there is something beneficial, either in a nature that can be grasped or in a specific nature” (Responsa of the Rashba 413). “Like the nature of the property (כח) of the magnet, which draws iron without anything, but by the wondrous power (בכח)” (Sefer Sha'ashu'im by R. Zabda 32). — And somewhat in the sense of the supernatural: “And on this day (the seventh day) there will be renewed in the bodies a likeness of power (כח) in generation, and in the souls the power (כח) of recognition and intellect” (Ibn Ezra, Genesis 2:3). “For the teraphim are in the form of human beings, and it is made to receive the power (כח) of the higher beings” (ibid. 31:19). “And all the beings under the heavens, their power (כחם) and their generations are according to the supernal order, with the roots below” (ibid., Deuteronomy 5:26). “Know that all the herbs that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for them known powers (כחות) Above that flow into them; and when the dew and the rain come down from heaven, blessings come from the supernal powers (הכחות) to the lower ones. And therefore the dew is good for the world, for the power (כח) of each and every herb comes down with it from the supernal powers (הכחות)” (Recanati, Genesis). — And especially the natural properties in plants and living creatures to digest food, so that blood or sap comes into being from it and the waste is expelled outward, and the plant and the living creature grow ever larger, and the like among the bodily and psychic faculties: “The Holy One, blessed be He, placed in man three faculties (כחות); some call them faculties (כחות), and some call them three souls. The first is the faculty (הכח) by which he grows and multiplies like the plant of the field; and the second, by which he moves about and changes his place, and all living creatures share with him in these two faculties (הכחות), and it is called the spirit of life; and the third, by which he discerns between good and evil and between truth and falsehood” (R. Abraham bar Hiyya ha-Nasi, Hegyon ha-Nefesh 2). “Three faculties (כחות) are in the life of man, and if you wish, call them by three names: neshamah, ruah and nefesh. Now the nefesh is the vegetative faculty (הכח הצומח), which is in the liver, and every living and growing thing shares in this faculty (בכח); and the ruah is in the heart etc.; and the neshamah is the highest, and its power (וכחה) is in the brain” (Ibn Ezra, Yesod Mora 7). “Consider, my brother, the four faculties (בכחות) that are in the body and their workings in it: the attractive faculty (כח המושך) is the one that receives the food and brings it to the stomach; and the retentive faculty (והכח המחזיק) is the one that holds the food in it until nature does its work; and the digestive faculty (והכח המבשל) is the one that cooks it, extracts the pure part of it and separates it from the unfit waste, and sends it to the body; and the expulsive faculty (והכח הדוחה) is the one that expels the waste remaining after the digestive faculty has taken what it needs from the food” (Hovot ha-Levavot, Sha'ar ha-Behinah 5). “And the brain is the dwelling place of the spiritual faculties (הכחות), and the source of sensation and the root of the nerves” (ibid.). “And He set up within it (within the palace of man) four more storehouses for four officers, that is, the attractive faculty (הכח המושך), the retentive faculty (והכח המחזיק), the digestive faculty (והכח המעכל) and the expulsive faculty (והכח הדוחה)” (ibid., Avodat ha-Elohim 9). “The first of the faculties (הכחות) is the nutritive faculty (הכח הזן) etc.; and the nutritive has the four well-known faculties (כחות) that serve it” (Kuzari 5:12). “Learn about the wonders of what He created in living things, of the expulsive and retentive faculties (מהכחות)” (ibid. 3:11). “For the Creator placed in the drop of semen a formative power (כח מציירת), which makes a plan and limbs and forms them” (R. Judah al-Harizi, Moreh Nevukhim 2:7). “Tell me the secret of the four faculties (הכחות) that are in the body etc.; for in each and every limb there are four faculties (כחות): one draws in the food and attracts it, and the second retains and cuts, and the third changes and transforms, and the fourth expels and casts out” (ibid., Iggeret Leshon ha-Zahav). “The vegetative faculty (הכח הצומח), which is found in man and in the plant; and this faculty (הכח) divides into seven faculties (כחות), and they are: the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, the expulsive, the nutritive, the formative and the augmentative; and in these faculties (הכחות) man shares with the plants and the other living creatures. And he has faculties (כחות) by which he is distinguished from them, from the plant, and they are: the sensory, the imaginative and the appetitive. And the sensory faculty (הכח המרגיש) is the one that grasps the objects of sense through the perceptions of the five known senses; and the imaginative faculty (והכח המדמה) is the one in which the impressions of the objects of sense remain after they have disappeared from sensation, and which combines some of them with others; and the appetitive is the faculty (הכח) by which a person longs for and seeks a thing, or flees from it, or loves it or hates it, and the other affections of the soul” (Ha-Ma'alot of R. Shem Tov Falaquera 2). “And this soul (the vegetative soul) has three faculties (כחות): the augmentative faculty (כח המגדל), the nutritive faculty (וכח הזן), and the faculty that generates its like (וכח המוליד לדומה). The augmentative faculty (כח המגדל) is a faculty (כח) that makes the plant grow until it reaches the limit allotted to it, and until that time it does not depart from it, and when it reaches the end of its limit it departs from it. The nutritive faculty (כח הזן) includes four faculties (כחות), and they are the attractive, the retentive, the digestive and the one that expels superfluities etc. The faculty that generates its like (כח המוליד לדומה) is a faculty (כח) that is in the drop of semen to generate a body like itself” (Sha'ar ha-Shamayim 3:1). “And the sage Ibn Rushd wrote and said that this faculty (הכח) (the faculty of memory) is what is called the cogitative faculty (כח המחשב), and by it a person thinks about things that are not known until he knows them. And the sage wrote in the book On Sense and the Sensible that they are three faculties (כחות), and these are they: the faculty of retention (כח השמירה), that is, that a person retains what he hears or what he sees, and this is what the foreigners call אשינטר"י; and the faculty of memory (וכח הזכרני), that is, that he remembers what he retained; and a faculty (וכח) by which a person comes back to remember what he forgot of what he had already retained” (ibid. 9). “And the nutritive faculty (וכח הזן) needs four faculties (כחות) to complete its form, and they are: the attractive faculty (כח המושך), to draw the thing that is fitting for it and that suits its nature; and it needs the retentive faculty (לכח המחזיק) to hold the thing drawn in until the digestive faculty (הכח המעכל) completes its action in it; and it needs an expulsive faculty (לכח מדחה) to expel the thing that is contrary to nature etc.; and it needs a transforming faculty (לכח משנה), and that is the one that makes the food like the one nourished” (R. Joseph ibn Tzaddik, Olam ha-Katan 1:5). “And the psychic faculties (הכחות הנפשיות) are divided into three parts etc.: the cogitative faculty (הכח המחשבי), and it is a judging faculty (כח) that decides about a thing that ought to be sought and about a thing that one ought to keep away from etc.; and the imaginative faculty (והכח היצרי) — when the cogitative uses it, it is called imaginative, and when the rational uses it, it is called cogitative” (Kuzari 5:12). “The faculty of will (הכח החפצי) will direct all the limbs that serve it with alacrity, diligence and joy” (ibid. 3:5). “Were he (the pious man) ruling over a country, he would conduct it with justice as he conducted his body and his soul; and he would curb the appetitive faculties (הכחות התאויים) and keep them from excess, after he had given them their share” (ibid.). “The imaginative faculty (הכח הדמיוני) does not distinguish and combine this, since it does not grasp the truth of things but only their accidents” (R. Isaac Abravanel, Mif'alot Elohim 4:2). — And the rhetorician said: “All that the company of his lower faculties (כחותיו) says shall be given to it, and in all that they desire they shall take their share” (Behinat Olam 1:5). — And in the sense of a spiritual awakening: “And the inclination will have no way to reach you to lead you astray, and you will be in the condition of the special treasure of God, and there will be renewed for you a supernal, strange power (כח) that you did not know, in all that you have accustomed your faculties (מכחותיך) to” (Hovot ha-Levavot, Heshbon ha-Nefesh 4). — °And the force (הכֹּחַ) acting in the world, nature and its workings: “The Khazar said: It (nature) is one force (כח) among the forces (מהכחות), as we have heard in the sciences, and we do not know what it is” (Kuzari 1:72). “As the naturalists do with the wondrous forces (בכחות) that they see, which, if they were told about them without seeing them, they would deny them” (ibid. 5). “That the Creator, blessed be He, guides them by one of the dispositions; call that disposition, if you wish, nature, or soul, or force (כח)” (ibid. 5:10). “And that seed, like that work, is attributed to the wondrous wisdom implanted in it, which they call nature; and it is a force (כח) that strives for the preservation of the species” (ibid.). “And just as these three faculties (הכחות) in the body of a living creature have one force (כח) from One, called the force (הכח) that guides the body, and it binds all the parts of the body and its faculties (וכחותיו) to one another, and the physicians call it nature — so there is in the world as a whole one force (כח) that binds all the parts of existence and its forces (וכחותיו) to one another and guides them” (Ikkarim 2:31). “The said matter, that is, the hyle, never ceased to be clothed in the force (בכח) of the four elements, and there was never a time when the forces (כחי) of the elements were not found in it; and likewise there was never a time when the forces (כחי) of the elements would be absent” (Toledot Adam, Joseph Israel Porlin, British Museum MS). — °כֹּחַ המשֵׁךְ, see משך. — k) °כֹּחַ, in the sense of the opposite of פֹעַל (act): a thing that is בְּכֹחַ (in potentiality) and not in act, that is only in possibility, in disposition, but is not yet in existence: “If the cause is in potentiality (בכח), the effect is in potentiality (בכח); and if it is in act, the effect is in act” (Kuzari 4:13). “And the soul is the perfection of a natural, organic body having life in potentiality (בכח), that is to say, the source of the vital actions in potentiality (בכח) and prepared for them” (ibid. 5:12). “We have said of the child who has been born that he is a writer, meaning that he is a writer in remote potentiality (בכח רחוק); and we have said of the boy before he begins to learn that he is a writer in potentiality (בכח) — now this potentiality (הכח) is nearer than the one before it; and we have said of one who engages in writing, at a time when he is asleep, that he is a writer in potentiality (בכח) — now this too is nearer than the first ones” (Millot ha-Higgayon 11). “For a man, before he intellects something, is an intellect in potentiality (בכח); and when he intellects one thing — as if you were to say, when he has intellected the form of this tree that is pointed to, and has abstracted its form from its matter, and the representation of the abstracted form, which is the act of the intellect — then he is an intellect in act” (Moreh Nevukhim 1:68). “Everything that is in potentiality (בכח) and has in itself one possibility may at some time not exist in act” (ibid. 2, Introduction 23). “And just as the sun gives the eye the light to see, and the seeing, by the light that reached it from the sun, is seeing in act after it had been seeing in potentiality (בכח); and by this light it sees the sun itself, which is the cause that the eye sees in act; and by the light the colors that had been visible in potentiality (בכח) become visible in act, and the seeing that had been in potentiality (בכח) becomes seeing in act — so too the active intellect” (Ha-Ma'alot of R. Shem Tov Falaquera 1). “Except that before the syllogism the thing was known in potentiality (בכח) in the premises, and by means of the syllogism it became known in act” (Ikkarim 1:16). “And people have already agreed to call the intellect of man, before the first principles reach it, intellect in potentiality (בכח), and to call it, after the first principles have reached it, intellect in act” (Emunah Ramah 1:7). “And it is clear that many of the existing things exist in potentiality (בכח) and do not exist in act, like plants in the seed and birds in the eggs” (ibid. 2:1). “We see that the human soul is at first intellecting in potentiality (בכח), afterward it is intellecting in act; and the passage from potentiality (הכח) to act is motion” (ibid. 4:1). “For to be moved is for the thing to be receptive in potentiality (כבח), and to move is for the thing to be in act etc.; and according to this you will find one motion itself in potentiality (בכח) and in act together, in one thing at one time, and potentiality (הכח) and act will be joined in it together at one time” (Tagmulei ha-Nefesh 2a). “And the intellect that was in it in act went back to being in potentiality (בכח)” (Sha'ar ha-Shamayim of Ibn Latif 24). “For that whose existence is in potentiality (בכח) cannot exist in act unless the form is joined to it, for it is the cause of its existence in act; and if matter were found bare without form, it would not be matter in potentiality (בכח), but something existing in act, and so it has form” (R. Isaac Abravanel, Mif'alot Elohim 2:4). “And it was explained there (in the first of the Rhetoric of Aristotle) that the meaning of in potentiality (בכח) is the art that acts upon the two contraries” (Nofet Tzufim 1). “The efficient cause of coldness is divided into two parts: one cools in potentiality (בכח), like opium, and the other cools in act, like snow” (Nathan Falaquera, Tzori ha-Guf 2:8, British Museum MS). “The efficient causes of moisture are five: that which moistens in act, like washing in the bath etc., and that which moistens in potentiality (בכח), like drinking milk and eating moist fish” (ibid.). — °יצא מִכֹּחַ אל הפֹעַל, הוציאו מכח אל הפעל: what was before only in potentiality, in possibility, afterward came to be in act, in existence: “For it is in the power (בכח) of the intellect to count thousands and thousands of thousands multiplied without end; this is in potentiality (בכח), but that it should bring it out to the bound of act — no” (Kuzari 5:1). “For whatever passes from potentiality (מן הכח) to act, something other than it brings it out, and it is necessarily outside it etc.; and if what brings it out is within it, and it had an impediment that was removed, there is no doubt that the remover of the impediment is the one that brings that potentiality (הכח) out to act” (Moreh Nevukhim 2, Introduction 18). “The active intellect, which is the last of the separate intellects, and it is what brings the intellect of man out from potentiality (מן הכח) to act, and it is the beginning of his passive intellect, just as the ray of the sun or other illuminating things bring the sense of the eye out from potentiality (מן הכח) to act” (R. Judah ibn Tibbon, Ruah Hen 3). “For matter is a dead body, but not entirely dead, for it possesses all the material forms in potentiality (בכח); and the spheres draw from it little by little by the word of God and bring it out from potentiality (מן הכח) to act, as the potter brings out from the clay each and every vessel into act” (Malmad ha-Talmidim, Bereshit). “For every change is a passage from potentiality (מהכח) to act etc.; but it does not follow from this that every passage from potentiality (מהכח) to act is a change; for change is the passage from potentiality (מהכח) to act that is in the thing acted upon, to be acted upon, not the passage from potentiality (מהכח) to act that is in the agent, to do its action” (Ralbag, Milhamot ha-Shem 6:1:24). “The sword is in the piece of iron in potentiality (בכח), and with all this it must have a possibility by which it can come out into act, and that is like the capability for melting and beating and scouring and sharpening, until it is a sword in act” (Tagmulei ha-Nefesh 6a). “By means of the senses and diligence in speculation he will attain perfection and go out from potentiality (מן הכח) to act; and therefore he said that it is more perfect for him to be created than not to be created, for when he is not created he has not gone out from potentiality (מן הכח) to act” (R. Abraham Bibago, Derekh Emunah 2:1).

he: לא נתברר מקורו ומהותו בודאות, ועי' הערה לקמן., ש"ז, —שֵׁם למין ממיני השממית, Eidechsenart; espèce de lézard; kind of lizard:  והאנקה וְהַכֹּחַאונק' תרגם כוחא. אבל כבר העיר ע' לֶו Aram. Lurchn. §19 כי קרוב לודאי שהיא היא המלה העברית שהניח אונק' בלי תרגום. השבעי' וכמו"כ ולג' תרגמוהו בקמיליאון, ר"ל אותו מין הלטאה המחליף גון עורו לפי רצונו. רסע"ג ואחריו ריב"ג תרגמוהו בחרדון בערב', שהוא מין לטאה גדולה, עי' ערך *חַרְדּוֹן. ואין בערב' שם דומה לזה לאחד ממיני הלטאה זולתי המלה כבח שהביא דוזי, וכבר העיר ע' לו שאולי יש איזה יחס בינה ובין המלה כֹח העברית. וממשמ' השרש כוח או כחח בודאי אין לעמד בודאות על מהותו של הבע"ח הנקרא בשם זה. והלטאה והחמט והתנשמת  (ויקרא' יא ל). — ואמר המשורר:  ומה יוכל עשה תיש לליש ומה כח בכח ואנקה (ר"ש הנגיד, ידידותך).
en: [Note: Its origin and nature have not been clarified with certainty; see the note below.] Masculine noun, — the name of a kind of lizard, German Eidechsenart; French espèce de lézard; English kind of lizard: “And the gecko, וְהַכֹּחַ [Note: Onkelos translated כוחא. But I. Löw (Aram. Lurchn. §19) has already remarked that it is almost certain that this is the Hebrew word itself, which Onkelos left untranslated. The Septuagint and likewise the Vulgate translated it chameleon, that is, the kind of lizard that changes the color of its skin at will. Saadia Gaon, and after him Ibn Janach, translated it by ḥardūn in Arabic, which is a kind of large lizard; see the entry *חַרְדּוֹן. And there is no name in Arabic similar to this for any kind of lizard, except the word כבח cited by Dozy, and Löw has already remarked that perhaps there is some relation between it and the Hebrew word כֹח. And from the meaning of the root כוח or כחח one can certainly not determine with certainty the nature of the animal called by this name.] (and the land crocodile), and the lizard, and the sand lizard, and the chameleon” (Leviticus 11:30). — And the poet said: “And what can a he-goat do to a lion, and what כח (strength) is there in a כח (lizard) and a gecko?” (R. Samuel HaNagid, “Yedidutekha”).

he: עי' הערה לקמן., ש"ז, — כדור למשחק, ירמוהו ויקפץ למעלה וישוב ויפול ארצה, Spiel-Ball; balle à jouer; balle: רמוברוב הספרים רומּוּ מלא ומם דגושה, אבל בקצת ספרים חסר, ואפילו לפי הספרים שבהם הוא מלא דגש המם מעיד כי העקר הוא חסר. ועי' עוד לקמן. מעט ואיננו והמכו כַּכֹּלבמלה זו כל הספרים מסכימים ואין שום שנוי בה לא בכתיב ולא בנקוד. ובדבר משמ' מלה זו, הנה השבעים ראו בה שֵׁם ותרגמוה בהשם היוני μολόχα שהוא שם צמח, ועפי"ז הגיהו קצת החדשים מלֻח במקום כֹּל. שאר התרגומים, ולג' ופשיטא, תרגמו מלה זו במשמ' א. כֹּל הרגילה, וכן המפרשים הקדמונים. החדשים התלבטו מאד בפרוש כתוב זה, והודו פה אחד כי מליצה זו, כַּכֹּל יקפצון, אם נפרש כַּכֹּל במשמ' כמו כֻּלם, אין לו שום טעם. ולכן הגיהו רובם הגהות מתחלפות בכתוב זה עד ששנוהו כמעט כלו ולא הגיהו בו אף מלה אחת כמו שהיא. במקום והֻמְכוּ הגיהו קצתם והַמַּכֶּה, ובמקום כל, הגיהו מלֻח, כמו שנזכר למעלה, ואחרים הגיהו יבול במקום כל, ובמקום יקפצון יקבצון, ואחרים הגיהו: והם ככל חציר יקטפון. כל אלה ההגהות מעידות עד כמה המליצה כמו שהיא, לפי משמ' הרגילה של כל, היא קשה ואינה מתישבת בדרך טבעי. והמפתח לפרוש כל הכתוב הוא במשמ' המלה כַּכֹּל, שאין שום ספק כי בזה צדקו השבעים שראו בו שֵׁם דבר, ומשמ' האמתית אנו למדים ממה שכתוב לפניו ולאחריו, והֻמְכוּ — יקפצון, מוכח כי הכֹּל שנזכר כאן בין שני הפעלים הוא דבר שיומך ויקפץ, והוא הכדור של משחק. ולמשמ' זו להמלה כֹּל יש גם סמך בערב'. כי הנה בלשון זו השם הכללי לכדור ולכדור-המשחק הוא כֹרה کُرة משרש כרי کرى, אבל בלשון הדבור בפרט בסוריה וא"י אומרים כֹרּה کُرَّة, בריש דגושה מן שרש כרר, ודבר ידוע הוא כי הריש והלמד מתחלפות בין שתי הלשונות תדיר, ולכן כֹּל יוכל להיות משקל זכר מכֹרַּה. ובאמת גם בערב' עצמה כבר נעשה חלוף זה, ובלשון הדבור ההמונית בסוריה וא"י אומרים להכדור גם כֹלַּה کُلَّة, אמר מחיט אלמחיט: ואלכֹלַּה ענד אלמולדינ הנה משתדירה מנ חדיד ונחוה ירמי בהא מנ אלמדפע ושי בקדר אלבנדקה מנ רח'אמ וע'ירה ילעב בהא אלצביאנ, ע"כ, ובעבר': הכֹלַּה אצל המשתמשים המלים שנכנסו בהלשון בזמן חדש הוא דבר עגל מן ברזל וכיוצא בו יזרק מן המקלע ודבר בגדל אגוז קטן מן שיש וכדומה ישחקו בו הילדים. פלישר (Fleiseher, kl. Schr. II, l, 769) סובר שחלוף זה נעשה בלשון תרקית, גלּה במקום כרּה, וממנה לקחוה הערבים וחזרו והקשו את הגימל לכף ואמרו כלה. אך אין זה מוכרח, ואין דבר בטבע הלשון הערבי' מונעת להניח כי החלוף הזה הוא ערבי, והמלה כֹּל העבר' היא אולי ראיה כי החלוף הזה הוא שֵמי. בפרוש זה א"צ להגיה את הכתוב זולתי במקום אחד: אינם במקום איננו, שהוא מוכרח מעצם הכתוב ששני הפעלים האחרים שבו הם ברבים, והפעל הראשון רֻמּוּ הוא פֻעל מן רמה במשמ' זרק, וכל הכתוב הוא תקון סופרים כעין תשובה על טענותיו של איוב על הצלחת הרשעים, ואמרו שאינם אלא ככדור שמשחק בו המשחק שירמהו ויֻמך ואחרי כן יקפץ למעלה רגע אחד, ולא יתר. ומזה ראיה כי איוב נכתב בזמן שהיה כדור המשחק נהוג גם בקרב היהודים. יקפצון וכראש שבלת ימלו (איוב כד כד).
en: See the note below. Masculine noun, — a ball for play, which one throws and it bounces upward and falls back to the ground, German Spiel-Ball, French balle à jouer, English ball: "They are exalted (רֻמּוּ) [note: In most books רוּמּוּ is written plene and with a doubled mem, but in some books defectively; and even according to the books in which it is plene, the dagesh in the mem testifies that the original is defective. And see further below.] a little while, and they are gone; and they are thrown down like the ball (כַּכֹּל) [note: In this word all the books agree, and there is no variation in it, neither in spelling nor in vocalization. As for the meaning of this word, the Septuagint saw in it a noun and translated it with the Greek noun μολόχα, which is the name of a plant, and on that basis some of the moderns emended מלֻח in place of כֹּל. The other translations, the Vulgate and the Peshitta, translated this word in the usual sense of כֹּל I, and so did the early commentators. The moderns struggled greatly with the interpretation of this verse, and admitted with one voice that this expression, כַּכֹּל יקפצון, has no sense if we interpret כַּכֹּל in the sense of 'like all of them'. Therefore most of them made varying emendations in this verse, until they changed almost all of it and did not leave even one word in it as it is. In place of והֻמְכוּ some emended והַמַּכֶּה, and in place of כל they emended מלֻח, as mentioned above; others emended יבול in place of כל, and יקבצון in place of יקפצון; and others emended: והם ככל חציר יקטפון. All these emendations testify how difficult the expression as it stands is according to the usual meaning of כל, and that it does not settle in a natural way. The key to the interpretation of the whole verse lies in the meaning of the word כַּכֹּל, for there is no doubt that in this the Septuagint were right in seeing in it a noun, and its true meaning we learn from what is written before and after it, והֻמְכוּ — יקפצון: it is evident that the כֹּל mentioned here between the two verbs is something that is thrown down and bounces, and that is the play ball. And for this meaning of the word כֹּל there is also support in Arabic. For in that language the general noun for a ball and for a play ball is kurah كُرة, from the root kry كرى, but in the spoken language, especially in Syria and the Land of Israel, they say kurrah كُرَّة, with a doubled resh, from the root krr; and it is well known that resh and lamed frequently interchange between the two languages, and therefore כֹּל can be a masculine form of כֹרַּה. And indeed in Arabic itself this interchange has already taken place, and in the popular spoken language in Syria and the Land of Israel they also call the ball kullah كُلَّة. Muhit al-Muhit says: ואלכֹלַּה ענד אלמולדינ הנה משתדירה מנ חדיד ונחוה ירמי בהא מנ אלמדפע ושי בקדר אלבנדקה מנ רח'אמ וע'ירה ילעב בהא אלצביאנ, end quote; and in Hebrew: 'The kullah, among those who use the words that entered the language in recent times, is a round thing of iron and the like, which is thrown from the cannon, and a thing the size of a small nut, of marble and the like, with which children play.' Fleischer (Fleiseher, kl. Schr. II, l, 769) holds that this interchange took place in Turkish, gulla in place of kurra, and from it the Arabs took it and hardened the gimel back into kaf and said kulla. But this is not necessary, and there is nothing in the nature of the Arabic language that prevents assuming that this interchange is Arabic, and the Hebrew word כֹּל is perhaps evidence that this interchange is Semitic. With this interpretation there is no need to emend the verse except in one place: אינם in place of איננו, which is required by the verse itself, since the other two verbs in it are plural; and the first verb, רֻמּוּ, is a Pu'al of רמה in the sense of throwing. The whole verse is a scribal correction, a kind of answer to Job's complaints about the prosperity of the wicked, saying that they are nothing but like a ball with which the player plays, who throws it and it is thrown down and afterwards bounces upward for one moment, and no more. And from this is evidence that Job was written at a time when the play ball was customary also among the Jews.] they bounce (יקפצון), and like the tops of the ears of grain they wither" (Job 24:24).

en: [Note: From כלל; the lamed was lightened in the isolated form and preserved in the inflections. It is an ancient word common to all the Semitic languages, in Arabic כֻלּ کُلّ; and in Hebrew too the kaf originally had the vowel sound of shuruk even in pause, and afterwards, in accordance with the general tendency of the Hebrew language, this sound changed to the sound of holam in the isolated form in pause, or at least when not in full junction with the following word, and they said כֹּל; but when joined by maqaf to the following word they continued to say כֻּל-דבר, and likewise in inflection the dagesh protected the shuruk sound and they said כֻּלֹּו, כֻּלָּךְ, etc. In a later period they began to say it with the holam sound also when joined by maqaf, and then they pointed it with a kamatz, כָּל, which is the sign of the holam sound that a word acquired at a later time, close to the time when the vocalization was fixed.], (כול), כָּל-, כֻּלוֹ, כֻּלֹּה, כֻּלָּהּ, (כֻּלָא), כֻּלָּךְ, כֻּלֵּךְ, כֻּלְּכֶם, כֻּלָּנוּ [Note: like בָּנוּ, לָנוּ, and like מודעתָנו Ruth 3:2.], כֻּלָּם, כּוּ-ָ, כֻּלְּהַם [Note: according to the opinion of the moderns, instead of כֻּלְּהֶם.], כֻּלָּנָה, כֻּלָּהְנָה [Note: instead of כֻּלְּהֶנָּה.], — a word indicating that the thing spoken of is not one thing only, or part of the thing, or some of the things that exist in the world or that were mentioned in what is said, but as many things as there are in the world, or the thing in its entirety, or as many things as were mentioned in the matter. It is used a) in the sense of the things that exist in the world or that were mentioned in the matter, German alles; French tout; English all: "Because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have everything" Genesis 33:11. "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and with gladness of heart, by reason of the abundance of everything, … and he shall put a yoke of iron upon your neck" Deuteronomy 28:47-48. "For she shall eat them for want of everything secretly" ibid. 57. "But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything, and have been consumed by the sword and by famine" Jeremiah 44:18. "I am the Lord who makes everything, who alone stretched out the heavens" Isaiah 44:24. "I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth, says the Lord; I will sweep away man and beast, I will sweep away the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, etc." Zephaniah 1:2-3. "You made him (man) to rule over the works of Your hands; You have put everything under his feet" Psalms 8:7. "The Lord has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of evil" Proverbs 16:4. "Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the Lord understand everything" ibid. 28:5. "Behold, my eye has seen everything, my ear has heard and understood it" Job 13:1. "I know that You can do everything, and that no purpose of Yours can be withheld from You" ibid. 42:2. "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for everything in the heavens and on the earth" 1 Chronicles 29:11. — *כֹּל יוכל: "To make known the might of the Holy One, blessed be He, that He is all-capable: without luminaries He makes the earth sprout" Midrash Tadshe 1. — כֹּל אֲשֶׁר: "Everything that is on the earth shall perish" Genesis 6:17. "The daughters are my daughters, and the sons are my sons, and the flock is my flock, and everything that you see is mine" ibid. 31:43. "Behold, yours is everything that belongs to Mephibosheth" 2 Samuel 16:4. "And everything that a man has he will give for his life" Job 2:4. — And with the definite article הַ, הַכֹּל: "Not like these is the portion of Jacob, for He is the Former of everything" Jeremiah 10:16. "So will I do for the sake of My servants, not to destroy everything" Isaiah 65:8. "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to the battle" Ezekiel 7:14. "Vanity of vanities, everything is vanity" Ecclesiastes 1:2. "And behold, everything is vanity  and striving after wind" ibid. 14. "He has made everything beautiful in its time" ibid. 3:11. "Everything goes to one place; everything came from the dust, and everything returns to the dust" ibid. 20. "For laughter they make a feast, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything" ibid. 10:19. "The end of the matter, everything having been heard: fear God" ibid. 12:13. "For everything comes from You, and from Your hand we have given You" 1 Chronicles 29:14. — And with the letters ב, ל, מ: "And the Lord had blessed Abraham in everything" Genesis 24:1. "Ordered in everything and secured" 2 Samuel 23:5. "And His kingdom rules over everything" Psalms 103:19. "One who vows [abstinence] from grain is forbidden in everything [made of the five species] and permitted fruit of the tree and vegetables" Nedarim 7:2. "For everything there is a season" Ecclesiastes 3:1. "And he gave him a tenth of everything" Genesis 14:20. — b) in the sense of the collection of the things mentioned above, or of the things that are known and familiar: "As the green herb I have given you everything" Genesis 9:3, that is, the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heavens and the creeping things of the ground mentioned there above. "Two of every [sort] shall you bring into the ark" ibid. 6:19. "And he brought it to me, and I ate of everything" ibid. 27:33. —  And with the definite article הַ, הַכֹּל: "And you shall take of the ram the fat and the fat tail, etc., and one loaf of bread, etc., and you shall put everything on the palms of Aaron" Exodus 29:22-24. "And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall lay the pieces, the head and the fat, etc., and the priest shall burn everything on the altar" Leviticus 1:8-9. "Their axles, and their rims, and their spokes, and their hubs, everything was cast" 1 Kings 7:33. "See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings, and the threshing sledges for wood, and the wheat for the meal offering; everything I give" 1 Chronicles 21:23. "The first fruits of grain, wine and oil, etc., and they brought everything in abundance" 2 Chronicles 31:5. — And in Mishnaic and Talmudic literature: "Everything is foreseen, and permission is granted" Avot 3:15. "Which courtyard is subject to tithes? etc. Rabbi Akiva says: any [courtyard] that one opens and another locks is exempt. Rabbi Nehemiah says: any [courtyard] in which a person is ashamed to eat is liable. Rabbi Yose says: any [courtyard] that one enters and no one says 'What do you want?' is exempt" Ma'aserot 3:5, כל חצר, every courtyard. "They stated a great general rule regarding the Sabbath: anyone who forgets the principle of the Sabbath and did many labors on many Sabbaths is liable only for one sin offering" Shabbat 7:1, כל איש השוכח, every man who forgets. "And they stated another general rule: anything that is fit to be stored, etc., and anything that is not fit to be stored" ibid. 3, כל דבר הכשר, any thing that is fit. "Anything that was put into hot water before the Sabbath may be soaked in hot water on the Sabbath, and anything that was not put into hot water before the Sabbath may be rinsed in hot water on the Sabbath" ibid. 22:2. "Abba Saul stated a general rule: anything that I am permitted to say, I am permitted to wait at nightfall for it" ibid. 23:3, כל דבר שאני זכאי באמירתו, any thing that I am permitted to say. "And what is an old sukkah? Any that one made thirty days before the festival" Sukkah 1:1, כל סוכה שעשאה, any sukkah that one made. "Who is a minor? Anyone who cannot ride on his father's shoulders" Hagigah 1:1, כל קטן שאינו יכול, any minor who cannot. "Who is a mamzer? Any [offspring of] close kin with whom [marriage is forbidden by] 'he shall not come' — the words of Rabbi Akiva; Shimon the Temanite says: any [union] for which one is liable to karet at the hands of Heaven, etc.; Rabbi Joshua says: any [union] for which one is liable to death by the court" Yevamot 4:13. "Anything whose time is fixed, etc., and anything whose time is not fixed" Nedarim 8:3, כל דבר שזמנו קבוע, any thing whose time is fixed. "This is the general rule (concerning a woman's vows): any [woman] who went out into her own authority for one hour — he cannot annul" ibid. 11:9, כל אשה שיצאה, any woman who went out. "Anyone who vowed [naziriteship] before the Temple was destroyed is a nazirite" Nazir 5:4, כל מי שנזר, anyone who vowed. "This is the general rule: any [case] in which she would have intercourse and would not be forbidden to him — he does not stipulate with her" Sotah 2:6, כל פעם, every time, כל מקרה, every case. "Which is a tam and which is a mu'ad? A mu'ad is any [ox] about which they testified for three days, etc.; and a tam is any [ox] that, when children handle it, does not gore" Bava Kamma 2:4, כל שור, any ox. "Rabbi Judah says: anything that has a distinguishing feature must be announced" Bava Metzia 2:1, כל דבר שמצא ויש בו שנוי, any thing that he found and that has a distinguishing feature. "Whoever has the money in his hand has the upper hand" ibid. 4:2, כל מי שהכסף בידו, whoever has the money in his hand. "This is the general rule (concerning the division of houses, courtyards, fields and the like): anything that can be divided and still retain its name is divided, and if not, it is not divided" Bava Batra 1:6, כל בית או חצר או דבר שיחלק ושמו עליו, any house or courtyard or thing that can be divided and retain its name. "What is an asherah? Any [tree] under which there is idol worship; Rabbi Shimon says: any [tree] that is worshipped" Avodah Zarah 3:7, כל אילן, any tree. "This is the general rule (concerning libation wine): anything whose benefit comes by imparting flavor is forbidden; anything whose benefit does not come by imparting flavor is permitted" ibid. 5:2. "Which is the right way that a person should choose for himself? Whatever is an honor to the one who does it" Avot 2:1, כל דרך, any way. "Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa says: Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures; and anyone whose wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure, etc. He used to say: Anyone with whom the spirit of people is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him; and anyone with whom the spirit of people is not pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him" ibid. 3:9-10, כל אדם, every person. "Anything that is within the wall is like the houses of walled cities, except for the fields" Arakhin 9:5, כל בית או חצר, any house or courtyard. "Everything that is in the sea is clean, except the sea-dog" Kelim 17:13, כל בע"ח, every living creature. "Wherever you are able to multiply doubts and doubts of doubts" Tohorot 6:4, כל מקום, every place, בכל מקרה, in every case. "Whatever is opposite the olive[-sized corpse] — beneath it and above it — is unclean; and whatever is not opposite the olive[-sized piece] — its inside and the house — is clean" Oholot 9:1, כל מה שהוא כנגד הזית וכל מה שאינו כנגד הזית, whatever is opposite the olive[-sized piece] and whatever is not opposite the olive[-sized piece]. "Who is one 'wounded by crushing'? Anyone whose testicles were wounded" Sifre Deuteronomy 247. "What is a forgotten sheaf in the stacks? Anything that one cannot stretch out his hand and take" ibid. 285. "What are oleloth? Any [cluster] that has neither shoulder nor pendant" Tosefta Peah 3:11, כל גפן, any vine. "There are three measures for a partition: any that is less than three [handbreadths], etc.; any that is three, and from three to four, etc.; any that is four, and from four upward" ibid. Kil'ayim 4:6, כל מחִצָה, any partition. "Whatever exists in the settled land exists in the wilderness, etc.; whatever exists on dry land exists in the sea" ibid. 5:9-10, כל בע"ח, every living creature. "And who is his teacher? etc. Rabbi Judah says: anyone from whom [he learned] most of his learning; Rabbi Yose says: anyone who enlightened his eyes in his Mishnah" ibid. Bava Metzia 2:30. "What is the breast? Whatever sees the ground from above until it reaches the neck from below" ibid. Hullin 9:13. "And what is tasteless spittle? Of anyone who has tasted nothing since the evening" ibid. Niddah 8:8. "Whoever is in good fortune, let him not despair of evil; and whoever is in evil fortune, let him not despair of good" Seder Olam Rabbah 28. "Any day on which there is an additional offering, such as the New Moon and the intermediate days of the festival, one must mention the matter of the occasion, etc.; and any [day] on which there is no additional offering, such as Hanukkah and Purim, etc." Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 7, 11c. "Who is a merchant? Anyone who brought [produce] twice or three times" ibid. Demai 2, 22c. "Who is a Torah scholar? Hezekiah said: anyone who learned the laws and in addition Torah, etc.; Rabbi Yohanan (said): anyone who neglects his business for the sake of his learning" ibid. Mo'ed Katan 3, 83b. "What are glowing (coals)? Rav Hisda said: any [coals] such that if one inserts a chip into them it catches fire by itself" Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 53b. "And what is [heat at which] the hand recoils? Rehavah said: any [heat] at which a baby's belly is scalded" Shabbat 40b. "Anyone on whose account his fellow is punished is not admitted into the compartment of the Holy One, blessed be He" ibid. 149b. "And what is a minor who does not need his mother? etc. Anyone who relieves himself and his mother does not wipe him; Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: anyone who wakes and does not call 'Mother'" Eruvin 82a. "Rabbi Judah says: In the morning the householder stands and says: Whatever the poor gather today shall be ownerless" Bava Kamma 69a. "Rava said: In any case in which he would return his own [animal], he must also return his fellow's; and in any case in which he would unload and load his own, he must also unload and load his fellow's" Bava Metzia 30b. "Rav Safra said: Anything for which by their laws they extract [money] from the borrower for the lender, by our laws we return it from the lender to the borrower; anything for which by their laws they do not extract from the borrower for the lender, by our laws we do not return it from the lender to the borrower" ibid. 62a. "A basket full of straw and a jar full of dried figs placed in a window — we see: in any case where, were they removed, the straw and the dried figs could stand by themselves, they form an interposition" Bava Batra 19b. "Anything by which he would acquire in the property of a convert, he acquires in the property of his fellow; anything by which he would not acquire in the property of a convert, he does not acquire in the property of his fellow" ibid. 57a. "What is the shirt of a Torah scholar? Any [shirt] under which his flesh is not seen; what is the cloak of a Torah scholar? Any [cloak] under which his shirt is not seen [by] a handbreadth" ibid. b. "This is the general rule (concerning a killer): any [killing] in the manner of descent — he goes into exile; not in the manner of descent — he does not go into exile" Makkot 7b. "If it (the bird) was sitting between two branches of a tree, we see: in any case where, if it slipped, it would fall on them, he is obligated to send [it] away" Hullin 140b. "What is 'near her old age'? Rav Judah said: any [woman] of whom her companions say, 'She is old'; and Rabbi Shimon says: any [woman] whom they call 'Mother, Mother' and she is not ashamed" Niddah 9a. "Ben Azzai says: Anyone whose mind is at ease on account of his wisdom, it is a good sign for him" Avot de-Rabbi Natan 25. "A parable of a dove that the hawks and the ravens were pursuing; she fled from them and sat on her nest, and people were saying: These eggs are from the hawk; and this one says: They are from the raven. One said to them: As long as they are eggs, it is not known whether they are of the raven or of the hawk; rather, leave them until she gives birth and they become chicks, and you will know from whom they are" Aggadat Bereshit 37, כל זמן שהן ביצים, as long as they are eggs. — And after a negative, in the sense of anything, aught, any thing, German Nichts; French rien; English nothing: "But now our soul is dried away; there is nothing at all" Numbers 11:6. "A land in which you shall eat bread without scarceness; you shall not lack anything in it" Deuteronomy 8:9. "But the poor man had nothing, save one little ewe lamb" 2 Samuel 12:3. "Your handmaid has not anything in the house, save a pot of oil" 2 Kings 4:2. "There is one who makes himself rich, yet has nothing" Proverbs 13:7. — And in the sense of any part, any piece: "So that he will not give to any of them of the flesh of his children whom he shall eat, because he has nothing left him, in the siege and in the distress" Deuteronomy 28:55. "And behold, the girdle was marred; it was profitable for nothing" Jeremiah 13:7. — f) in the sense of many different things, German allerlei; French de toutes sortes; English of all kinds: "And when you come into the land and have planted all kinds of trees for food" Leviticus 19:23. "There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, who brought fish and all kinds of wares and sold on the Sabbath to the children of Judah and in Jerusalem" Nehemiah 13:16. "Onyx stones and stones to be set, stones of antimony and of diverse colors, and all kinds of precious stones" 1 Chronicles 29:2. — And with the definite article ה, הַכֹּל, in this sense: "All this have I seen in the days of my vanity: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evil-doing" Ecclesiastes 7:15. — g) בְּכָל, in the sense of every time, German jedesmal; French chaque fois; English every time: "And it came to pass, whenever the stronger of the flock conceived, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the flock in the gutters" Genesis 30:41. "For what great nation is there that has God so near to them as the Lord our God is whenever we call upon Him?" Deuteronomy 4:7. "That Your eyes may be open to the supplication of Your servant and to the supplication of Your people Israel, to listen to them whenever they cry to You" 1 Kings 8:52. — *כָּל-שֶׁכֵּן, כל-שכן he will do, כש"כ that he will do, like על אחת כמה וכמה, German desto mehr; French d'autant plus; English so much the more: "Rabbi Eliezer says: Repent one day before your death. His disciples asked Rabbi Eliezer: Does a person know on which day he will die? He said to them: All the more so, let him repent today, lest he die tomorrow" Shabbat 153a. "Rabbi Tarfon said to Rabbi Judah: Today your face is shining. He said to him: Last night your servants went out to the field and brought us beets, and we ate them without salt; and had we eaten them with salt, all the more so would our faces have shone" Nedarim 49b. "Two houses, one inside the other — if both are by sale, [or] both by gift, they have no right of way through each other; all the more so if the outer is by gift and the inner by sale, (or) the outer by sale and the inner by gift" Bava Batra 65a. "For one does not make a breach before the honest man, and all the more so before the thief" Tanhuma Metzora 13. — And in סהמ"א: "[Something] brought from outside the Sabbath limit for the sake of this Israelite is permitted to any other Israelite, and all the more so in Mehoza, where gentiles are common" Halakhot Pesukot, Festivals. "And I examined the customs of people in most of the generations mentioned in the books, and I found them far from this kind of commandments, except the zealous and the abstinent among them, as is mentioned of them; but the rest — how much they needed to be roused and instructed! And all the more so most of the people of this our time, who have made light of the wisdom of the commandments of the limbs, all the more so of the duties of the hearts" Hovot HaLevavot, Introduction. "And in the knowledge of the Creator there is no change, and He does not know you, all the more so [does He not] know your intention and your deeds, and all the more so [does He not] hear your prayer and see your movements" Kuzari 1:1. "And she confessed the thoughts and undertook not to mention them with her tongue, all the more so not to do them" ibid. 3:5. "And I see how many people put on tefillin and fix mezuzot and it has not entered their hearts what is written in them, all the more so they do not perceive the first intention in them" Malmad HaTalmidim, Va'ethanan. "For there is no doubt that Moses did not ask each and every man of that numerous people, all the more so the hewers of wood and drawers of water" ibid., Nitzavim. "But the other intellects that are above the active intellect, and all the more so the First Cause, which is the Creator, blessed be He — it is impossible for the human intellect to apprehend anything of them" Ruah Hen 3. — And the liturgical poet said: "My song is silenced and my voice no more, and here I am, yearning and longing to hear it; my house is leaking and my hiding place laid bare, and my daily offering is removed, and all the more so the additional offering" Yemenite prayer book, Yom Kippur, אפסו בעוני. — And in one word: "For one who is hungry in the evening and puts off his eating to the second evening cannot eat even [the amount] of one meal, and all the more so [that] of several meals" Responsa of the Geonim, Harkavy 397. — And especially *לֹא כָּל-שֶׁכֵּן: "And if prayer, which is light, he did not pray except outside the city — speech, which is weighty, not all the more so?" Mekhilta Bo, Petihta. "If the one who opens [the pit] is liable, the one who digs it, not all the more so?" ibid. Mishpatim, Nezikin 11.
